items.title: Almost all of Amazon’s new Echo gear is available now
paragraphs: You can read all about the new products and buy most of them, too. The fancy Echo Show 16 is coming later this year.
You can read all about the new products and buy most of them, too. The fancy Echo Show 16 is coming later this year.
Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Amazon used to blast out dozens of products onstage at annual hardware events. If this October is any indication, the company has wisely changed its strategy to put more focus on each new product with its own launch. The latest round of launches focuses on Echo products, including speakers, smart displays, as well as a smart photo frame.

All products, save for the new Echo Show 16 (which might be the most interesting of the bunch), are available to buy today. This includes the Echo Dot, the Echo Studio with Home Camera, the Echo Time, and the Alexa Photo Frame. The Show 16 isn’t launching until December 16th, though you can preorder it now to save $100 off the cost.
I’m going to spin through each of the products below, just so you can view them all in one place in case you’re considering making a purchase (or a few) soon.

The latest Echo Dot features 50 percent more bass, and faster on-device processing for handling conversations with Alexa Plus. There’s also an extra mic to better hear you around the house, plus Omnisense, a temperature- and presence-sensing tech, which can seamlessly control smart home devices.
The latest Echo Studio simply adds a camera and Alexa Plus smarts into the mix. After launch, Amazon will enable pairing with Fire TV devices to let your video calls show up on the big screen.

While not Amazon’s first bedside alarm clock, this one’s focused on helping you sleep better, and it doesn’t have a camera. It can detect your sleep stage via ultrasound and use smart alarms to ease you into the day, but only if you want it to.

A 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen that comes in a few design options. It’s a frame that features Alexa, and doubles as a smart speaker. It works with Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members.

Amazon’s most powerful (and best-sounding) smart display yet, with eight woofers and two tweeters sandwiched between its stand and screen. It’s VESA-compatible, and there’s a pricier nanomatte screen option.

items.title: Russell Brand tells court allegations had devastating impact on him
paragraphs: Russell Brand has said a documentary that made allegations about his behaviour had a "devastating" effect on him, and made friends and colleagues turn against him.
The entertainer has begun giving evidence as his defence case gets under way at his trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.
Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of attempted indecent assault.
The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies all the charges.
Asked whether consent was important to him, he told the court: "Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed many ways more important than sex itself."
After Brand entered the witness box on Wednesday morning, defence barrister Ian Winter KC began by taking him through the indictment, asking him if he had committed the offences.
After each question, Brand replied "no" loudly towards the jury.
Brand was then asked about a documentary that aired in 2023, which included some allegations against him.
Asked by Winter what impact the documentary had had on his friends and colleagues turning their backs on him, Brand said: "It was devastating."
Winter questioned whether Brand had been able to persuade any friend or acquaintance who might have been able to give evidence on his behalf to appear in court.
Brand, wearing a black suit with an open neck white shirt and a loose black tie, replied: "I have not."
Winter asked: "Will they touch you with a bargepole?" Brand said: "No."

Brand also claimed in court that he was told he could not stay with his son at Great Ormond Street hospital in London when the child was having open heart surgery, following the documentary and a newspaper investigation.
He told the court: "Due to material that had been published in the public eye they had to bar my attendance and presence.
"They were unclear about what legal reason there was but that was the reason they gave to my wife Laura and I."
Brand told the court: "My entire life has been consumed by these allegations," adding that he had "devoted myself to these matters".
Winter asked Brand if he recalled meeting the first complainant, who alleges he raped her at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999.
Brand said yes, explaining that he found her "loquacious" and "interesting".
When asked if there was any truth in the allegations that he raped her, he said: "No."
Brand was then asked about another woman, who alleges that the entertainer grabbed her breasts before dragging her into a toilet and raping her.

Brand said he recalled been invited to a party in London at a bar in 2004, and said a friend had introduced him to the complainant by saying "something like 'there's a bird here who really wants to meet you mate'."
When asked if he remembered what he said to her upon meeting, he told the court: "I would have said something like, 'You're really, really beautiful'."
The barrister asked whether he had grabbed her breasts. "Absolutely not," Brand replied.
When questioned if he would have behaved in the way that had been alleged, he said it would have amounted to "disgusting behaviour".
"I was increasingly focused on my promiscuity," he said. "That's not the way I would have behaved because it's not only criminal but vulgar."
Brand said he remembered going into the toilet with her but said "no" when asked if he had dragged or forced her there.
"Did your penis enter her mouth at all whilst in the cubicle?" Winter asked. "No," said Brand.
Another complainant, who worked at MTV, alleges that Brand tried to drag her into a toilet at work in 2001.
At the time, he was one of the channel's star presenters. She said she managed to wrench herself away.
Asked if he had intended a non-consensual sexual encounter, Brand told the court: "Absolutely not."
Brand was also asked about his wedding to singer Katy Perry in October 2010 and whether it brought a "sea change" to his life. He said the marriage brought him "staggering fame".
Being cross examined later, Brand agreed with the prosecution's suggestion that he blamed Channel 4 documentary programme Dispatches for the allegations.
Asked if the media had been fair to him, Brand said he "would reject that suggestion strongly".

items.title: At least 31 dead and 80 injured after two trains collide in Spain – latest updates
paragraphs: The death toll from today’s train collision has risen to 31, according to the latest information from local government in Castile-La Mancha.
All Spanish Cup football games cancelled as mark of respect
EU 'ready to support' Spanish investigation into train crash
At least 30 dead, 80 injured, with concerns death toll could rise further - what we know
Aerial footage from the crash scene - video
At least 30 dead, 80 injured, but numbers likely to rise, local president says
Death toll may rise further, local government spokesperson warns
At least 30 dead in Spanish train crash, local government confirms
Spanish royals express concern for and support to all affected by train crash
'Europe mourns in you,' EU's von der Leyen responds to train collision in Spain
At least 30 dead after two train collide in Spain - what do we know
Spain's transport minister working to 'obtain all possible information'
Spanish PM, opposition leader 'shocked' by train crash in Toledo
Spanish health minister fears 'major tragedy' after train collision in Toledo
Toledo crash brings back memories of deadly crash in Adamuz
Death toll likely to rise, local government spokesperson warns
At least 10 feared dead after collision in Toledo province
We are expecting to hear from Spain’s transport minister Óscar Puente at the top of the hour, at 2pm local time (1pm UK).
Spain’s former labour minister Fátima Báñez was reportedly on one of the trains caught up in this morning’s crash.
Speaking just now on RTVE, Antonio Sanz, the Andalusia government’s emergency minister, confirmed she is believed to have been on board and has not yet been reached since the incident.
The death toll from today’s train collision has risen to 31, according to the latest information from local government in Castile-La Mancha.

All games of the first round of Spanish Copa del Rey football competition planned for today have been postponed as a mark of respect following the train crash in Urda, Spanish football federation said in a statement.
“The great Spanish football family remains united in grief over this tragedy, offering its support to the authorities to help the victims of this devastating accident,” the RFEF said in a statement.
A revised schedule will be published in due course.
The European Commission has offered to help with the investigation into today’s train crash in Urda.

“Our thoughts and our feelings are with the victims, their families and friends, and all those affected, and the Commission, together with the European Union Agency for Railways, is closely following the situation, and we stand ready to support the Spanish authorities in any way that may be needed.”
But she noted it was “too early, absolutely too early, to draw any conclusions” as the emergency response continues.
Von der Leyen has not yet spoken with Spain’s PM Pedro Sánchez this morning, the spokesperson said, who also pointed reporters to her message of solidarity on social media (11:32).
Today’s crash is already the fourth worst train accident in Spain recorded since the seventies – and the death toll is still expected to rise.
In 1972, 86 people died and 112 were injured in a head-on clash between two passenger trains in El Cuervo (Sevilla).
In 2013, 80 people died and more than 140 were injured in Angrois, Santiago de Compostela (A Coruña) after a high-speed train detailed outside the station.
And earlier this year, 46 people died and 152 were injured after two trains collided in Adamuz (Córdoba).
At least 30 people have died and 80 have been injured after two high-speed trains collided in Spain’s Toledo province, with fears the death toll could still rise higher (12:22).
The number of people affected is still expected to rise (10:46, 12:04), local authorities said, with growing concerns about a “major tragedy” (11:03).
The affected trains are understood to be Iryo 7076 with 146 passengers plus one baby on board, and AVE 2080 with 397 passengers on board, making it 544 people in total on board of both train (11:00).
Early inquiries point to a possible signalling failure that contributed to the crash, Spanish media reported (12:32).
The incident comes less than a year after a similar crash in Adamuz, the province of Córdoba, which killed 46 and injured 152 in January this year (11:00).
Spain’s high-speed railway network ranks as the largest in Europe and the second biggest in the world after China, carrying 25 million passengers in 2024.

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said he was “shocked” by the accident (11:05), with transport minister Óscar Puente working at the emergency control centre to “obtain all possible information about what happened” (11:16).
The Spanish king Felipe VI expressed his sorrow and solidarity with all affected (11:38, 12:07).

Meanwhile, El Mundo is reporting that the Iryo train flagged a failure in its LZB signalling system shortly before the crash, but the train behind did not receive the information due to a potential human error.
Investigators believe the AVE high-speed train travelling behind crashed into the stationary Iryo service, according to the newspaper.
The president of Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano García-Page, is now briefing the reporters.

He confirms the latest figure of 30 dead – 24 in the AVE train and six in the Iryo train – but says the authorities expect this number to rise further as emergency services are yet to reach the most affected parts of the wreckage.
He also says some 80 people were injured, with 30 people with minor injuries, and 50 with moderate and more serious injuries of varying severity.
He thanks all emergency services for their help.

Unlike other party leaders, the far-right Vox party’s Santiago Abascal appears to be going ahead with his political plans for today as he continues campaigning ahead of next month’s parliamentary election in Spain.
In his comments, he repeatedly attacked Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez for “constantly putting the Spanish people at risk.”
He explicitly rejected calls to suspend the campaign, insisting that would only to “exploit the grief and mourning to silence complaints and protests regarding the decay of our infrastructure.”
Spanish King Felipe VI appeared in front of cameras on his visit to Bétera, where he is attending some military exercises.
His brief reaction was largely in line with his earlier written statement.
Visibly shaken, Felipe VI said he wanted to “express my deep regret over this horrific incident,” acknowledging “a high number of fatalities and many injuries.”

“My primary concern is to express my sorrow over this terrible tragedy and to convey our condolences, sadness, support, and affection to the families during such an incredibly difficult and painful time.”
He also thanked emergency services responding to the incident for their help.

items.title: Everything announced at Amazon’s October 2026 hardware launch
paragraphs: Amazon had plenty of new gadgets to share at its Echo hardware event this year, along with updates to the AI-powered Alexa Plus after it became available to everyone in the US in February. But the big news this year is screens: devices with big, beautiful ones, and those that lack them entirely.

There’s the Alexa Photo Frame, which Amazon devices chief Panos Panay describes as “the world’s smartest photo frame” and that doubles as a full Alexa speaker. There’s also the new Echo Time smart alarm clock, the screenless Echo Studio with Home Camera, a fully redesigned Echo Dot, and Amazon’s latest flagship smart display, the Echo Show 16, which comes with a whopping eight woofers and can run the full Fire TV experience by touch.
You can catch up on all our coverage below, including the six biggest announcements and our hands-on with the Echo Show 16 and Echo Time.

Amazon has just taken the wraps off a bunch of new devices as part of a string of fall announcements. Today’s news focuses largely on new Echo speakers, with a few new smart home gadgets sprinkled in.
Here’s a roundup of all of the updates Amazon revealed on Wednesday.

Amazon’s smart home map interface that shows you where all your connected devices are has been overhauled with new graphics, features, and dynamic effects. The new Alexa Home Map is now an interactive 3D view of not just everything that’s inside your property, but outside of it too — using compatible Ring cameras to provide a 360-degree view that animates cars and people moving nearby.

Even just visually speaking, it’s a considerable upgrade from the 2D map that was introduced to the Alexa app in 2023. This new version looks similar to Samsung’s SmartThings Map View, and makes it easier to see exactly where all of your Echo devices, Ring and Blink cameras, Fire TV, lights, locks, thermostats, and other connected devices are located around your home.

Amazon just announced its newest smart alarm clock — the Echo Time. The baseball-sized smart speaker with a screen, the Time looks like an Echo Dot with Clock and an Echo Spot had a much bigger baby. It features a 3.2-inch touchscreen that prominently displays your choice of a huge selection of clockfaces and includes a sleep-sensing feature that promises to rouse you at just the right time in your sleep cycle to help you feel more rested. It costs $199.99 and is available to order now.

I spent some time with the Time at Amazon’s event in New York City and was impressed by several upgrades over the Spot, one of my favorite smart alarm clocks. The biggest is that you can set an alarm using the touchscreen, so you won’t wake your partner when you try to set one with your voice late at night.

Amazon’s latest Echo Show smart display is big, gorgeous, and eye-wateringly expensive. Announced today, the Echo Show 16 costs $499.99 (wall mount included) and is available to preorder now. There’s a Nanomatte display option for $569.99, plus a $100 preorder discount ahead of its release later this year.

After spending time with the device at a small media event in New York City this week, I think the Echo Show 16 could be the versatile family hub Alexa users have been asking for. The sleek hardware brings with it a completely new software experience, including better smart home controls, a much-improved calendar interface, and a real photo frame option — all fully customizable.

Amazon is giving its premium smart speaker a camera. The new Echo Studio with Home Camera, announced today as part of Amazon’s big blast of announcements, has a built-in camera for monitoring a room while you’re away, showing things to Alexa, and, soon, to use with video calls on Fire TV devices. It’s an iteration on the revised Echo Studio announced last year, which had a brand-new design.

The Echo Studio with Home Camera also offers some audio updates. Amazon says a new feature called “Advanced Room Adaptation” will continuously tune sound to the space that the speaker is in. There’s also an “Adaptive Volume” feature that raises or lowers volume depending on where you are in a room so that “your music or audiobook maintains the same volume as you move about.”
Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Amazon’s screen-equipped smart speakers have long been able to display your family’s photos, but its new Alexa Photo Frame is purpose-built for that task. It’s designed to compete with other digital picture frames from companies like Aura, and Amazon’s incorporates a smart speaker with access to Alexa Plus’ capabilities through voice commands. However, unlike the Echo Show and Amazon’s other smart home hubs, the Alexa Photo Frame only ever displays your photos, and you’ll never be served an ad.

The Alexa Photo Frame is available starting today; it’s $199.99 for a black frame or $229 if you want to upgrade to a frame made from birch or walnut wood. It pulls images from Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members, but otherwise the frame doesn’t require a subscription. The Amazon Photos app can back up photos from your Android or Apple devices and pull images from iCloud Photo, but importing from Google Photos isn’t supported yet.

items.title: 'Dissident republicans may be responsible' for explosive device at hotel - PSNI
paragraphs: Police believe dissident republicans may be responsible for a "viable postal device" which was delivered to a hotel in Londonderry.
Ammunition Technical Officers (ATO) were tasked to the hotel at Ebrington Square in the Waterside after the package was discovered at about 15:20 GMT on Tuesday.
They carried out a controlled explosion on the device, which was later taken away for a forensic examination.
Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Supt Gillian Kearney condemned it as "shameful and utterly abhorrent", adding that "those responsible clearly do not care who or what they harm".

"We are keeping an open mind as to who is responsible, and we are working through a number of lines of enquiry, one of which, at this time, is that dissident republicans may be responsible," Kearney said.
She said the investigation is at an early stage and has appealed to anyone with information to come forward as "it could make all the difference".
Ulster Unionist councillor Darren Guy, who chairs the local policing and community safety partnership believes the incident was timed to cause maximum disruption.
He also said it may have been linked to the MoD being represented at a careers event at the hotel in September.
"Recently, there was a careers event held in that hotel where I believe an RAF [Royal Air Force] stall was there for the careers event at that time.

"I think this was specifically done this week to cause as much disruption as possible during the 40th Halloween celebrations with thousands of international visitors visiting the city and the amount of families, especially young families going out to enjoy the many things on offer.
"It is totally reckless and these people don't think about anyone else but themselves."
Sinn Féin councillor Christopher Jackson said it was too early to "speculate" about any link between the alert and the jobs fair.
"We need clarification from those responsible," Jackson said.
He said this was "a disgusting attack on the city and the people of Derry".
"There is no justification whatsoever for carrying this out and putting people in danger, especially when the city is gearing up for the 40th anniversary of the Halloween festival.
"Derry is a warm and welcoming place and it's disgusting why someone or some organisation did this."
Foyle SDLP MP Colum Eastwood told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme the incident must have been terrifying for those members of the public in the vicinity of the hotel .

"This was clearly a viable device which is really frightening for the staff and the visitors to the hotel and to the hundreds, probably thousands of kids who were at that funfair yesterday and have been over the past number of days," Eastwood said.
"I don't know what entered someone's head to think this was a good idea.
"It is appalling, reckless and achieves absolutely nothing."
Julie Middleton, Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) assembly member for Foyle, told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme on Wednesday that she was "deeply disturbed and disgusted".

"There is no excuse to leave a viable device anywhere at all, but in the middle of Ebrington Square, where you have people at their work, families out enjoying some half-term fun and tourists visiting and unfortunately this was designed to cause disruption and with any viable device, it was obviously designed to cause harm."
Middleton said many children would also be in the vicinity enjoying the fun fair.
"To think anyone would place something like this near our children, or anyone for that matter, is just deeply wrong."

items.title: What we know about the crash so far
paragraphs: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was "shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo".

"I remain in constant contact with the Minister of Transport, and with the president of Castilla-La Mancha," Sánchez said on X, adding that emergency services were working on the ground "to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations".
"My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families."
Sánchez and other Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.
Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" by the accident and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.
A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.
A huge emergency response is under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.
Spanish news agency have reported that hospitals in the area have suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash.

A blood transfusion centre in Madrid has also appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de Transfusión said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".
It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and Alcázar de San Juan have cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.
This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.
In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain, its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

items.title: Amazon’s new Echo line is here: the 6 biggest updates
paragraphs: Amazon has just taken the wraps off a bunch of new devices as part of a string of fall announcements. Today’s news focuses largely on new Echo speakers, with a few new smart home gadgets sprinkled in.
Here’s a roundup of all of the updates Amazon revealed on Wednesday.
Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Amazon’s new Echo Show 16 has a 16-inch display in an anodized aluminum frame that the company says is nearly 40 percent thinner than its predecessor. There’s a new Nanomatte display option to reduce glare, along with an audio architecture with micro woofers and two tweeters for clearer audio.

The Echo Show 16 features a wide-angle 13-megapixel camera, which Amazon says offers the “widest field of view” on an Echo Show device so far. It has 20 percent more computing power and an upgraded Omnisense fusion platform, allowing Alexa to turn up the heat when the room is too cold or turn on a light when you enter the room.
The Echo Show 16 is available for preorder today and costs $499.99, with the Nanomatte option priced at $569.99.
Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Amazon is launching a new digital photo frame with a semi-matte, 10-inch touchscreen. The device syncs with Amazon Photos, allowing Alexa Plus to automatically pull up pictures based on who’s in it, when it was taken, and sentiment. You can also choose people you want to feature in your frame, as well as ask the device to show you specific pictures.
The Alexa Photo Frame costs $199.99 with a black frame or $229 for the birch and walnut frames.
Photo: Jennifer. Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Amazon is rolling out an upgraded Echo Dot with a built-in smart home hub that can control devices around your home without a separate hub. Like the Echo Show 16, the Echo Dot also has the company’s Omnisense fusion platform to detect room temperature and presence. It has Amazon’s custom AZ3 chip as well, along with four microphones, a new full-range driver for 50 percent more bass than the previous generation, and a built-in Eero Wi-Fi extender. You can buy the Echo Dot today in black, white, green, and pink for $99.99.

Amazon built a camera into the Echo Studio. With this update, you can tap into a livestream of the room while you’re away from home, or ask Alexa questions about something in front of the camera. As an example, Amazon says you can hold up a board game to ask about the rules, or show it a box of cereal to order a different flavor. The Echo Studio with Home Camera will soon connect with compatible Fire TVs, too, giving you the ability to hold video calls on a larger screen.
The Echo Studio with Home Camera is available in black for $249.99, while its optional stand costs $39.99.
Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge
Amazon has revealed the Echo Time, a smart alarm clock with a circular, 3.2-inch touchscreen that you can customize with different clockfaces and layouts.

The Echo Time offers an optional smart alarm feature that can wake you up when you’re in a lighter sleep — 10 to 60 minutes before your alarm — rather than at the exact time you want to wake up. It uses Amazon’s Omnisense technology to determine when to wake you up based on temperature and presence. The display also adjusts throughout the day, gradually brightening in the morning before dimming at night.
The Echo Time is available today for $199.99 in black, white, and pink, while a Kids Echo Time starts at $209.99. There’s also an adjustable stand available for $39.99.
Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

A new Alexa Home Map feature creates an interactive 3D map of the inside and outside of your home. It displays your Echo devices, Ring and Blink cameras, Fire TV, lights, locks, thermostats, and other smart home devices, which you can control directly through the map.

Amazon says you can create a map by entering your home address, scanning each room with a compatible iPhone, and then placing each smart home device. You can access your map in the Ring app, too, where you can view live animations of people and cars outside your home.

Alexa Home Map is rolling out in preview later this year on iOS in the Alexa Home Map, Alexa, and Ring apps. It’s also coming to larger Echo Show devices, the Ember Artline Fire TV, and new Alexa Tablets.

items.title: Voters in Texas agree: They hate data centers
paragraphs: Ask Texas NAACP president Gary Bledsoe what it’s been like to see data center developers descend upon Austin and its surrounding suburbs and he can rattle off project after project facing opposition from locals.

There’s the fight in Taylor over plans to build a data center at a site that’s supposed to be a park. Temple, around 40 miles away, is another sore spot, Bledsoe says. The mayor and City Council members there face recall attempts over data center developments. And some 30 miles outside of Austin, San Marcos became the first city in all of Texas to ban data centers.

Nowhere in the world are data centers growing more explosively than in Texas. With the midterm elections looming, the data center fight “is the issue in Texas,” says Bledsoe. The state’s NAACP recently joined dozens of other groups across the political spectrum to form a coalition to stop — or at least stall — data center construction. Their grievances are just as diverse as their membership: concerns about how much water the industry consumes in a state as dry as Texas, qualms about tax subsidies, and objections to new gas plants and wind farms built to meet rising electricity demand. Together, Bledsoe estimates the coalition — named We the People Texas — represents as many as 1 million voters across the state.

If there’s one thing a broad range of voters can agree on this election season, it’s that they hate data centers and are unhappy with the status quo. A majority of Texans — 57 percent — oppose the construction of data centers, an August poll found. That included 43 percent of Republicans, 75 percent of Democrats, and 54 percent of independents.
“We have almost nothing in common in so many other ways. And yet you get us in the room with this issue, and it’s like a wall”

After initially proclaiming his state the “epicenter of AI development,” Texas Gov. Greg Abbott is now fighting for reelection against underdog Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who is seen as having a rare shot at taking a reliably red state. The state’s high-profile Senate race is no less of a nail-biter, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton running neck and neck against Democrat James Talarico. In each race, candidates have to win over voters who think data centers are coming for their water, land, and livelihoods. Republican and Democratic hopefuls alike are trying to distance themselves from an industry that’s taken deep root in the state — and so far, voters aren’t buying it.

“You’re talking about Democrats, libertarians, independents, Republicans, all in one fight … we have almost nothing in common in so many other ways. And yet you get us in the room with this issue, and it’s like a wall … fighting one big enemy,” says Jet Parker, who cofounded a group called Save Rural Texas that is now part of the We the People Texas coalition.

Save Rural Texas came together this year after a local county commissioners’ meeting about plans to build a new data center in the Texoma area that borders Oklahoma. Residents, including Parker, successfully delayed that project. That victory led Parker, a corporate coach and speaker, to write up a handbook for other communities trying to block data center projects, and she now spends much of her time traveling around the state to train grassroots groups.

She’s got a warning for Republicans: If they keep backing data centers, they’ll lose Texas. “You just pissed off a lot of people in rural Texas who are supposed to carry you across the [finish] line,” Parker says.

Abbott is in particularly hot water. “You brung it, so you dance with it. That’s Texas talk, you know,” Parker says. “That’s what Abbott’s done, but we’re the ones having to dance with it … we didn’t want to be in the dance at all.”

For years, however, Texas has taken among the most welcoming stances toward data centers in the country. The state passed a sales and use tax exemption for data centers in 2013 under former Gov. Rick Perry. In 2015, Abbott expanded the exemption to include hyperscale data centers, which can span millions of square feet and house tens of thousands of GPUs. As a result, qualifying data center developers don’t have to pay state taxes on equipment and electricity for up to 20 years. That essentially rolled out the red carpet for companies that need abundant electricity to power energy-hungry data centers.

Since then data centers have had a massive growth spurt in order to support new generative AI models — and that’s costing the state. The tax exemption was initially expected to cost taxpayers $14.6 million in 2014 and 2015. But in 2025, state officials estimated that the tax break would lead to $3.2 billion in lost sales tax revenue over two years.

The state’s energy woes go further than that. Electricity bills have grown by 35.4 percent on average over the past five years as demand rises and utilities build expensive new infrastructure to meet that demand. Bledsoe is concerned about air pollution for communities around new gas plants. Data center electricity demand could erase decades of air quality gains in Texas, one recent study found. Parker, meanwhile, can’t stand solar and wind farms built near farmland. Neither wants to see new transmission lines snaking through their communities.

Data centers can also put pressure on already stressed water supplies, especially in a drought-prone state like Texas. While they can reuse water used on-site to cool servers, the larger part of data centers’ water footprint comes from electricity use. Data center proposals have driven a surge of gas and nuclear power projects, both of which need a lot of water for their own cooling systems.

Data center electricity demand could increase nearly tenfold by 2030, the state’s largest grid operator estimates. Meanwhile, data centers in Texas consumed about 25 billion gallons of water last year, around 0.4 percent of total water use, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). By 2030, that figure could grow to up to 2.7 percent of the state’s total annual water use, HARC estimates. And water consumption can be much higher when zooming into certain communities. Another study by the University of Texas at Austin estimated that data center water use statewide could rise to as high as 9 percent by 2040.

Virginia has historically been the state with the most data centers, but it’s running out of space. Virginia still beats Texas 287 to 170 when it comes to the number of planned data center projects as of April, according to Pew Research. But as data centers get bigger, they’re moving out of cities and into rural areas — particularly in Texas. Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power it draws, and in this measure, Texas already takes the crown with 26GW of existing and under-construction capacity compared to 13GW in Virginia.

Facing backlash to data centers, Abbott has changed his tune. In June, he directed the state Public Utility Commission to require that data center operators cover the costs of new infrastructure built to serve them. Since then, he has also announced statewide moratoriums on permits for data center projects pending audits on their electricity and water use. He’s also said that he would support a repeal of the sales tax exemption for data centers and greater oversight of data centers’ water and electricity use.

Even so, he’s reportedly taken millions in campaign contributions from data center interests, and We the People Texas coalition members are not convinced he’s turned the page. “Is he doing enough? Absolutely not,” Parker says.

The NAACP sent a letter to Abbott’s office last month criticizing his moratoriums for not going far enough because the state is only auditing projects that connect to the power grid. However, more so than any other state, Texas has data centers building their own power supply on-site, without needing to connect to the grid. Bledsoe’s concerned that these private energy projects will be subject to less regulatory scrutiny, while also harming air quality in nearby neighborhoods. Projects that already have permits are still being built. And an October investigation by advocacy group Public Citizen and FracTracker found public records indicating that state agencies are still processing permits for data centers, although Abbott’s office denies that they have issued any approvals since he directed them to pause permitting. To Bledsoe and other coalition members, he says, the temporary moratorium looks like “an attempt to run out the clock before the election.”

Data center hyperscalers including AWS, Microsoft, Google, Meta, and others have formed their own trade group called the Data Center Coalition (DCC). For what it’s worth, DCC isn’t endorsing any candidates. But in an interview with The Verge, Jess Heck, the group’s director of Texas government affairs, says, “It’s very clear that our members share the same goals as Gov. Abbott and the legislature. We want to be true partners, good neighbors in every Texas community where we operate.” Heck didn’t confirm whether any of its members are providing any campaign support for Abbott.
“An attempt to run out the clock before the election”

Eduardo Leal, press secretary for Abbott’s campaign, said in an email to The Verge that “Under [Abbott’s] standards, data centers must pay for their own electric infrastructure, add power instead of only adding demand, reuse their own water, reduce the cost of electricity for Texans, not disrupt residential neighborhoods, and eliminate reliance on outdated taxpayer-funded incentives.”

Abbott signed a state Senate bill into law last year that directs the Public Utility Commission of Texas to reassess how it allocates transmission costs in order to keep rates from rising disproportionately for residential customers. And this June, he proposed more measures to force companies to cover the costs of infrastructure upgrades needed to serve their data centers.

Abbott’s biggest competitor, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has eked out a narrow lead recently in some polls after strengthening her language against data centers — calling for a moratorium on development until the state legislature passes more protections. “I think her campaign has made a ton of inroads into moderate Republican communities because of her stance on data centers,” says Anthony Elmo, public education funding defender for Good Jobs First, which recently cofounded another coalition pushing for data center reforms in Texas alongside other advocacy groups.

Hinojosa has skyrocketed from a relatively obscure local official to a serious contender for the governor’s seat, largely on a populist message that caters to residents’ frustration with Big Tech companies grabbing land for data centers. Even so, she might not be convincing enough for conservative rural voters.

Candidates from both sides of the aisle were pretty soft on data centers up until the party conventions earlier this year, says Miriam Cobb, who cofounded the Texas Coalition Against Data Centers earlier this year (which is also part of We the People Texas). Texans can see the political posturing from Hinojosa, too, she says. One of Hinojosa’s major donors has been the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, which recently formed an “American Infrastructure Alliance” with OpenAI and data center developers.

“[Voters] know she wasn’t against it from a place of understanding or sincerity, it’s something she knows she has to say now,” Cobb tells The Verge, adding that she’ll be writing in an independent candidate come Election Day. Even with many conservatives — some of them now claiming to be single-issue voters on data centers — skeptical of both parties’ candidates, Cobb still expects Republicans to lose seats.

Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate, is attempting to atone for his previous support of data centers. He voted for the sales tax exemptions as a state senator in 2013, although he now says he’d support a repeal. In September, he announced an investigation into hundreds of data centers’ water use. Paxton also launched an investigation into the case in Taylor over whether it’s legal for land deeded for parkland to be developed into a data center. And he’s aligned himself with Abbott’s proposals to impose stronger light and noise restrictions on data centers, limit construction in rural areas, and push developers to cover the costs of new energy infrastructure. But he also reportedly received hundreds of thousands of dollars in campaign funding this year from data center interests.
“Trump keeps saying, you know, ‘Let them in, let them in, let them in’”

Talarico, meanwhile, has a similar plan to stop data centers “from jacking up our utility bills.” But he also claims to want to “empower local communities to decide whether they want a data center in their town,” a jab at Republicans including Paxton who have either stayed mum on whether counties should be allowed to make permitting decisions on data centers rather than the state or have actively curtailed their ability to do so. Abbott signed the so-called “Death Star” bill into law in 2023 barring counties and municipalities from crafting regulations that contradict state law. Some Republicans have cited the Death Star law in legal challenges to local moratoriums on data centers.

While the Senate race between Talarico and Paxton is in the national spotlight over the prospect of a Democrat flipping the seat, it’s probably less important for Texans concerned most about data centers, advocates tell The Verge. The race is too politically polarized to flip voters on the single issue, Cobb says, and neither candidate has given a very convincing position on how to rein in data centers anyway. Neither campaign responded to press inquiries from The Verge.

Working at the federal level, the best thing the senator-elect could do would be to push back against President Donald Trump’s data center agenda and ensure Texas can moderate data center development without interference, she says.
“We want assurances that you’re gonna let us deal with it instead of what’s been happening, where Trump keeps saying, you know, ‘Let them in, let them in, let them in,’” Cobb tells The Verge.

Cobb still sees construction traffic clogging two-lane rural roads leading to data center projects that have avoided Abbott’s partial moratorium. Residents are worried about the traffic jams blocking emergency vehicles, especially when fire weather kicks up. In some areas, Texans have seen property values drop, she adds. Farmers are giving up land that their families have tended to for generations. In other neighborhoods, an influx of new workers arriving for the data center “gold rush” is exacerbating housing shortages and making rent more unaffordable for locals. In either case, data center opposition coalition members say they’re worried about a loss of culture.
“It’s not for nothing,” Cobb says. “They have real community … and now they’re losing it.”

items.title: Amazon’s first digital picture frame lets you add voice notes to photos
paragraphs: is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Amazon’s screen-equipped smart speakers have long been able to display your family’s photos, but its new Alexa Photo Frame is purpose-built for that task. It’s designed to compete with other digital picture frames from companies like Aura, and Amazon’s incorporates a smart speaker with access to Alexa Plus’ capabilities through voice commands. However, unlike the Echo Show and Amazon’s other smart home hubs, the Alexa Photo Frame only ever displays your photos, and you’ll never be served an ad.

The Alexa Photo Frame is available starting today; it’s $199.99 for a black frame or $229 if you want to upgrade to a frame made from birch or walnut wood. It pulls images from Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members, but otherwise the frame doesn’t require a subscription. The Amazon Photos app can back up photos from your Android or Apple devices and pull images from iCloud Photo, but importing from Google Photos isn’t supported yet.

The frame has a 10-inch touchscreen display with a “semi-matte, anti-glare finish” to simulate the look of physical prints. A light sensor adjusts the display’s brightness throughout the day, and it sits on a detachable stand.

You can select specific people or albums through Amazon Photos, or let Alexa Plus curate what’s displayed. Alexa selects the best images based on lighting, when people are smiling, and the current season, so you may get more Halloween costumes this time of year, while intelligently skipping images like receipts or screenshots. Alexa can also display similar photos with unique connections as side-by-side pairs, such as pics of a child 10 years apart with a similar pose. If there’s something specific you want to see, like last summer’s beach trip, you can just ask Alexa to dig those up.

You can use the Amazon Photos app to add voice notes to images that will play through the frame. An option to record them on the frame itself is coming later. If you plan to buy the Alexa Photo Frame as a gift and purchase it through Amazon, you can preload photos or albums with voice notes that play once the recipient sets it up.

items.title: How a grocery merger could expand a surveillance network
paragraphs: is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.
Kroger’s $1.65 billion proposed acquisition of Giant Eagle might not only consolidate the grocery market, but also a vast surveillance network that includes Flock cameras, a new report warns.

Beyond standard concerns that a merger could decrease competition and increase prices, the American Economic Liberties Project (AELP), which advocates for competition policy reforms, says that the consolidation could also expand customer surveillance by a single company. It comes at a time where Americans are particularly on-edge about surveillance technologies like Flock cameras and surveillance pricing, heading into a midterm election largely defined by affordability issues.

A combined Kroger-Giant Eagle — which would add Giant Eagle’s 200-plus stores to Kroger’s 2,700 — could pose risks in two ways, according to AELP. The first is by enabling Kroger to acquire data on customers across a broader geographic area, which it can use to serve customers personalized pricing based on inferences about their backgrounds and shopping behaviors. It could also use that data to fuel its retail media arm, which repackages consumer insights for other brands. The second is by expanding or combining an existing physical surveillance network consisting of technologies like Flock cameras and Cooler Screens, a company that previously touted its ability to scan shoppers’ faces but backed off that messaging after public backlash. Kroger has denied using in-store facial recognition to serve customers’ prices, but has acknowledged in its privacy policy that it uses facial recognition at some stores for security purposes. Kroger and Giant Eagle did not immediately respond to The Verge’s requests for comment.
“Buying bleach or yogurt now comes with the prospect of being scanned, tracked, and profiled”

Similar privacy concerns were raised during Kroger’s earlier attempted merger with Albertsons, a much larger deal that courts blocked in late 2024 after the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general challenged it. AELP argues that the proposed merger with Giant Eagle is also deserving of scrutiny, because of the way it could significantly reduce options in places like Columbus, Ohio, and also because of Kroger’s buying patterns and incentives. They urge the FTC and Ohio attorney general to seek to block the merger, though experts have predicted they might not, both because of the relatively small size of the deal compared to Albertsons, and the Trump administration’s more open approach to settlement deals than the prior administration.“Buying bleach or yogurt now comes with the prospect of being scanned, tracked, and profiled,” the report says. “With every store Kroger buys, the data and surveillance apparatus grows.”

items.title: Amazon’s new Echo Studio speaker has a camera
paragraphs: is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Amazon is giving its premium smart speaker a camera. The new Echo Studio with Home Camera, announced today as part of Amazon’s big blast of announcements, has a built-in camera for monitoring a room while you’re away, showing things to Alexa, and, soon, to use with video calls on Fire TV devices. It’s an iteration on the revised Echo Studio announced last year, which had a brand-new design.

The Echo Studio with Home Camera also offers some audio updates. Amazon says a new feature called “Advanced Room Adaptation” will continuously tune sound to the space that the speaker is in. There’s also an “Adaptive Volume” feature that raises or lowers volume depending on where you are in a room so that “your music or audiobook maintains the same volume as you move about.”
The new Echo Studio with Home Camera will cost $249.99 and come in graphite. Amazon will still sell the standard Echo Studio at its $219.99 price.
Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Amazon is also updating the Echo Dot, and the new version is powered by Amazon’s custom-designed AZ3 chip and has a fourth microphone to improve your conversations with Alexa. The Dot also now has a built-in smart home hub, supporting Zigbee, Matter, and Thread, and has a built-in Eero Wi-Fi extender that Amazon says can add up to 1,000 square feet of coverage.
The updated Echo Dot is available starting today for $99.99 in graphite, glacier white, agave green, and coral pink.

items.title: Our first look at Amazon’s big new Echo Show 16
paragraphs: Amazon’s latest Echo Show smart display is big, gorgeous, and eye-wateringly expensive. Announced today, the Echo Show 16 costs $499.99 (wall mount included) and is available to preorder now. There’s a Nanomatte display option for $569.99, plus a $100 preorder discount ahead of its release later this year.

After spending time with the device at a small media event in New York City this week, I think the Echo Show 16 could be the versatile family hub Alexa users have been asking for. The sleek hardware brings with it a completely new software experience, including better smart home controls, a much-improved calendar interface, and a real photo frame option — all fully customizable.
But at double the price of the $250 Echo Show 11 and $200 more than Apple’s new HomeView smart display, it may be too expensive, even for diehard Alexa fans.

The Echo Show 16’s signature feature is its new customizable homescreens. Called Screen Styles, you can choose from a family organizer, a smart home dashboard, an Alexa widgets screen, or a digital photo frame. Unlike existing Echo Shows, these homescreens can stay on all the time or appear when you approach, giving you quick access to your calendar, a new meal-planning feature, or your most-used smart home devices.

This kind of easy interaction has largely been missing from smart home displays, which have traditionally been voice-first devices, with the screen providing additional visual context for the voice assistant inside. Over the years, Amazon has slowly added more functionality to its smart displays, and the Echo Show 16 feels like the culmination of those efforts.

With its size and slim bezels, the Show 16 looks a lot more like a tablet than a smart display, specifically the new Alexa Tablet Pro 12. It even has the same anti-glare Nanomatte display as an upgrade option and sports a MediaTek processor rather than Amazon’s AZ3 chip. “A lot of the same work went into this as the tablet,” Amazon’s head of devices and services, Panos Panay, confirmed to me.

When mounted on one of two optional stands, the Show 16 starts to resemble a small iMac, giving off some strong home-computer vibes, though it verges on too big for a kitchen counter. It’s much thinner than the Echo Show 15 or the 21 (also $499), with significantly slimmer bezels.

In my hands-on, the Show 16’s full HD screen felt responsive, and the display was bright and clear with deep blacks. The sound is better than a tablet and on par with the Show 11, thanks to a slim speaker box that runs the length of the screen and packs in eight custom woofers and two tweeters. Luke Combs’ “The Way I Am” was clear and loud, and the sound was smooth, though it lacked a bit of depth. I didn’t get to test the new microphone positioning (four total) to see whether Alexa can hear any better in this form factor.

While the hardware is impressive, the software is where the experience steps up. The Show 16 is designed as a household hub, a central place to see the family calendar, check the week’s meal plan, view family photos, control smart home devices, and see who’s at the video doorbell. It also runs the full Fire TV interface and comes with a newly redesigned Alexa remote that feels much nicer in the hand.

Along with the Screen Styles, you can choose from one of two ambient screensavers that appear when you’re away from the device: a photo frame or Alexa Recommendations. You can also skip an ambient screen entirely and keep your homescreen accessible at all times.

Alexa Recommendations is the same concept as the customizable rotating screen you see on current Shows. This can show the weather, news, photos, and other options, along with display ads. Amazon didn’t demo this option at the event, but according to Aidan Marcuss, the incoming VP of Alexa and Echo, this screen “will continue to offer the broad variety of content, just as it does now.” I asked whether this includes full-screen ads; he confirmed it does, but they’ll appear only there, not on any other home screen, and you can turn off Alexa Recommendations.

Another key interface change is a new favorites bar you can access from most screens. It opens a programmable quick bar that lets you switch between the device’s functions, including third-party Alexa skills and integrations. This small change makes the device easier to navigate by touch than the current Show interface. It opened promptly in my hands-on, and selecting an app took me directly to the relevant screen.

Of course, this is an Alexa Plus device, and you can still navigate by voice and chat with the assistant, which has had a brain boost. Daniel Rausch, the current VP of Alexa and Echo, who is transitioning into a new role at Amazon next month, says the latest version of Alexa Plus can do deeper research and is smarter. “It has access to more models and now has more depth of reasoning, is more capable of multitasking, and better at breaking down both complex tasks and vague tasks,” he said.

Alexa Plus has a new “next best actions” feature that makes proactive suggestions based on your conversations with it. The demo showed Alexa offering suggestions such as where to buy hardware cloth when you’ve been talking to it about building a chicken coop, or suggesting hiking trails and YouTube videos when you’ve been planning a trip to Scotland. These suggestions appear in a new Alexa Plus interface on the Show, built around “Cards.”

These cards, which also appear in the new Alexa app and on Alexa.com, act as Alexa’s memory, letting you return to a conversation and pick up where you left off; you can also pin cards to the Show in the Alexa Widget face. The cards interface uses the screen real estate better than the current way of talking to Alexa on the Show, which just fills the blue screen with white text.

Another feature that takes advantage of the big screen is an improved map view. This is a ground-up rebuild of the map view that launched in 2023, and it gives you access to all your smart devices in a 3D interface you can zoom in on to control lights, locks, cameras, and more in situ.

The map updates in real time, so when you toggle on a light, the room on the map lights up. It now gives you a bird’s-eye view of your home and neighborhood and can tap into any exterior Ring cameras you have. If someone approaches your house, you’ll see a figure on the map and can tap it to get a live view from the camera that spotted them.

The new UI and its features will eventually come to all current Show devices, though Amazon didn’t share a timeline. However, Marcuss confirmed that while the new customizable homescreens are included for free on the Show 16, it will require a subscription on the older devices. He didn’t confirm exact pricing.

As a category, smart displays have often felt like solutions looking for a problem; they promise to do too many things, but rarely do any very well. Based on my short time with the Show 16, Amazon may have solved that problem and delivered a genuinely useful device. But whether it’s a solution worth spending $500 on remains a big question.
Photos by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

items.title: Spending time with the Echo Time — a smart clock that senses you sleeping
paragraphs: Amazon just announced its newest smart alarm clock — the Echo Time. The baseball-sized smart speaker with a screen, the Time looks like an Echo Dot with Clock and an Echo Spot had a much bigger baby. It features a 3.2-inch touchscreen that prominently displays your choice of a huge selection of clockfaces and includes a sleep-sensing feature that promises to rouse you at just the right time in your sleep cycle to help you feel more rested. It costs $199.99 and is available to order now.

I spent some time with the Time at Amazon’s event in New York City and was impressed by several upgrades over the Spot, one of my favorite smart alarm clocks. The biggest is that you can set an alarm using the touchscreen, so you won’t wake your partner when you try to set one with your voice late at night.

The Time’s screen is an upgrade over the Spot’s 2.83-inch version: It’s fully round, whereas the Spot uses a cramped semicircle, and it shows a much bigger clock, which improves glanceability across the room.

The Time also prioritizes the clock at all times, so no matter what you ask Alexa to do — turn the lights on, play music, show you who’s at your video doorbell (on a very tiny screen) — it will revert to the clock as soon as the action is completed. If you’re playing music and have a timer running, small icons above the clock let you tap into them for more detail while keeping the clock visible.

The Time’s screen can dim down to under 0.3 nits. I saw this demoed, and it was barely visible in a very bright room, which is impressive, but I’ll have to get it on my bedside table to really test it.

Like the Spot, the Time has no camera, making it more suitable to put on your bedside table than an Echo Show. It does add an ultrasound transducer to the Dot’s ultrasound sensor, which detects motion. Combined, these enable a new smart alarm feature that uses the sensors to track your breathing and small movements to estimate your sleep stage, and wake you at an optimal moment up to an hour before your alarm goes off. Sleep sensing is opt-in, and you can quickly disable it by pressing the mute button.

If you’re a serial snoozer, the Time has a selection of special alarm tones that start quietly and “build energy” every time you hit that snooze button (by tapping the top of the speaker or by telling Alexa to snooze), to help make waking up less painful.

If you don’t like waking up to loud noises, the Time has a sunrise wake-up feature that gradually brightens the clockface with warm colors to help you wake up. This seemed very subtle in the demo I saw, but the room was brightly lit. If the Time were right next to your face, I could see it being effective for light sleepers.

The Time has the same hardware as the new Echo Dot, also announced this week, so it features a built-in smart home hub (Zigbee, Thread, and Matter), meaning you can pair smart lights in your room with it to brighten them along with the clockface. I’ve been using light to wake up for several years now and can’t imagine going back to a jarring alarm.

Amazon went all out on clockface options with Time; there are hundreds to choose from, and you can customize them to your heart’s content. The Time also comes in pink, black, or white, and there are two jazzy kids’ editions in galactic grape and cosmic lime.

These cost $209.99 and include a year of Amazon Kids Plus, which features a Sleep Studio that provides guided bedtime routines that prompt your kids to put on their PJs and brush their teeth. It also offers Wind Down prompts and can slowly dim the lights. The kids’ clockfaces feature cute animated characters, plus analog faces for kids learning to tell time.

On paper, the Time fixes many of the Spot’s problems and feels like a more polished device — and at nearly twice the price, it should be. My main concern is its size; it feels a hair too large for a bedside clock, though it’s smaller than the popular Hatch Restore. That’s a big screen for the bedside — though not as big as your phone — and if it could replace that on your bedside table, I can see it being a useful gadget. An optional stand ($39.99) lets you adjust the screen angle and makes it feel less bulky, but I’ll have to test it in my bedroom before making a final verdict.
Photos by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

items.title: Amazon’s Alexa Home Map is getting a smarter 3D redesign
paragraphs: Amazon’s smart home map interface that shows you where all your connected devices are has been overhauled with new graphics, features, and dynamic effects. The new Alexa Home Map is now an interactive 3D view of not just everything that’s inside your property, but outside of it too — using compatible Ring cameras to provide a 360-degree view that animates cars and people moving nearby.

Even just visually speaking, it’s a considerable upgrade from the 2D map that was introduced to the Alexa app in 2023. This new version looks similar to Samsung’s SmartThings Map View, and makes it easier to see exactly where all of your Echo devices, Ring and Blink cameras, Fire TV, lights, locks, thermostats, and other connected devices are located around your home.

You can control core device functions like adjusting speaker volume or checking security cameras from the map, and some features update dynamically in real time to provide an easy overview of what’s currently running — such as dancing music notes over active speakers, and a glow for any smart lights that are currently switched on that matches whatever color they’re set to.

For the exterior view, a small live preview will appear on the map when one of your cameras detects movement. An interactive timeline is also available that lets you rewind the last 24 hours across every camera at once, so you can stay informed with package delivery times and other movements while you’re away from home. There’s even animation effects that match what the weather is really like outside, and Amazon says it’s planning themed modes for Halloween and Christmas.

As this is a digital replica of your house specifically, there’s obviously some setup required. Amazon uses your address to automatically pull a 3D model of your house and neighborhood from Mapbox, and you’ll then have to walk through every room and scan it for an accurate interior layout. Scanning requires an iPhone that has a LiDAR/structured-light sensor, though Amazon said it’s currently testing a plain-video scanner for iOS and Android. Your existing Map View maps can’t be repurposed so you’ll have to follow this process, and an average home apparently takes between 15-20 minutes to scan.

When the map model is set up, you can drag your devices onto it from the app tray. It’ll show multiple floors and even where your furniture is located. There are a few viewing modes too, including light and dark modes, and the ability to filter for specific devices like lights.

The new Alexa Home Map will start to roll out in preview “later this year,” though Amazon hasn’t specified a date. It’ll be available on the iOS Alexa Home Map, Alexa, and Ring apps, the new Alexa Tablets, the Ember Artline Fire TV, and larger Echo Show devices — including the new Echo Show 16.

items.title: Will Instagram's 90-minute videos make it impossible to switch off from socials?
paragraphs: It's official: the internet is eating itself. Instagram has just announced it's testing 90-minute video content, and my poor, brainrotted head cannot take it. Now, whether it's short-form, attention-stealing slop or long-form video rambling, it doesn't seem to matter to IG, as long as there's content.

Not to be a grandma, but I remember when the Instagram logo was a skeuomorphic vintage camera, so I feel I've earned the right to whinge. The app has evolved a lot since its debut, but the move to long-form video means yet another social media app is gunning for our precious attention, and I'm really feeling the fatigue.

On Monday, Instagram began testing the 90-minute clips with a handful of US-based creators. The 'Features' project has already been tested in Brazil and is aimed predominantly at podcasters and comedians. Whether other long-form creators will migrate from the safety of rival platforms like YouTube remains to be seen, but I already find the concept of extended video content on IG rather tiresome.

I'm a woman of structure. I like that TikTok is for brainrot and YouTube is for slightly more nuanced, long-form brainrot. But it's no secret that podcast content is ruling the social feed – it's cheap to produce, and so long as you can wrangle some semi-interesting yappers to host, you've got a steady flow of hour-long content each week.

I've already seen video content infiltrate my other precious apps like Spotify. Do I watch podcast videos on the platform? Absolutely not, but the fact that it's even there suggests I may be in the minority. Social media brands are competing to become the next 'every app', and with little distinction between them, it all feels a little like a desperate plea for my watch time.

I see a not-so-distant future where an evening can be swallowed by circling the drain of social media. 15 minutes on TikTok as an appetiser, catching up with your favourite zillenial podcasters on IG for main, and a nice YouTube video essay for dessert. Simply put, it's becoming too tempting to switch off.
For more social media news, check out Instagram's new brand identity that's more than just a wordmark, or take a look at the best social media platforms for artists and designers.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).
