items.title: How rebuilding old mosques is bringing Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims together in Punjab
paragraphs: Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.
The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.

He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.

“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”

Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.

“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”
Bibi Rajinder Kaur, a Sikh, donated family land to build a mosque in her village. ‘There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,’ she says
Gajju Khan, who hopes to live long enough to see the mosque in his village completed

During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.

But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.

About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.
Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.
Jaspal Sharma says donating some of his land to build a mosque was a neighbourly duty
The new mosque in Malerkotla, Punjab, welcomes worshippers for evening prayers

“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”

For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.

“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.
Sadna Qasai, one of the many mosques in Punjab that fell into ruin after partition

“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.

Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.
Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.
Sikh men in Punjab’s villages have been coming together to fund and help build or revive old mosques

“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

items.title: Australia must ‘re-win the argument for democratic politics’ in wake of Haines incident, Alastair Campbell says
paragraphs: Tony Blair’s former communications guru, Alastair Campbell, says the UK political system was too quick to revert to overheated rhetoric and polarisation after attacks on MPs, urging politicians to “re-win the argument for democratic politics”.

More than a week after independent MP Helen Haines was allegedly targeted in an attack outside her electorate office in northern Victoria, causing her to lose both legs, Campbell said the tenor of political debate in Australia should better reflect Haines’ own approach.

Speaking to the Guardian’s Australian Politics podcast on Wednesday, the commentator said the killings of British MPs Jo Cox, David Amess and former politician Ann Widdecombe had not brought about lasting change in political culture.
“They were followed by everybody saying the right thing about how our political debate culture had to change, about how we had to address online hate and polarisation, all this stuff,” he said.
“But it didn’t take long before we kind of got right back into it. So I think it is about how we genuinely try and generate a different way of talking to each other and about each other now.”
A 43-year-old man has been charged over the alleged attack on Haines and the incident continues to be investigated by police.
The co-host of popular podcast The Rest is Politics, Campbell said Haines’ eventual return to parliament would help bring about change.
“It’s very rare these days that an individual act or incident lasts more than half a news cycle, and so we just move on. I think remembering is so important.

“In a way, the fact that she is still with us and is going to still be part of the political debate, maybe that will help people … that people will see that that is the consequence of the actions that were taken against her.”
A former journalist, Campbell is the author of more than 20 books, including diaries documenting his years working inside 10 Downing Street.
He is due to visit Australia for a speaking tour next month.
Campbell said politicians and the media should reflect on how they speak to everyday people, and why their professions are so poorly trusted.

“It’s made more difficult at the moment because you’ve got Donald Trump in America as the loudest, most talked about politician on the planet, and he represents a lot of the things that I think we don’t want in our politics.
“We’ve got to re-win the argument for democratic politics because it’s under a lot of pressure right now,” he said.
Discussing the rise of populist politics, Campbell said the world was still struggling to grasp the effects of the 2008 global financial crisis.

“If I think of one thing that maybe ties the rise of Trump to Brexit, to the protests that we’re seeing in different parts of Europe, I think is that we haven’t really come to terms with the consequences of the financial crisis, and the sense that there was socialism for the banks who caused it, and austerity for the people, and the people who are still struggling to see their living standards rise.
“That, ultimately I think, is a big driver of what the Americans call affordability, what we call cost of living, just the sense that people don’t feel that they’re able to get on.”
Campbell revealed he occasionally watches clips of Paul Keating’s parliamentary attacks as Australia’s prime minister in the 1990s.
The bestselling author’s latest book is Persevilience: The Word the World Needs Now, published by Allen and Unwin.

items.title: Losing my legs ended my football dream - now skiing gives me freedom
paragraphs: Adam Golebiewski has been able to train in snow
ByLouise HosieBBC ScotlandReporting fromHuntly and Ken BanksNorth east Scotland reporter
A promising footballer who lost both legs after a car crash has a new passion in life - after finding "freedom" in skiing.
Adam Golebiewski was only 17 when the crash happened in 2024 in Macduff, Aberdeenshire. He needed a double amputation below the knee.
The former goalkeeper celebrated his 18th birthday during his rehabilitation in hospital, and was fitted for prosthetics.
Since then he has become a father, and - now aged 20 - is showing a flair for para cross-country skiing. Adam's coach thinks the Parlaympic Winter Games could be a target.
Adam faced three months of rehabilitation at Woodend Hospital in Aberdeen following the crash which was caused by a drink driver.
He was able to walk again on crutches, and was "thankful and grateful" to be home with his family that Christmas.
Adam's dreams of becoming a professional goalkeeper were shattered, but in the face of adversity he found a new joy.
He now trains at the Nordic ski centre in Huntly, next to the field where he used to play football with junior side Deveronside.
There, he uses a special sit-ski with a board and wheels. The board is replaced with skis when he trains on snow - something he had the chance to do in America earlier this year.
With no previous experience of the sport, he has just qualified to enter international competitions as a para biathlete - which combines cross-country skiing and shooting.
'I don't think of my injuries when I am on the board'
His sights are now set on para biathlon World Cup events in Finland and Sweden over the next six months.
"I don't actually think of my injuries when I'm on the board - I just forget that I have them," he told BBC Scotland News.
"I just feel so free and I just forget about everything else."

Of his training travels, he explained: "In Colorado, I didn't really know anybody and I was quite nervous to go and try it out, but once I was on the snow I was completely fine - even though I fell about 40 times.
"Then Italy, that was another good experience where I I tried biathlon, which is skiing and shooting.
"The last trip I was recently on was Oberhof in Germany which was again just an improvement from the first time being away on snow, and I learned a lot more again."
He said his mind was "completely focused" on what he is doing.
Adam needed a double amputation as a teenager two years ago
Adam's coach, Simon Bate of Snowsport Scotland, said he had made impressive progress.
Bate believes the Parlaympic Winter Games in 2030 could be a future goal.
"From when I first met him as an 18-year-old and he just had this real maturity and positive outlook," he said.
"He's always been very very up for what we've suggested in terms of the training, he's really keen to work hard."
Bate added: "He's definitely got the potential - and I think he's going to do well."
Adam hopes to be an inspiration to others facing difficult times.
"I think they should just give it a go because you never know what could happen," he said.
"Since I've started skiing, I've loved every minute of it.
"I never knew any of this would happen so quickly. It's just given me a bit of freedom again."
Adam says he hopes to be an inspiration to others
A drink-driver who caused the crash in which Adam was injured was later detained for 32 months.
Arran Paterson, 19, admitted causing serious injury by dangerous driving, being over the drink-drive limit, and driving without insurance.
Adam had been a passenger in Paterson's car which crashed into a wall. Two other teenage passengers were also seriously injured.
Patterson was also disqualified from driving for five years and four months.

items.title: Bonfire Night policing in Scotland will be 'largest operation since Trump visit'
paragraphs: Police Scotland are preparing for a large-scale operation on Bonfire Night
Scotland's biggest police operation since the visit of President Donald Trump last year is to take place on Bonfire Night, in the face of a "unique" combination of safety concerns.
As many as 1,700 officers could be deployed on and around 5 November to deal with fireworks-related disorder, a European football match involving Celtic and potential protests in Glasgow.
Additional public order vehicles and drivers are being brought in from 18 English and Welsh police forces under mutual aid arrangements.
Police Scotland says the plan, titled Operation Amberlight, is intended to ensure the safety of the public and emergency services.
The force has already vowed that anyone caught up in disorder around Halloween and Bonfire Night will face "very real consequences".
This will be enforced through Fireworks Control Zones (FCZs), which ban the use of pyrotechnics in certain areas of Edinburgh and Glasgow from 30 October.
In recent years, emergency crews have been pelted with petrol bombs and missiles - though police said there were fewer instances of this last year.
Police tackle Bonfire Night disorder in 2025
The deployment will beef up Operation Moonbeam, the annual police response to fireworks-linked criminality which is now in its ninth year.
Moonbeam involves local police divisions receiving additional specialist support in case trouble breaks out on their patch.
This year's Bonfire Night will see police coping with two further challenges - both in Scotland's biggest city.
Celtic will take on Turkish side Beskitas in a Uefa Europa League match at Celtic Park.
Officers say they are also aware of images circulating online, suggesting "planned protest activity" will take place in Glasgow the same night.
The force is planning what it calls "one overarching policing operation" to ensure a co-ordinated approach.
Operation Amberlight's gold commander, Ch Supt David Robertson, said: "Bonfire Night remains one of the busiest nights on the calendar for Police Scotland.
"We are committed to supporting local policing divisions with dedicated nationally co-ordinated specialist capabilities.
"Operation Amberlight builds on what is already in place to further enhance our capability and capacity to respond to the unique challenges we may face on 5 November.

"Whilst we have seen improvements in recent years, we are not complacent, and with these additional challenges, our enhanced model will see the largest deployment of police forces since the visit of President Trump."
The worst Bonfire Night disorder in recent years took place in 2023, when more than 60 officers were injured across the country.
Youths targeted officers with petrol bombs and fireworks in the Niddrie area of Edinburgh.
Similar incidents were reported in other parts of the city, while fire crews were targeted in Dundee, Glasgow, Blantyre in South Lanarkshire, and Blackburn in West Lothian.

Further instances of anti-social behaviour around Halloween in 2024 saw another officer injured and bus services withdrawn from Niddrie despite police seizing a cache of fireworks and petrol during pre-emptive raids.
This year, Fireworks Control Zones (FCZs) banning the use of pyrotechnics in certain areas are scheduled to come into force in Edinburgh and Glasgow from 30 October.
Under the restrictions, it is a criminal offence to set off a firework within the FCZ boundary or throw one into a zone.
The FCZs run from 30 October to 8 November in Edinburgh and until 9 November in Glasgow.
The police response to President Trump's visits in July 2025 - Operation Roll 2 - cost £21m and involved 7,340 officers.

items.title: 6 Music Festival 2027 heads to Newcastle
paragraphs: 6 Music presenter Lauren Laverne said: "Having grown up in the North East, I know just how much music means to people here and the important role it plays in local culture and communities.
"It's fantastic to see the festival return to the North East, and I can't wait to join listeners, artists and presenters for what promises to be a brilliant celebration of live music."
In 2026, the festival saw performances from the likes of Bloc Party, Courtney Barnett and Jacob Alon.

Mawdsley said: "Since it was last here, Newcastle has become a true music city with many of our artists being recognised not least by awards like the Mercury Prize, which has shortlisted Sam Fender, Jade and Knats in the last two years, but there is a real collaborative spirit in the city.
"Music is a vital element of our cultural lifeblood, and we can't wait to welcome 6 Music listeners to learn more about how vibrant the city has become."

items.title: Sydney must close its beaches – level 1
paragraphs: A dead whale washes up on the rocks near Sydney, Australia. Local leaders close nearby beaches to keep people safe. They are worried that the big dead animal will bring hungry sharks near the shore.

Workers cannot easily move the whale. The water is dangerous, and the rocks are sharp. Also, the body is already breaking down into parts. Experts say that many whales are swimming near the land this month.
Local people and rangers want to do a special ceremony for the animal. Leaders tell visitors not to swim in the sea right now.
Difficult words: wash up (when water carries something onto the land), shore (the land along a sea or lake), break down (to separate into smaller parts over time).

items.title: Sydney must close its beaches – level 2
paragraphs: Officials closed famous Australian beaches after a dead young whale washed up on rocky shores near Sydney. Lifeguards shut the beaches to keep swimmers safe because the whale carcass can attract dangerous sharks.

Local teams are trying to figure out how to handle the situation, but removing the heavy animal is extremely difficult. The ocean is rough, and the body is already breaking down. Experts say that more whales are migrating along the coast this season, which makes these events more common.
Indigenous groups are preparing special cultural ceremonies to respect the animal. For now, local leaders ask people to stay away from the water until the coast is clear and safe again.
Difficult words: carcass (the dead body of an animal), migrate (to move from one region to another according to the seasons), common (happening often).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Sydney must close its beaches – level 3
paragraphs: Popular beaches in eastern Sydney were closed to the public after a dead young humpback whale washed ashore in a rocky bay.

Local authorities shut down swimming and surfing spots as a safety precaution and warned that the whale carcass is likely to attract sharks to the coastline. Emergency teams and local rangers face significant challenges trying to remove the body because the animal is in an advanced state of decomposition, and the rough ocean conditions make the area inaccessible for boats or heavy machinery. Community leaders and experts noted that with growing whale populations along the coast, such events are becoming more common. Indigenous rangers plan to perform cultural ceremonies to honor the whale, while scientists advise the public to stay out of the water and let nature take its course if retrieval remains impossible.

Difficult words: precaution (an action taken in advance to prevent something dangerous, unpleasant, or inconvenient from happening), carcass (the dead body of an animal, especially a large one), retrieval (getting something back or removing it from a specific location).

items.title: Jim Chalmers is blaming Australia’s accelerating inflation on Trump – but voters aren’t buying it
paragraphs: Jim Chalmers is blaming the latest shocking inflation figures on the worsening Middle East conflict, and he has a point.
The trouble is, voters aren’t buying what the treasurer is selling.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics said that the 9.4% jump in fuel costs in September was largely responsible for inflation accelerating from 4% to 4.3%.
Petrol and diesel prices were on average 24% higher than a year earlier, the data shows.
We are clearly paying an economic price for Donald Trump’s pointless and damaging war on Iran – and you can’t pin that on the government, whatever your political leanings.
Then there’s the sudden boom in spending on datacentres, which is pouring money into an economy that is already struggling to deliver the workers and materials needed to build homes and roads.
Again, this is driven by the global rush by tech companies to put in place the infrastructure to power their artificial intelligence revolution.

Earlier in the day, Michele Bullock, the RBA’s governor, made the same point: overseas developments were complicating the central bank’s already tough task of bringing inflation all the way back to 2.5%, preferably by the end of next year.
Taking the lion’s share of the blame for worsening cost of living pressures may not be completely fair, but it is the price of incumbency – as the latest Essential poll showed.
Nearly a third of voters believe that government spending is the top cause for rising cost of living.
Only 24% said overseas events like the global oil shock was the main reason, and 19% said it was supermarket price gouging.
While government spending may not be the main reason that inflation has tracked higher since the middle of the year, it is part of the mix.
Economists including Chris Richardson, the country’s top budget watcher, have argued that public spending is too high and is not helping in the battle to bring inflation down.
Government expenditure as a share of the economy is around record highs.

This is hard to reconcile with Chalmers’ protestations that the government has nothing to do with the latest jump in cost of living, particularly when RBA officials frequently refer to the capacity pressures that existed when the war on Iran started in late February.
It’s also important to note that the RBA’s preferred measure of underlying inflation – removing the biggest price moves – also lifted from 3.6% to 3.7% in the year to the September quarter.
Regardless of who or what is to blame, and to what degree, voters are likely to get angrier still next Tuesday when the Reserve Bank surely delivers the year’s fifth interest rate hike.

In Senate estimates before the latest price statistics were released, Reserve Bank officials confirmed they were more worried about inflation becoming entrenched than they were about rising unemployment, which recently reached a five-year high.
So it’s hard to see anything but more pain for mortgage holders come Melbourne Cup day. Another rate rise will bring the cash rate to 4.85% – the highest since the GFC.

If you’re starting to fret about that comparison, Sarah Hunter, the RBA’s chief economist, offered the reassurance that there were no signs the economy was “in or heading into a recession in the near term”.
Perhaps, but there is no doubt we are heading into more dangerous territory, and the future is looking darker, not brighter.
Families are approaching Christmas with rates at their highest since 2008, sky-high petrol costs and rising unemployment.
For many households, it will be a tough summer that will add to an increasingly entrenched pessimism about the future.
The share of Australians saying they think the country is on the wrong track has been steadily climbing and reached 61%, according to the latest Essential poll.
The pressure is now on Chalmers to use December’s mid-year budget to somehow change the narrative as the government approaches the third year of this parliamentary term.
It will be a tough ask, and there are no obvious answers.
There is, at least, one thing we can agree on. As the treasurer is fond of saying: the Middle East conflict can’t end soon enough.

items.title: ‘Emotional intimacy’ from AI chatbots would be banned under Australia’s digital duty of care laws
paragraphs: The federal government wants to ban AI chatbots which seek to create “emotional intimacy” after prime minister Anthony Albanese raised the alarm in a heartfelt speech about children treating these agents as their “best friend”.

But Labor is coming under increasing pressure to empower the telecommunications ombudsman to become a watchdog for social media and AI to give Australians an external complaints mechanism and allow the “naming and shaming” of big tech.

The digital duty of care bill passed the House of Representatives on Wednesday and will be debated by the Senate in coming weeks. The government hopes to pass the bill by the end of 2026, but its pathway through the upper house remains unclear. The Greens support the bill, while the Coalition has said it will not vote for it, though Labor still appears keen to win the opposition’s support and remains open to amendments.

The planned framework would apply new online safety standards to social media, games, apps and chatbots. Labor said it would place “an overarching obligation” on tech platforms “to provide a safe online environment for all Australians” and replace a range of existing online codes and standards with a broader duty-of-care requirement to protect users from certain “harmful” content. It would also require social media platforms to offer an “opt-out” feature for its algorithm and suggested content.

The communications minister, Anika Wells, has suggested content that that promotes misogyny, terrorism, suicide, self-harm and eating disorders would be captured by the laws. On Wednesday, the government accepted amendments from crossbencher Kate Chaney which would add certain AI chatbot activity to the list of harms, requiring platforms to ban “material or conduct that simulates emotional intimacy and encourages or fosters a child’s dependence on it in place of human relationships”.

In an emotional address on Tuesday night, where he again implored the Coalition to consider voting for the bill, Albanese said: “the stories we hear about people identifying a chatbot, a non-person as their best friend, should be a huge wake up call for every member of this parliament to be prepared to act.”

The opposition voted against the bill in the House, alongside One Nation. Political opponents have accused Labor of an “Orwellian” system of “censorship” and of seeking to influence conversations online – claims Wells strongly denied.
“If they really care, the test is simple here, they should bring an amendment, not a slogan to ‘kill the bill’,” Wells told ABC radio on Wednesday.

Another Chaney amendment accepted by Labor would require the algorithm opt-out features to be “accessible, easy to use” and “prominently available” on platforms, amid concerns that social media firms may offer only small or hard-to-find features.

The bill now moves to the Senate, where the Greens have set up an inquiry to probe the laws due to report back in late November. Senator Sarah Hanson-Young backed a digital duty of care, calling for the government’s legislation to be strengthened. The Greens want Australians to have the right to pursue private legal action against platforms and for penalties to be increased.
“Australians also need an external complaints pathway, free from the profit-driven whims of big tech’s content moderation,” she said.

Independent MP Sophie Scamps had proposed changes to the bill to expand the remit of the telecommunications industry ombudsman. She said such a watchdog – which does not currently exist for big tech – would allow ordinary social media users to seek remedies to their accounts being hacked or inaccessible, including compensation, and investigate broader issues to name and shame companies behaving badly.
Labor did not accept this amendment in the lower house and Wells declined to voice support for such an idea, but the Greens will push for such a reform in their Senate negotiations.

The telecommunications industry ombudsman, Cynthia Gebert, said her office would be well placed to carry out such a role for big tech. She said such roles were funded by the industries they regulate and that expanding its remit could be financed by big tech.

“There are some real strengths in the DDOC [digital duty of care] because it’s putting the onus on platforms to make things safe … but I think the area that needs to be strengthened is giving people somewhere to go if they can’t get their complaints resolved with the platform,” Gebert said.
“It risks leaving Australians in the safe place they are now, where they get automated responses or escalation procedures that don’t go anywhere.”
Gebert said the government should make it mandatory for big tech to be part of an ombudsman scheme, saying it would “hold industry to account and drive system improvement”.
“[The telecommunications industry ombudsman] can help with your Telstra account, but we can’t help with your Gmail account. Consumers come to us sometimes and ask, ‘why this, not that?’,” she said.
“We want to help but don’t have the powers to do so now.”

items.title: Gulliver fans celebrate three centuries of Jonathan Swift’s classic satire
paragraphs: In March 1726, an Irish clergyman visited London and arranged for a courier to deliver a manuscript to a publisher under cover of night. The dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin knew his novel would cause trouble and wanted to publish it anonymously.

His name was Jonathan Swift and the story was called Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World. The satirical work was published that October and is better known 300 years on as Gulliver’s Travels.

An immediate sensation, it skewered Georgian pretensions and entered popular culture through translations, children’s versions, comics and films. The anniversary is now being celebrated at Swift’s alma mater, Trinity College Dublin, and at events around Ireland.

Exhibitions, festivals, seminars, art competitions and workshops are exploring the origins of Swift’s masterpiece, its retelling through a feminist lens, and its prophetic depiction of a society in thrall to a form of artificial intelligence.

“Lemuel Gulliver’s first voyage to the land of Lilliput is the one most familiar to audiences today,” said Stephanie Breen, an assistant librarian and co-curator of the exhibition at Trinity. “This exhibition, however, brings viewers on a journey to all of the lands Gulliver encountered – Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa and beyond and the country of Houyhnhnms.”

The exhibition, which runs until December and is available online, draws on the university’s collection of hundreds of editions and popularisations of Gulliver’s Travels, including engraved illustrations, pop-up versions, a 1976 Marvel comic and the only known surviving copy of an abridgement printed in 1761.

The voice of Gulliver’s wife, Mary, who is neglected and left at home “big with child” until his eventual, grumpy return, was imagined through contemporary works such as Alison Fell’s The Mistress of Lilliput and Lauren Chater’s Gulliver’s Wife, said Aileen Douglas, a professor of English and exhibition co-curator.

Gulliver’s experiences in Laputa, a floating island dedicated to arts and science, resonated with our era’s anxieties about technology, said Douglas. Its inhabitants seek to extract sunbeams from cucumbers and obtain knowledge via an “engine” of wires, handles and paper that can produce tracts on philosophy, poetry and mathematics “without the least assistance from genius or study”.
In the kingdom of Luggnagg, Gulliver is at first enchanted and then horrified by the Struldbruggs, a race that is immortal but continues eternally to age and sicken.

A panel discussion about the role of art in challenging power, and Gulliver’s attacks on human vanity and scientific arrogance, is to be held at Trinity on Wednesday. At the cathedral, a children’s choir will perform the premiere of a work by the composer Seán Doherty, along with organ recitals and extracts of Gulliver’s Travels read by the Swift scholar Brendan Twomey. An exhibition and lecture series at the Robinson library in County Armagh runs until December.

Born in 1667, Swift combined posts in the Church of Ireland with pamphlets and essays that pioneered deadpan, savage satire, including A Modest Proposal, which suggested alleviating the plight of the Irish poor by selling their children as food to the wealthy.
He wrote Gulliver’s Travels in Dublin and at an estate in County Meath, where it is said that some very tall and very small farm workers inspired the storytelling.

When shipwrecked on Lilliput, Gulliver discovers diminutive inhabitants who are waging war against a rival kingdom in a dispute over which end of a boiled egg should be cracked – a satire on Europe’s sectarian conflicts. Gulliver captures the Blefuscudian fleet and douses a fire at a Lilliputian palace by urinating on it.

Marooned among giants in Brobdingnag, Gulliver’s stories about his “own dear native country” inadvertently reveal its corruption and cruelty, prompting the Brobdingnagian ruler to pillory humanity as “the most pernicious race of little odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon the surface of the earth”.
Swift’s publisher, Benjamin Motte, did not know his author’s identity but the book’s success, and Swift’s literary record, enabled many to guess, said Douglas. “People sort of knew it was him.”

items.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
paragraphs: A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.
The US-based operator of Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".
It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".

Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (£6,000) from $1,800.

The company said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.
The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.
The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website.
Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds.
The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia.
There were around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in Cambodia, Bloomberg reported, citing the cruise operator's founder.
The Villa Vie Odyssey is equipped with several bars and restaurants, a pool deck and a pickleball court, according to its website.
Permanent residencies in its cabins range from $120,000 to $440,000. These cabins are also also available for rent from $3,500 a month.
Last year, the company launched a lifetime residence programme for people to spend their retirement years at sea.

In 2024, days after US President Donald Trump won his second term, Villa Vie Residences announced a four-year "Skip Forward" package. Its CEO told Fox Business at the time that it was the "perfect product for those who said they'd leave the country if 'XYZ' wins the election".

items.title: ‘Backdrop for countless local love stories’: Geelong gingko named Victorian tree of the year
paragraphs: For more than 160 years, a humble ginkgo tree raised from seed in Geelong’s botanic gardens has been the backdrop to “countless local love stories”. Standing beneath it is the most popular spot to get married at the park, its branches forming the backdrop of many wedding photos.

Now, in addition to being the largest ginkgo biloba in the state – and possibly Australia – at a whopping 20 metres tall, it has a new claim to fame. The much-adored Geelong icon has been crowned Victoria’s tree of the year.

The National Trust of Australia (Victoria), which runs the awards, announced on Tuesday that Geelong’s ginkgo beat eight other finalists to the 2026 title, receiving 27% of 4,435 public votes cast. Second place went to the smooth bark apple myrtle in Prahran, while Apollo Bay’s myrtle beech was voted third.

To be eligible, trees have to be listed on the National Trust significant tree register, which recognises 2,500 trees in Victoria for their cultural, scientific, and historic value. More than 40 were nominated this year, then narrowed down to nine by a panel of 12 experts and arboriculturists.
The executive manager of gardens and landscapes at the National Trust Victoria, Justin Buckley, said the ginkgo was a “very popular winner”.
“It’s a really special tree, and very well loved in that area,” he said.

The ginkgo was planted in 1859, just two decades after the township of Geelong was formally established. The seeds were transported from China, rumoured to have been delivered by a ship’s captain making a stop at Geelong’s port.

Since then, generations of botanic garden workers and volunteers have helped it thrive. Not all have been able to see the unusual stalactite-like growths from its trunk and branches, which only occur in much older female gingko varieties, or enjoy its fruit – which has a reputation for being smelly.

Ginkgos, also known as maidenhairs, are among the most ancient trees on earth, dating back to the Jurassic period more than 160m years ago. In Japan, they’re a symbol of hope, longevity and peace, after six survived the 1945 atomic blast in Hiroshima. They were thought to be extinct in the wild for many centuries before being revived.
Botanic gardens supervisor Sheree Parker said the ginkgo was one of the first trees planted in the park and was also its “most visited and talked about”.
“It’s just starting to awaken now after being dormant,” she said. “We’re really excited.
“It’s our most popular destination to get married as well. We have a lot of weddings on this lawn and a lot of couples like to get married underneath the ginkgo.”
The city of greater Geelong staff had been strongly lobbying for the ginkgo to be crowned since the finalists were announced, posting regularly to social media encouraging people to vote.
“As … the backdrop for countless local love stories, she holds a special place in all our hearts,” they said a post earlier this month.
The competition was established in 2016 to celebrate Victoria’s best-loved trees, while also calling for greater protection of green spaces.

A recent urban greening framework, released by Stonnington city council, found over the past decade, more than 17.9 hectares of tree canopy had been lost on private lands in the inner Melbourne suburb alone.

The National Trust is urging the Victorian government to give automatic statutory protection to trees on its register and those of local councils, while also introducing a “retain first” planning principle making tree removal a genuine last resort.

In the past year, the Victorian government introduced uniform protection of canopy trees, but Buckley said it remained “quite limited” and there was “large scope” for significant trees to be removed without a permit.

“The reason we continue to draw attention to trees through this competition is because they really don’t have adequate protection, certainly not the same protection that heritage buildings have,” Buckley said.
“You can’t just think, well, we’ll take this one out, we’ll put another tree in there and everything will be fine. Big significant trees are virtually irreplaceable.
“As we need to accommodate growing populations and more housing … there’s going to be a lot of pressure on trees.”

items.title: Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in US after Brazil cancels his passports
paragraphs: Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has arrived in the US, hours after Brazil cancelled his passports, sources have told the BBC.

The right-wing candidate left the country after its Supreme Court ordered that he surrender his passports amid an investigation into alleged money laundering. Bolsonaro has not been charged and has denied the allegations.
His passports were cancelled on Tuesday after he missed a deadline to hand them over to authorities, prompting widespread speculation that he may have left Brazil.
Sources told BBC Brasil and BBC Mundo that Bolsonaro met with his younger brother, Eduardo, in Florida - though his exact travel route from Brazil to the US is unclear.
Neither brother could be directly reached for comment.
His reported arrival in the US came hours after a senior US official confirmed the US State Department would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the country.
The BBC has contacted the White House, State Department and embassies in both the US and Brazil.
On Monday, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to hand his passports over to police within 24 hours as part of its alleged money laundering probe.

At the time, Bolsonaro said he had no plans to leave the country, and insisted that he would stay in Brazil to lead the opposition to his left-wing rival, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who on Sunday won the election.
After he missed the deadline, Bolsonaro's lawyers told BBC Brasil that they were "completely in the dark" about his whereabouts.
"We knew nothing about this, and we still have no information about what happened," one lawyer said.
Bolsonaro has not made any public statements since Monday afternoon local time, when he posted a video on social media.
Federal officers checked border crossings to establish if Bolsonaro may have travelled to neighbouring Argentina, a police source told BBC News Brasil.
However, Argentine authorities told the BBC there was no record of the senator entering their country through any border crossing.

Bolsonaro was already under investigation for alleged corruption over the financing of a film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup and is under house arrest.
A separate inquiry involves alleged links to a Brazilian lawyer, who is accused of laundering more than $1bn through a fraud scheme.
Police said earlier this month they had discovered Mr Bolsonaro had access to the bank accounts of a company owned by the lawyer.
Bolsonaro denied doing business with the lawyer, and described the passport confiscation as an attempt to intimidate him.
In addition to that investigation, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered police on Tuesday to examine Flávio Bolsonaro's electoral campaign over alleged foreign funding.
The 45-year-old senator suffered a stinging defeat on Sunday when he was beaten by Lula in a presidential run-off, which Bolsonaro had been widely expected to win.

His younger brother Eduardo Bolsonaro lives in the Texas, in the US, but was in Miami on Sunday, where he cast his vote at a polling station and attended an election viewing event which was streamed to his followers.
Sources have confirmed to the BBC that Flávio has already met with his brother, Eduardo, in Florida, though details of his exact travel route from Brazil are unclear.
It's also unclear who travelled with him or whether Flávio Bolsonaro intends to stay and live in the US.
Opinion polls had put him narrowly ahead of Lula and analysts pointed out that Bolsonaro's win in the first round of the election on 4 October, meant he was likely to take victory in the run-off.
But after an early lead in the count, he was overtaken by the veteran incumbent, who became the first presidential candidate to overturn a first round loss to win in the second round.
Lula won 51.79% of the vote, compared to Bolsonaro's 48.21%.
Despite trailing by 4.4 million votes, Bolsonaro has not conceded and has called for the election to be annulled.
He argues that he was put at a disadvantage because polling was extended by two hours on election day - even though the extension was requested by both his party and that of his rival.
He called the extension, which was ordered by a Supreme Court justice, a "dirty trick".
However the party he represented, the Liberal Party, has accepted the result, although it did say that the extension of voting "merits investigation".
Ayelén Oliva, Vinícius Mendes, Cecilia Barria Ricardo Senra and Ione Wells contributed to this report.

items.title: Neil Young again sues Trump campaign for playing Rockin' in the Free World at rally
paragraphs: Rock veteran Neil Young has filed a $10m lawsuit against a fundraising committee that supports US President Donald Trump, citing "unauthorised" use of his 1989 song Rockin' in the Free World.

The Canadian-American star alleges that the Trump 47 Committee infringed on his copyright when it played the song before Trump took the stage at a 12 October rally in Ohio. Playing the song amounts to an "unauthorised public performance", the lawsuit says.
The singer-songwriter sued the Trump re-election campaign in 2020 over its use of the same song and Devil's Sidewalk. Young said the parties settled the matter shortly thereafter.
The BBC has contacted the Republican National Committee for comment.
The White House referred the BBC to the Republican National Committee for comment.
Through his company Silver Fiddle Music, Young alleges that the song was played without a license or Young's permission at a political event in Youngstown, Ohio on 12 October.
In the US, music used at campaign rallies often requires a public performance licence for it to be played for an audience, even if a campaign has already purchased a legal copy of the recording.

According to US Congress, because sound recordings do not have a general public-performance right, permission is only needed from the musical-work copyright holders, which can be obtained directly from the copyright holders themselves or through performing rights organisations.

The five-page federal lawsuit says that Trump "was personally aware that a license would be required to play the Song at rallies," and that Young "has not, and would not, grant the required license". It also says the song has been played "numerous times at other rallies".

The Grammy Award winner, 80, who has strongly opposed Trump's politics, characterises the song as "a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten".
Young says that the song is "the opposite of everything that Donald J Trump stands for".
In 2020, Young sued Trump's re-election campaign for copyright infringement over the same song, as well as Devil's Sidewalk.
The new lawsuit claims that the campaign, at the time, "asserted no defence and immediately settled shortly after it was served", promising to never use the song without permission again.
Young posted about the lawsuit on his website on Tuesday, thanking Trump for coming to so many of his shows in the 1980s and 1990s, but stopped short of allowing him to play his music.
"I am sorry it came to this, but money and transactions are something you understand," he wrote.
Young, The Rolling Stones, Rihanna, Adele, REM and the estate of Prince have previously criticised the president for using their music at campaign events.

items.title: A bust-up between mathematicians is fuelling fears that AI could undermine science
paragraphs: A bank of white freezers hums away at a former watch factory in central London. Inside: dozens of small boxes with barcoded glass tubes, collectively containing one hundred billion genes. Just two boxes may hold 10 times more information than all the text on the internet, says Dr Oliver Vince, the facility's co-founder.

His firm, Basecamp Research, plans to collect as much DNA as possible to create an artificial intelligence that can speak the language of biology, in the same way that US and Chinese tech firms have hoovered up written material online to create Large Language Models (LLMs), the basis of current AI systems.
Vince, like many in business and academic research, believes AI will supercharge scientific research. But increasingly, it also comes with controversy.

Last month, OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, said it had solved one of maths' great unsolved problems, relating to the famous Navier–Stokes equations. The company said its AI agents had cracked it in 88 hours. The body that runs a prize for whoever can solve the problem said it had "apparently been settled", but that its review would take time.

But hours before the announcement, Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, went public with concerns. He formed an independent team with Levent Alpöge, a mathematician employed by day by the rival company Anthropic.

They had been working towards the same goal, and kept their drafts in OpenAI's coding tool, Codex. Buckmaster said that his co-researcher was tipped off that news of their progress had "reached" OpenAI, though he did not specify how. He asked whether his research, stored in Codex, could have fed into OpenAI's own work, though he stressed he was "not accusing anyone of anything".
One threat is to scientific journals, the guardians of scientific integrity, which are seen to be failing to deal with a tsunami of AI-generated distortions.
"Generative AI has basically disrupted the whole scientific process," says Dalmeet Singh Chawla, a science journalist who has spent a decade reporting on research misconduct.

He tells the BBC that publishers' integrity staff - the people who screen submissions for accuracy and reliability - will need to "drastically increase [in number and effort] if they're anywhere near the fight". He says: "Right now, it seems like they're not."

On the face of it, AI seems just the right tool to power scientific research. Scientists deal with huge amounts of information. Telescopes and particle accelerators, for example, collect billions of data points – too large for the brain to comprehend. AI can pick the scientific highlights from the surrounding humdrum.
The poster child of scientific AI is the UK-based firm Google DeepMind, which in 2020 solved one of biology's biggest problems: how proteins in living things fold into their precise shapes.

It may sound dull, but proteins are the tiny machines that make life work, and the shapes they fold into determine what they can do; from building cells and fighting infection to helping form the tissues and organs of the body.

Before AI, scientists had to conduct time-consuming experiments in the lab. Then, Google DeepMind developed an AI model called AlphaFold that accurately predicted 200 million protein folds in just one year.

The equivalent experimental work would have taken hundreds of millions of years in laboratories. The firm gave the results away for free to researchers. The head of DeepMind and the project's lead scientist were both awarded the Nobel Prize for Chemistry.
Dr Pushmeet Kohli, who leads DeepMind's science work, told me that AlphaFold could be seen as a "watershed moment".

items.title: 'Biggest night in club's history' as fearless Fleetwood stun Arsenal in EFL Cup
paragraphs: Given their league positions, form and pedigree, there could surely only have been one winner.

Fleetwood played Arsenal on Tuesday with an 84-place gulf between the teams and most home fans arriving in hope rather than expectation. But remarkably, it was the hosts who booked their place in the Carabao Cup quarter-final thanks to their penalty shootout win over the Gunners.

For the side known as the Cod Army, who won six promotions in 12 years in an impressive journey from non-league, this result will surely be remembered longest of all. Against the reigning Premier League champions, the club from a small seaside town in Lancashire created history in claiming one of the biggest cup upsets ever.
Aaron Loupalo-Bi gave the hosts the lead after 21 minutes but, after the break, Viktor Gyokeres pulled the visitors level.

And from there, they might have been expected to take charge, but Fleetwood remained resolute, prospering from a wasteful performance from Arsenal that included Max Dowman being sent off for kicking out after a robust challenge from Harrison Neal.

Fleetwood, who sit 18th in League Two having won just once in their past eight league games, dared to dream and took the game to penalties, with fans spilling on to the pitch after Conor Haughey's decisive spot-kick.

"The biggest night in the club's history in terms of opposition coming to town and we've managed to beat the champions," boss Matt Lawlor told Sky Sports in the aftermath of his side's stunning victory.

"I'm a big football fan and I watch National League all the way through to the Premier League, Championship. So for me it was a tough game to prepare for, but I'm just so glad that the lads have the feeling the way they are and took that performance in to make that town, the club, everyone proud."

Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, left-back Jake Batty added: "Our league form's not been as good as what we'd want it to be and for some reason [in] cup competitions everyone gets a bit of a fire in their belly. We just came up with some magical moments and obviously that's one to tell the grandkids, isn't it?
"We've struggled. We're not known as a big club in League Two. We get a few thousand fans each game, and just the buzz around the town, you could see the fans in the shootout and all game.
"That's what we encourage to bring on Saturday. That's what we want on Saturday.
"Why can't we replicate that and get 5,000 fans behind us every game and, and give us that momentum?"
Batty added that on reaching the quarter-finals for the first time since their arrival in the English Football League in 2012, Fleetwood should be "fearless" and hope for a home tie.
"It's unbelievable for the town and hopefully we can get someone else at home and do exactly the same thing," he said.
"I don't think we should be scared of any team."
On 20 April 2024, Fleetwood's relegation from League One was confirmed, capping off a miserable season for the club on the pitch.
That same day, Arsenal beat Wolves 2-0 at Molineux to go top of the Premier League. They would finish that campaign second, but won the title two years later.
Meanwhile, Fleetwood have held their heads above water in League Two - and the league is very much in mind for boss Lawlor, with his side facing Bristol Rovers on Saturday.
"It's really hard to address the players. I've just said to enjoy it and then we've got a league game on Saturday," he added.
"I didn't want to be the bearer of the reality, but we've got a game."
It was Haughey who ultimately struck the winning penalty to send the hosts through, yet it was goalkeeper Jay Lynch who tipped the shootout in their favour.

He pulled off superb saves during the match to deny Ben White and Martin Odegaard, then kept out Bruno Guimaraes' penalty, and was left hoarse in the aftermath of a stunning victory at a windy Highbury.
It was a victory which he likened to Grimsby's triumph over Manchester United in the competition last season.
"My voice has gone from organising the defence," Lynch told Sky Sports.
"We took heart from Grimsby beating Man United last year. We kind of compared it.
"It was a typical night in Fleetwood. We were expecting a storm, we knew the conditions would be horrible, so we thought it might go in our favour.
"It's amazing for the club, the town. Honestly it means everything to everyone."

items.title: King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summit
paragraphs: King Charles has confirmed he will discuss the legacy of slavery at a summit with Commonwealth leaders as he begins his Caribbean tour.
The king arrived in the Bahamas to a ceremonial welcome and attended a youth rally at Clifford Park, the site where the country officially gained its independence from British colonial rule in 1973.
His visit comes amid renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for the atrocities of transatlantic slavery and engage in reparations talks.
Charles’s nine-day tour, which includes a solo state visit to Guyana, will culminate in presiding over the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) hosted by Antigua and Barbuda.
In his speech in the Bahamas on Tuesday, Charles said: “Some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness.

“It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future.”
He said the Chogm leaders would discuss matters relating to the legacy of slavery next week in Antigua.
But a statement from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee said the king’s comments on Tuesday “fall short of what justice requires”.

“Our culture is not born out of darkness; our culture was born out of agency and out of the will to survive despite the horrors, trauma and degradation. Our culture is a testament to the power of the human spirit, not simply a reaction to the worst examples of it.
“We therefore do not need King Charles to tell us how outstanding our culture is … We need him to speak about his role in the darkness and how he plans to atone for it actively.

“The royal family and the British government were responsible for the darkness. His comments fall short of what justice requires – a full and formal apology – and they do not speak to the steps needed to remedy the wrongs committed in the name of the crown he wears.”

Dr Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, the committee’s chair, told the Guardian that while she appreciated the king’s attempt to “connect with Bahamian culture” in his speech his words felt “like hollow platitudes”.

She added: “I am very proud of my Bahamian people and the beautiful spirit and hospitality that they shared. My critique is not an attempt to rain on their parade. It is because of this pride that I feel we deserve so much more than what was offered.”
The chair of the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, Prof Hilary Beckles, said what the Caribbean was looking for was “proprietary justice, beginning with remorse”.

Beckles added that when speaking to Caribbean young people the king should “dig deep within his consciousness” and give to them “the empowerment that he would give to his own children” to survive in a rapidly changing world. Anything short of that would be to condone and minimise the legacy of harm and suffering that continues today, he said.
Charles is to travel to Guyana on Thursday where the president, Mohamed Irfaan Ali, recently called for the monarch to take the next step and offer to apologise.
The king follows the guidance of his ministers, and it is understood the government has not advised him to offer an apology or reparations, in keeping with established policy.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will join Charles in Antigua for the gathering of Commonwealth leaders.

Charles acknowledged the “appalling atrocity of slavery”, describing it as something “which forever stains our history, when he attended the ceremony marking Barbados’s historic transition to a republic in 2021.

A year later he described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to “deepen my own understanding of slavery’s enduring impact”, in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: “At the request of host governments, the king’s programme will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future that are having a transformative effect on the region, as it confronts the challenges of today.

“For his majesty, this tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past. This will therefore also be reflected in differing ways and words during the tour, as you would expect.”
Additional reporting by Press Association

items.title: 'An annoying buzz': The search for stealthier drones
paragraphs: Schmidt is one of a growing number of people living with the noise of drones dispatched by companies including Amazon and Walmart as they seek to speed up home deliveries.
Delivery drone services, not long ago a novelty, are becoming part of everyday life for many people in the US.

Among them, Amazon Prime Air is in the process of expanding deliveries to nearly 500 cities and towns, delivering items that fit into a space the size of a shoe box. It has also launched to customers in and around Darlington in the north of England.
Smaller drone delivery services are popping up too: in some US cities, customers can order flying treats from their local pizza joint or ice cream parlour.
Even in cities where noise is already a steady part of life, the sound of drones seems to irk in a particular way.
While the steady passing of traffic might blend into the background, the sudden whine of a drone's rotors can pierce the everyday hum.

The sound tends to be "particularly noticeable, even when overall sound levels are relatively low," says Antonio Torija Martinez, professor in acoustic engineering and psychoacoustics at the University of Salford.
Unlike planes, drones operate at low altitudes and may fly directly over residential areas.
"They can expose communities that have not previously experienced significant aircraft noise, and who may therefore be more sensitive to changes in their local soundscape," says Torija Martinez.

He points to research showing that people respond strongly to a noise when they consider the source to be "novel, intrusive or frequent". People who benefit from a drone delivery service, for example, may be less bothered by the noise.

However, complaints about the sound of drones are likely to grow, he warns: "At the moment we are seeing some of these problems localised in some areas, but… as the drone sector expands, more and more of these complaints will happen."

In the US, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulates commercial drones, but it has come under fire for allowing noisy drone delivery operations. The FAA says operators and local community leaders have primary responsibility for addressing any community concerns.
Might better technology muffle the irritating buzz?
One startup, Greenjets, set out to tackle both "noise level and the frequency of that noise," as Darren James, future technologies lead at the company, puts it.
The London-based business has designed a propulsion system it claims can reduce drone noise by at least two thirds.

While standard drones use spinning propellers that slice through open air, creating that high-pitched buzz, Greenjets encloses spinning blades inside a pod, to muffle the sound and direct the noise away from the ground.
Its system also quietens things down through slower rotor speed and by using materials that reduce vibration noise.
Making quieter drones isn't just about keeping the noise down for neighbours who are already sick of airborne deliveries.

Greenjets' low-noise tech has been used by police and harbour security teams in Germany. It has also helped conservationists in Africa, who are seeking to track poachers from above without being detected.
Battlefield drone operators also have good reason to keep the noise down, to avoid alerting the enemy of the approach of their unmanned vehicles.

"There are some efforts to reduce the sound of drones. The US Special Forces are interested, at an experimental stage," says Robert Tollast, a research fellow at Whitehall think tank The Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

But he stresses that drone speed, rather than stealthiness, tends to come first for larger drones used in the war between Russia and Ukraine. "Make it faster, not less quiet, seems to be the approach," says Tollast.
For Detroit-based entrepreneur, Greg Sharrow, it was the challenge of broadcasting a classical music performance back in 2012 that set him on the path to quieter drone design.
He needed to film a violinist from a tricky angle and a drone seemed the only solution – expect that it would be far too noisy.

As a starting point, "I knew that most of the noise from the drone was coming from the propeller, not the motor," he says. Specifically, it was the tips of the blades that he realised were creating the noise as they swiped through the air.
"I asked myself a very simple question, what would a tipless propeller look like and how would it function?"
The result was to create a propeller with twisted loop-shaped blades with no points.

It turned out it was easier to test his propeller in water than it was to repeatedly fly a drone, which led Sharrow to initially develop a less noisy boat propeller. Now, however, his company, Sharrow Engineering, is focusing on developing "ultra-quiet" drone rotors.
"We have validated that the technology works in drone applications and that it is dramatically quieter," says Sharrow.

Companies at the forefront of drone deliveries say they are also working to reduce the noise of their fleets. A spokesperson for Amazon says it has made "measurable sound improvements" to its drones and its latest designs use custom-designed propellers "that produce almost half the perceived sound of the prior generation, with a milder tone".

Drone maker Wing, which provides its vehicles for Walmart deliveries, says its propellers are designed to minimise noise. It also varies its flight paths to prevent repeated overflights over any single home or neighbourhood.

For Schmidt, fed up with the noise of drones, the only truly satisfactory solution would be to halt drone deliveries in her area. "I would like them to completely stop until they figure out how their services stop being a nuisance," she says.

items.title: Multiple sclerosis patient living in 'horrific pain' due to UK-wide drugs shortage
paragraphs: Jill Kenning experiences constant pain in her eye, which she compared to being "stabbed with a hot poker"
ByToni Connor and Luke SprouleBBC News NI
A woman with multiple sclerosis (MS) has said she is living with "horrific pain" after being unable to get a drug she uses to manage her condition.
Jill Kenning has used Nabilone for 17 of the 18 years since she was diagnosed with MS and said the drug had been vital for managing her pain and helping her live a normal life.
She said she had spent most of her time in bed since running out of the drug last Tuesday.

Northern Ireland's devolved health department said there was disruption to supplies of the drug across the UK, meaning Nabilone was out of stock with wholesalers and not expected to be available again until December.
A spokesperson said they would not say why there was disruption as the information was "commercially sensitive".
According to a tracker published by the industry reference guide MIMS, the average number of drugs in short supply in the UK has trended upward this year, external.
The number of drugs in short supply reached 157 this week, up from a low of 107 in January.
Kenning, from Coleraine in County Londonderry, was diagnosed with MS in 2008 after experiencing problems with her sight.
She subsequently developed numbness down the left side of her body and was treated by a neurologist.
After a severe relapse, which resulted in a four-week hospital stay, she was prescribed Nabilone which she said made a massive difference to her quality of life.
"It helps me basically that I can get out of bed in the morning," she said.
But she said that without the drug she experienced constant pain in her eye, which she compared to being "stabbed with a hot poker".
Earlier this year, pharmacists warned of medicine shortages in Northern Ireland
After contacting her health trust for her regular repeat prescription, she said she was told there were no supplies of Nabilone available.
She was told to contact her neurologist and has since been prescribed other medication.
Kenning said the alternatives had not been effective and that her health had declined to the point where she had to stay in hospital for several nights.
"I don't want to be here any more because the pain is so bad," she said.
"I have been living on painkillers... I can't sleep, I'm sick, I'm not eating."
Kenning said more should have been done to prepare patients for the disruption.
"How do I live my life? How do I cope with the pain?" she said.
"I'm not only fighting for me, I'm fighting for all the other patients that are on this drug."
Multiple sclerosis is a disease that affects nerves in the brain and spinal cord.
The nerves in these areas are surrounded by a protein called myelin, which helps signals from the brain get to the rest of the body.
The myelin becomes damaged in people with MS because the immune system mistakes it for something that shouldn't be there and attacks it.
This means signals from the brain struggle to get through properly.
Northern Ireland's Department of Health (DoH) said both licensed doses of Nabilone were out of stock from wholesalers across the UK.
It said the shortage began affecting 1mg capsules in July, with the 0.25mg strength becoming unavailable more recently.

The DoH said it was working with the UK's Department of Health and Social Care and health trusts to manage the disruption, and that guidance had been issued to healthcare professionals on alternative treatments, including unlicensed imports of Nabilone where available.
A spokesperson said the DoH recognised "that medicine supply disruptions can be concerning for patients and the healthcare professionals who care for them".

"If patients cannot access their prescribed medication or have concerns about an alternative, they should speak to their specialist healthcare teams for advice about their treatment options," the spokesperson said.
Are you affected by specific drug shortages? Share your experience.

items.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
paragraphs: Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.

Official data released in the last week, external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.
The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.
The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.
China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children.
The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.
At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.

No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.

The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.
"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.

The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.
China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy, which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.

The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.
The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.
But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.
Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.
Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.

Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.

The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.
The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.
Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.
It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

items.title: Trump shows off tanker with ‘1m barrels of oil’ and floats Venezuela as 51st state
paragraphs: Donald Trump suggested Venezuela would become the 51st state of the United States on Tuesday as the president showed off a tanker he claimed had “one million barrels of oil on it” from the country, nine months after deposing its president.
At a campaign rally in Corpus Christ, Texas, Trump touted a US oil deal with Venezuela, which the US attacked in January, capturing its long-serving leader Nicolás Maduro.
Trump claims the agreement – struck with the South American country’s interim government, which is backed by Trump’s administration – will cover “billions” of barrels of oil.
Venezuela “will become a prosperous country, and who knows? Maybe some day soon it’ll become a prosperous 51st state,” Trump said at the podium on Tuesday. “That’s possible.”
Venezuela is on a growing list of countries and territories Trump has spoken of acquiring, including Greenland, Canada and Mexico.

With tens of millions of Americans set to vote in next week’s midterm elections, Trump’s aggressive foreign policy – including his controversial war on Iran, and tariffs on goods from much of the world – have challenged his popularity, according to opinion polls, with his approval ratings falling to record lows.

But on Tuesday, the president sought to point to the Venezuela operation as an example of his success. US fuel prices, which surged after the start of the Iran war, piling pressure on Americans’ cost of living, “will soon come plummeting down”, he claimed in a social media post.

“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” he said at the rally, pointing out the ship off the Texan coast. “The oil provided is being provided to the United States at zero cost to the American taxpayer.”

Moments before Trump took the stage in Texas, he claimed on his Truth Social platform: “By unleashing Energy Dominance from Alaska, all the way down to Venezuela, I have made the Western Hemisphere the Energy Capital of the World.”

The deal has also drawn skepticism as critics complained that the Trump administration has not pushed a transition to democracy in Venezuela, where elections have not been held since Maduro was detained by US forces and taken to New York to face criminal charges after a raid on his Caracas residence.

The urgency of the oil agreement stems from Trump’s opting into the war with Iran in February. Gas prices have shot up nationwide after Iran closed the strait of Hormuz, a passageway for 20% of the world’s oil supplies.

items.title: Metropolis: more than four decades of street photography – in pictures
paragraphs: Metropolis: Street Photography 1985–2025 transitions from the tough, film-noir streets of 1980s New York, to the time surrounding the fall of the Berlin Wall, to the modern, colour-saturated, hard-shadowed geometry of contemporary Australian streets. Spanning classic monochrome grit and vivid colour abstraction, this remarkable collection examines how photographers have documented the relentless energy of our ever-changing cities. Ultimately, it is a celebration of the unscripted characters, strange encounters and the absurd comedy that unfolds when people share public space. On now until 17 November at The Photographic Gallery, Sydney Continue reading...

items.title: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
paragraphs: King Charles has arrived in the Bahamas for a nine-day tour of the Caribbean - the first time he has visited the region as monarch.
The King, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was given a ceremonial welcome at the airport before attending a youth rally.

Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during the visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.
Appearing at his first engagement, he told young people it is "only right" to "acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past".

Upon arriving on the island, he met island's Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour on the runway.
The King was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended the island's independence celebrations as Prince of Wales in 1973.
