The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University in the US.
The lyrics are critical of Israel's military actions in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack.
After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out.
He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza.
Sheeran said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group.
His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity with Macklemore, and fans to express frustration.
Sheeran then addressed the controversy during the start of a gig in Philadelphia.
He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue".
He described the 7 October 2023 attacks as "horrific" and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate".

items.title: Pentagon designates Confucius Institute in US as national security threat
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.
The Department of War has designated Chinese-funded Confucius Institutes on American university campuses as a national security threat.
China's Foreign Ministry responded Monday, saying it opposed what it called “smears and stigmatization” targeting the institutes.

In a video address Friday, Secretary of War Hegseth described Confucius Institutes as “Chinese government-backed propaganda cultural programs” that had infiltrated universities in nearly every U.S. state. He said Congress had banned the institutes several years ago, but they had returned in new forms under different names.

“It turns out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds of American students,” he said.

He said the Pentagon had added those organizations to its list of institutions threatening national security and had “systematically dismantled every single one of these organizations” over the past two months.
Hegseth did not identify a specific instance of intellectual property theft involving a Confucius Institute in his remarks.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a news conference Monday that China opposed what he described as “smears and stigmatization targeting Confucius Institutes.”“Educational exchanges and cooperation between China and the United States help deepen mutual understanding between the peoples of both countries. They are two-way, mutually and win-win, and should not be disrupted or undermined,” he said.
Days before Hegseth’s remarks, the Department of War announced October 19 that it had successfully completed initial research security audits at 30 universities across the United States.

The Pentagon said all 30 universities covered by its initial audits had addressed identified relationships with foreign entities on the National Defense Authorization Act’s Section 1286 list of entities of concern.

According to the Department of War, the audits resulted in more than 80 “termination-related actions.” Those included ending relationships with listed entities, as well as precautionary terminations involving entities not specifically on the list

items.title: Pakistan defends attacks on Afghanistan, denies civilian casualties
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

Pakistan’s government has defended its attacks on Afghanistan as an act of “self-defense” and rejected killing Afghan civilians. Pakistan’s Foreign Affairs Ministry, in a statement Monday posted on X, said that its attacks are “directed against terrorists and their logistical support based in Afghanistan,” and rejected the civilian casualties “attributed” to the attacks.

Pakistani forces and the Afghan Taliban have recently clashed along the border, and Pakistan also has carried out airstrikes in Afghanistan. The Afghan Taliban called Pakistan’s airstrikes in Afghanistan “an act of aggression and crime in violation of all accepted principles.”
The United Nations Mission in Afghanistan said in September that it had documented more than 1,100 civilian deaths and injuries from cross-border attacks in Afghanistan so far in 2026.
Pakistan accuses the Taliban of sheltering the militant group Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which has taken responsibility for attacks inside Pakistan.
The Afghan Taliban publicly deny harboring any militant group, but a U.N. report, released in August, said that the Taliban continue to support TTP.
A spokesperson for the U.S. State Department told VOA in an email statement in July that Pakistan has the “right to defend against terrorist attacks.”
“The Pakistani people have suffered greatly at the hands of terrorists,” the unnamed spokesperson said at the time.
The U.N. said that the Pakistani Taliban’s attacks inside Pakistan have increased.
Pakistan has said that the attacks inside Pakistan have resulted in more than 3,500 casualties so far in 2026.

Ismail Khan, an editor at Pakistan’s Dawn newspaper, told VOA that both sides blame each other, and relations between the two countries have deteriorated. “Borders are closed [between the two countries]. There is no trade and no negotiation is underway,” he said.
Khan added that some countries, including China, Turkey and Qatar, have tried to get Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban to resume negotiations, but those efforts have not yielded results.
“In the end, both countries have to negotiate and find a way out,” he said.
But Khan said the situation is likely to continue for now because both “Pakistan and Afghanistan are not ready to negotiate.”

items.title: Afghanistan sees drop in men’s university enrollment as women remain barred
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

University enrollment among men in Afghanistan in 2026 has fallen nearly one-third from levels before the Taliban’s takeover, while women’s enrollment has remained at zero for the third consecutive year.

A new U.N. report says enrollment at public and private universities in Afghanistan totaled approximately 208,000 students, all men, in 2026, down from about 430,000 students, including 124,000 women, in 2020.

“Women remain excluded from formal participation, male enrollment is substantially lower than in 2019, the academic workforce has shrunk, and private institutions face continuing financial pressure,” the report said.
The Taliban barred women from university education in December 2022 and from medical training institutes, which offer diplomas in nursing, midwifery and other health fields December 2024.
Since seizing power in 2021, the Taliban have placed sweeping restrictions on women’s rights and freedom.

Under the Taliban, women and girls are not allowed to get an education beyond 6th grade. They are barred from working with government and non-government organizations, going to parks, gyms, public baths, and beauty salons.
The group has issued more than 100 decrees that curb women’s and girls’ rights and freedoms, including their right to get an education.

Meanwhile, the Taliban have tightened their control over men’s higher education by imposing numerous restrictions, such as conducting new oral exams on religious topics, dress codes, removing hundreds of books and other learning materials, and discontinuing over a dozen subjects related to human rights, democracy, gender, governance and other social science fields, according to the U.N.
Farid, a university student in Kabul, told VOA that students have few incentives to pursue higher education.
“There are only a few opportunities for graduates. This makes people not be motivated to continue their studies,” said Farid, who did not want his full name disclosed for security reasons.
He added that most of the students also face financial problems, forcing them to discontinue their studies.
“The economic situation has worsened. Students are not even able to pay for commuting to the university daily,” he said.
Farid added that students are also worried about their job prospects after graduation.
Mohammad Asif Nang, former deputy minister for education in Afghanistan, told VOA that the future of higher education in Afghanistan is uncertain.
“For example, a young man loses hope of a better future when he cannot find himself in a system based on competition, merit and professional qualifications,” he said.
“These trends affect not only higher education itself but also the future supply of qualified professionals across Afghanistan’s education, health and wider service sector,” the U.N. report said.

items.title: Surprising things we have learnt from Anthropic's blockbuster share listing
paragraphs: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has become a key figure in the current AI era.
Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic just released the required paperwork ahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market.
The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by.
Anthropic also detailed some of the the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology.
Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing.
Every public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong.
Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole.

"Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.

It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies.
But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models".

One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology.
Anthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing.

The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance.
Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.
The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn billion for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even.

Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added.
Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment.
"As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added.
Despite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about.
At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day.
Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined.
Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants.
The leasing of data centres alone is costing the company $321.4bn so far this year.
Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth.
Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said.
Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.
A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10mn in the past year.
An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.
Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract".
The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue.

Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted.
Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year.
Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".
The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.
For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good.
"Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.
That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."
"We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission. "

Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice and making more efficient power grids and batteries.
Decades of scientific progress could be condensed into years, accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy.

Anthropic said AI could provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities.
"Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said.

items.title: Star Trek actor Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov, dies aged 90
paragraphs: Walter Koenig, who played the spirited Russian crewman Pavel Chekov in the original Star Trek TV series, has died aged 90.

The US actor was a mainstay on the show as the eager and earnest navigator of the Starship Enterprise, from season two in 1967 until it ended in 1969, later reprising his role in the six original cast movies from 1979 through to 1991.
In the mid-late 1990s, Koenig portrayed a very different character, the ruthless Psi Corps telepath Alfred Bester, in another sci-fi space series, Babylon 5.
His Star Trek co-star George Takei led the tributes, external on social media on Monday, writing: "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend."

Representatives for Koenig said in a statement given to the BBC: "Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world."
They confirmed he had died "of old age at home in North Hollywood" on Sunday night, "surrounded by his daughter and niece".
Koenig's Chekov added heart and humour to the adventures of the crew, led by William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk.
Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu, added: "Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course."
Born in Chicago and raised in Manhattan, Koenig was the son of Soviet Jewish immigrants whose family had lived in Lithuania.
He studied at the famous Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre in New York, alongside the likes of James Caan, Christopher Lloyd and Dabney Coleman.
His big break came as the capable young Chekov, who would often joke that everything was invented in Russia.
The character was introduced to appeal to younger audiences, with his Beatles/Monkees-style mop-top haircut.

But Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry's studio also publicised the role as a response to criticism in Pravda, the main newspaper of the Soviet Communist Party, about the lack of a Russian character. This was a claim Koenig later denied.

The American show, which aired during the Cold War and Space Race between the US and Soviet Union, imagined a future in which nations worked together to explore the galaxy, and Chekov's Russian heritage fitted that ideal.
Koenig once said that the character's purpose on the NBC show was to "set out the bones of the plot and let McCoy, Spock and Kirk fill it in", according to the Hollywood Reporter., external
He was arguably more integral to the movies, being nominated by the Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror for his work on The Wrath of Khan (1982) and The Voyage Home (1986).

Koenig's seventh Star Trek film appearance was a brief one in Generations (1994) - mainly a next generation film - and he later voiced President Anton Chekov in the modern series Star Trek: Picard in 2023.
He also wrote an episode of the original show's animated series spin-off, in 1973, titled The Infinite Vulcan.

items.title: Two UN-sanctioned North Korean tankers spotted repeatedly off China
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

Two North Korean oil tankers sanctioned by the United Nations Security Council have been repeatedly spotted off China’s coast, according to the public record by vessel-tracking Marine Traffic website, raising concerns that they may be circumventing sanctions while continuing to operate at sea.

The vessels, NAM SAN 8 and CHON MA SAN, have previously been suspected of engaging in prohibited ship-to-ship transfers, according to local media reports. A former member of a U.N. panel of experts on North Korea sanctions said their movements raise concerns that they could be using at-sea transfers to evade sanctions.

According to MarineTraffic, NAM SAN 8 was spotted on Oct. 24 near Xiaoqu Shan, in the Hangzhou Bay and Ningbo-Zhoushan area off eastern China. CHON MA SAN was also detected near Tang Yu on the same day, having moved south from its previously observed position.

Neil Watts, a former member of the U.N. Panel of Experts on North Korea sanctions, told VOA in an email on Oct. 23 that tracking images showed both vessels had spent time in territorial waters among the islands in the Ningbo-Zhoushan area, which he described as “an area synonymous with illicit ship-to-ship transfers of cargo from North Korean vessels.” Such transfers allow cargo to be moved between vessels at sea without entering a port, potentially making it more difficult to trace the cargo’s origin and destination.
Both the CHON MA SAN and NAM SAN 8 were added to the U.S.'s sanctions list in 2018 and are subject to port bans and asset freezes, Watts said.
“By not entering port and doing transfers at sea, they are using a ‘workaround’ tactic to create plausible deniability and thereby skirt around the consequences of their designation,” he said.
Both tankers are subject to an asset freeze and a ban on entering the ports of U.N. member states, including China.

Under Security Council Resolution 2397, member states must seize, inspect and impound vessels in their ports and may take similar measures against vessels in their territorial waters when there are reasonable grounds to believe they have been involved in prohibited activities or transported prohibited items. The U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) placed both ships on its Specially Designated Nationals List. That designation bars any American dealings with both craft.

“It is concerning that these tactics seemingly enable these vessels to escape the consequences of their designation and keep operating when the designations were intended to stop their illicit activities that are in violation of U.N. Security Council sanctions,” Watts added.
VOA requested comment from the Chinese government on the vessels’ activities and China’s enforcement of the relevant sanctions but received no response.

items.title: Political battle intensifies within Labour over Rosebank oil field
paragraphs: Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor John Healey visited the St Fergus Gas Terminal on Wednesday
Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra is wading into the political battle which is intensifying over the Rosebank oil field.
He is making a direct appeal to Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to approve the plans to allow production to begin in the North Atlantic.
Environmentalists have long campaigned against the proposals for drilling in the UK's largest untapped oil field, 80 miles north-west of Shetland.
That the debate is now taking place within the Labour Party is a sign of the UK's recent journey on the politics of energy.
When Labour came to power in 2024, it was with a manifesto pledge not to allow any new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea.
Rosebank is the UK's largest untapped oil field
A legal challenge thrust the future of the Jackdaw and Rosebank developments into the hands of the then-Energy Secretary, Ed Miliband.

At that point, senior offshore industry figures didn't hold out much hope of getting the go-ahead, given Miliband's deep commitment to renewable energy and his close political ties to Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
All that was before the outbreak of the war between the US, Israel and Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz and made an ongoing cost of living crisis even worse.
A new government under Andy Burnham entered 10 Downing Street with greater political freedom on the issue - and a new energy secretary to make the decisions.
Strictly speaking, Jackdaw and Rosebank aren't applications for new drilling licences, just the adjudication of existing ones.
But in political terms, the change of tone within Labour has been clear.
What had been an article of faith on energy has become something much more flexible.

It's a shift that's also plain to see within the SNP, with the Scottish government that once favoured a presumption against new oil and gas drilling now issuing a careful welcome to the Jackdaw announcement.
Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh announced that production could begin on the Jackdaw gas field.
She said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, the project would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.
Campaigners have called for the Rosebank plans to be rejected
Environmentalists said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
The UK government has always insisted that these decisions are part of a quasi-judicial process, judged on strict environmental criteria, not politics.
But as attention turns to Rosebank, the politics are seeping in.
Within hours of Jackdaw being granted approval, a briefing campaign began suggesting that Fahnbulleh was "minded" to reject Rosebank.
Now, in the week of the Budget, reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval.
Neither cabinet minister has given their view publicly, of course.
Fahnbulleh has insisted that the decision is "a regulatory process not a policy process," adding: "It sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because in the end only I can make it."
Even though she isn't looking for advice, the Scottish Labour leader is willing to offer it.
Marra is in Westminster meeting both Healey and Fahnbulleh in the run-up to the Budget on Wednesday.
Marra believes that on jobs and investment, the case for Rosebank is clear.
Michael Marra will be meeting both the chancellor and the energy secretary
"I supported Jackdaw and Rosebank because I think they're really crucial for the Scottish economy, for employment, and for the public finances as well," he told me.
"We need to make sure that we're a country that people feel they can invest in.
"You've seen what's happened with Jackdaw in recent days - a real boost to the morale and the investment climate in the north east of Scotland."
He's also arguing for increased levies on banks in the Budget, to contribute towards the cost of help on the cost of living.
That second request looks set to be granted - which is likely why Marra feels able to make it publicly.
On Rosebank, we still can't say for sure how things will go.
But the fact this debate is even being had is itself a symbol of our new energy reality.

items.title: Paralelo Transversal organises Chilean house under cantilever roof
paragraphs: Chilean studio Paralelo Transversal has designed a rectangular house with a large hip roof and a terrace that cantilevers over a ravine in Puerto Varas, Chile.
Completed in 2025 on a 1.2-acre site near Lago Llanquihue, the 155-square-metre house, known as Casa Ensenada, was oriented around its roof.
“In southern Chile, rain is not an exception but part of everyday life, so we wanted the roof to become more than a protective element,” architect Sebastián Silva of Paralelo Transversal told Dezeen.
“It creates a place beneath the rain, extending daily life beyond the enclosed rooms while bringing the different parts of the project together under one continuous gesture.”
The roof serves as the organising element for the program, circulation, relationship to the landscape and the home’s structure.
“Its section thickens toward the center while remaining remarkably thin at its perimeter,” Silva said.

“This allows it to be perceived as a light, continuous sheet while providing the structural depth required for long-span trusses capable of resisting both Chile’s seismic conditions and the strong winds of Patagonia.”

The house sits on a sloped site with a stream. Residents and visitors approach along the stream before the access ramp turns towards the house, where they enter at the junction of public and private zones.
The narrower side of the plan contains a large, open kitchen, dining and living room that bleeds onto the cantilevered terrace.

Oriented toward the northeast to capture winter sunlight, the house opens its living spaces to the landscape – the valley of Vicente Pérez Rosales National Park on one side and Calbuco Volcano on the other – through floor-to-ceiling windows with thin black frames.
The other side of the house widens to hold three suites. On either side of the house, the perimeter wall pushes under the roof canopy to form a covered bench and a planted garden.
The warm, contemporary material palette continues across the exterior and interior with exposed concrete slabs, large spans of glazing, tongue-and-groove timber and standing-seam metal roofing.

The concealed joints allowed the roof to be precise while reducing the visual impact of construction tolerances. The team collaborated closely with engineers and local builders to achieve its long spans and thin edge.
“Looking back, we believe the project fulfilled its original ambition of integrating architecture and landscape without compromising comfort, construction logic or budget,” Silva said.
“More importantly, it reinforced our belief that a project becomes stronger when one clear architectural idea is capable of organizing structure, climate, materiality and space simultaneously.”
Previously, Paralelo Transversal created a sail-like skylight that brought sun, shadows and air into a home on the outskirts of Santiago.
Other homes recently completed in Chile include a mass timber forest hideaway by Iragüen Viñuela Arquitectos and a seaside home with stacked terraces by Croxatto and Opazo Architects.

items.title: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
paragraphs: Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.
The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.
Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.
The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.
Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".
Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.
Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.
Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.
Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.

As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".
"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.
Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".
Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.
Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.

It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.

However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields.
"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.
Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.
The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.

items.title: LS Lowry review – matchstick men, or the broken denizens of a smog-filled hellscape?
paragraphs: While people queue at the British Museum to see the Battle of Hastings, this excellent survey of LS Lowry at the MK Gallery in Milton Keynes takes you back to another, maybe more decisive part of our past – the age when Britain was the most industrialised society on Earth. Laurence Lowry was born in 1887 and worked for 41 years as a rent collector, a job that took him all over his native Greater Manchester observing its people and places. He had the city’s grime and grind in his soul. The MK wants to show him as a fully rounded artist, to uncover the Lowry with a song in his heart, but it’s the misery of his urban hell that holds and harrows you.

In his 1930 painting Coming from the Mill it’s the end of the shift and scores of people emerge from a factory’s bleak yellow gatehouse as if leaving prison. Their daily captivity has left them broken and exhausted and the little abstracted figures hunch forwards as they walk without pausing to laugh or chat, going to their separate homes, each one withdrawn, wretched. They are not the painting’s protagonists – they are passive victims. The architecture of industry dominates the picture as it rules their lives. How can any of these little people, dwarfed by the mill that eats their time and energy, attain individuality? No wonder they all look the same except for minor variations in their drab clothes. They’ve been reduced by the Industrial Revolution to matchstick people.

Lowry is the Franz Kafka of industrial Britain. He is not a naive artist who painted crudely because that’s the best he could do. Nor is he a patient social realist laying bare the injustices of capitalism – although Friedrich Engels would surely have recognised his Manchester. He is a modern expressionist who finds his inner melancholy reflected in the industrial sublime. He drinks in its despair, feasts on its poetry of alienation. As you journey through Lowry’s North, you sink ever further into his personal slough of despond.

Slough of Despond would make a good alternative title for his 1924 drawing The River Irwell at the Adelphi. Heaps of mud and ash choke the slow-moving river that runs through Salford, its shores lined with decaying sheds and slums against a smoggy, chimney-lined sky. It’s Lowry at his purest as he depicts the stunning, crushing presence of the city itself. He draws and paints the black, gnarled spires of urban churches with as much relish as those monstrous mills. In the second world war he was a fire-watcher with a privileged view of the blitz: a drawing of freshly bombed buildings in Piccadilly, Manchester shows husks of charred brick still wreathed in smoke.

This show digs out other, less well known dimensions to his talent. But his paintings of the Lake District are even more chilling than his cities. Lake Landscape, painted in 1950, is a vista of low curving hills divided by silvery still water, receding in abstract, musical pulses of sadness. No people or animals inhabit this eerie world. When he paints people close up it’s even more disturbing: a young man with staring eyes, a father and sons who all seem equally desperate. He lightens up to paint his ideal woman with a simplified doll-like face apparently intended as his tribute to Pre-Raphaelite red-lipped beauties but the result is weirdly robotic. Her face is on the exhibition merchandise, perhaps because Halloween is coming.

The most bizarre painting, however, is his 1963 work In a Park. At first glance it’s another city crowd scene until you realise everyone in this fenced enclosure has something different about them. A one-eyed face screams while people walk around the white-earthed, empty space with spinal deformities, facial palsies, amputated limbs. The catalogue gets itself in knots – is Lowry mocking the disabled or questioning how we define disability?
But this painting is not about disability in a political sense at all. It uses it as an image of humanity in general: all people are broken and alone, misshapen in Lowry’s hopeless universe.

Lowry is a tricky customer. If it is pure snobbery to look down on him for being popular it is also patronising to see this troubled artist as a warmly sentimental nostalgist of the north. He is a painter of modern life in the age when that meant huge crowds staggering home in the shadow of smoking chimneys in cities blackened by carbon. At his best, Lowry is a great modern artist. His 1919 painting Pit Tragedy shows working-class people waiting for the worst news. They are statuesque, tragically posed in the grey dusty light. A woman turns towards us, her head veiled. Her pain is lost in the past but lives on here, observed and recorded by Lowry, visionary of the industrial age.
LS Lowry: The Theatre of Life is at MK Gallery, Milton Keynes until 28 February

items.title: Commuters appalled by accidental optical illusion ad
paragraphs: TFL recently caused a stir when commuters spotted a public safety ad that appeared to depict a woman in a hijab with the tagline "Are they trying to hide something?" The controversial design was met with a mixture of confusion and outrage, forcing TFL to respond.

While the best adverts often spark conversation, TFL's controversial ad has ignited the wrong kind of public engagement. With its unintentionally ambiguous design, the ad demonstrates why the Corporate Memphis art style might not be the best choice for PSA ads.
Disgusting insinuation in this campaign. Absolutely appalling @MayorofLondon @TfL @ACT https://t.co/Bdl1PdDbzcOctober 25, 2026

The design in question is supposed to feature a man looking over his shoulder, but thanks to the featureless style of Corporate Memphis, some commuters saw otherwise. "Disgusting insinuation in this campaign. Absolutely appalling," one X user wrote. "Suspicion, paranoia and ethnically ambiguous abstract art - 1984 is here in full force," another added, while another joked, "This is a wonderful Rorschach test."
It took me ages to see the balding man. TfL accidentally created its own version of this image. https://t.co/KvsE6zUFwCOctober 25, 2026

Since the ad was clearly misinterpreted by many, TFL was forced to respond, informing the OP that the poster was being investigated. It later claimed the poster had been "installed without TFL's permission."

"Our media partner, our teams and contractors have been instructed to inspect trains and remove any unauthorised posters that are found on our network. The incident has been reported to [British Transport Police] as flyposting is an illegal activity," TFL explained in a now deleted X post.

TFL are now claiming the 'Are they hiding something?' poster is unauthorised flyposting... but official news sources covered these posters going up, including variants of that exact poster. TFL say they have reported it to British Transport Police, but... it looks like BTP themselves ran the campaign.October 26, 2026

While the origin of the ad remains unclear, the controversy points to a wider issue with ad campaigns. Creating the right language and visual tone is key to a successful campaign, and this ad (whether fake or not) completely missed the mark. Paranoia-inducing copy and ambiguous design created a recipe for disaster, and now TFL have to deal with the fallout.
For more ad controversy, take a look at why 2026 is the year of the cancelled ad, or check out why Sydney Sweeney's racy ad sparked a Gen Z culture war.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: 'Safety first' as wedding guests stranded on island after Storm Boelo
paragraphs: Guests attending a wedding on Lower Lough Erne in a County Fermanagh island ended up stranded after the ferry took on water during Storm Boelo.
At the weekend, the storm saw gusts of wind reach almost 80mph in some areas and led to flights and ferries being cancelled.

Guest Shéa Clarke, who was on Lusty Beg island said that, despite the weather spirits were high, the staff were "great and obviously it's too dangerous to cross and the boat can't cross so safety comes first".
"You could see the waves were rough and the wind was going," he said.
"Some people have slept in cars, some people have slept on sofas there's been eight people in one room sleeping on the floor.
"But the spirit has been good the craic is 90," adding as "long as we don't run out of Guinness or chips".
A boat has since been taking guests off the island.
A Met Office yellow warning for strong winds, mainly along the Antrim and Down coasts, lasts from 18:00 GMT on Monday until 03:00 Tuesday.
Olivia Millar, a cabin crew member based in London, was also a guest at the wedding and said the plan was to be in South Africa on Monday night.
"It hasn't felt like real life but everyone's been amazing and we've just made the most of it.
"We've drunk to pass the time and had a really good barbecue yesterday".
Staff at Lusty Beg Island Resort & Spa took care of guests who couldn't get off the island.
Michael Cadden, managing director at hotel, said they are "delighted at how staff and customers have dealt with this".
"The ferocity and the longevity of this storm was unlike anything we've experienced on the island before.
"This was a crisis, but we've now arranged to transport and are getting all our staff and customers safely home".
Kacper Dymarczyk, a bartender, was locked down with the guests and had to work through the storm.
"It was great craic, seeing other people drinking" he said as he laughed.
Dymarczyk added that there was "no concern" of running out of anything as they are "well stocked at all times".

Meanwhile in the Republic of Ireland, an ESB spokesperson said there are "a number of homes, farms and businesses still without electricity" on Monday morning, and that teams are working to restore the power to all properties.
About 5,000 homes, farms and businesses were still without electricity on Sunday evening in the Republic of Ireland.
In the Republic of Ireland, wind and rain warnings have also been issued for most counties along the south and west coasts on Monday evening.
Much improved weather conditions are expected on Wednesday with calmer and sunnier weather in the forecast.
Although some faults occurred overnight in Northern Ireland, and are showing on NIE's Powercheck tool, external, they are not believed to be storm related.
NIE said around 12,500 properties were without power at one stage after Storm Boelo.

items.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
paragraphs: Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

items.title: Part of Antarctica named after former BBC science correspondent
paragraphs: The naming of geographical features in Antarctica follows strict rules.

The Amos Channel was recommended by the UK Antarctic Place Names Committee, which looks after names for sites within the British Antarctic Territory, as well as South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.
Athena Dinar, from the British Antarctic Survey, said: "Jon's passion for Antarctica and engaging journalism offers something for every reader, viewer or listener.
"The naming of an Antarctic place in his honour is a fitting recognition of his outstanding contribution to the promotion of Antarctic research."

Amos joined the BBC in 1986 as a local radio reporter in Cambridge. He was part of the team that launched the BBC News website in 1997, and ran the online science desk for many years. He later worked as a BBC science correspondent across TV, radio and online, before leaving the organisation in 2024.

"Jon consistently highlighted the importance of Antarctic research, explaining not only what science is being done there, but why it matters for society, climate understanding and the global environment," said Fiona Fox, from the Science Media Centre.

items.title: AI giant Anthropic files for an IPO that could break records
paragraphs: Anthropic is taking a big step toward a blockbuster stock listing that would rank among the biggest IPOs ever. Patrick Sison/AP Photo hide caption

The artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, maker of the hugely popular Claude AI models, has taken a major step toward holding an initial public offering that analysts expect to be one of the biggest ever.
Anthropic filed final paperwork with regulators on Monday for an IPO under the ticker symbol ANT that reports have said could value the company at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.

That would put it in league with Elon Musk's rocketry and AI company SpaceX, which was valued at around $1.8 trillion when it listed in June. Anthropic's listing prospectus did not say how many shares the company will offer or at what price range.

The filing of a public version of a registration statement called a Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission is a major milestone in Anthropic's meteoric rise. It was launched just five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI researchers, led by Dario Amodei, who were concerned that that company, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.

Anthropic has since become a juggernaut, and OpenAI's biggest competitor, with some of the most widely used AI models on the market. But the company has faced controversy, including a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used and questions about Amodei's dire warnings on AI risks.

Still, the prospectus highlighted Anthropic's bullishness about the technology. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.

In its prospectus, Anthropic highlighted breakneck growth — in revenue, income and losses. The company said its revenue in the first half of the year rose 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, vs. a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
Anthropic has yet to turn an annual profit, and said it booked a loss of nearly $81 billion in the January to June period, up from $13 billion during the same six months last year.

In a statement emailed to NPR, Raj Joshi, senior vice president in the corporate finance group of Moody's, the ratings agency, called Anthropic's swing in adjusted operating income from negative to positive territory "a strong positive for the AI ecosystem."
U.S. stock indexes were up on Monday after Anthropic's early-morning announcement.

The filing comes at a volatile time in the stock market for AI-related companies, as investors waver between exuberance about the positive effects AI could have on the economy and concern about safety and the tsunami of investment in the technology.

The IPO, which could happen as soon as November, will be one of the most eagerly anticipated public share offerings in years. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, is also planning an IPO, but those plans are temporarily on ice, with Altman ruling out a listing this year as "ill-advised" in the face of swirling AI safety concerns.

"Going public has a lot of advantages. It brings in capital for growth. It makes it easier for you to raise additional capital elsewhere. And it makes it possible for your existing investors to cash out," said Jim Angel, an associate professor and markets specialist at Georgetown University.

But, he added, "there's concern that we may be in an AI bubble. We're in a very dynamic industry, to say the least, and we can expect a lot of volatility in the markets." Still, Angel said, it makes sense for Anthropic to "strike while the iron is hot" and list shares now to get as high a valuation as possible.

With SpaceX already trading publicly, Anthropic's IPO could test investor appetite for AI businesses at a time when markets are jittery about whether they can be profitable enough to justify the mind-boggling sums of money being invested in AI. SpaceX's shares soared briefly after the listing, but have come back down to around $150, where they started trading.
In May, at its last private fundraising round, Anthropic had a post-money valuation of $965 billion.

The balancing act for companies trying to ride the AI wave is real. The data center and infrastructure provider CoreWeave saw its share price plummet this month when investors got nervous about its ability to finance its expansion plans and its bond yields leaped. Other major players, including Intel, Meta and Nvidia, have also been buffeted by concerns and watched their share prices slide in recent weeks.

Debt financing has been a growing concern as AI-related companies scramble to raise money to meet demand at a time when interest rates are poised to keep rising as the Federal Reserve tries to douse stubborn inflation.

The S-1 filing that tees up the IPO flagged what Anthropic sees as the risks from AI — and to its business model. Among them are the risk that its AI models could develop faster than the company can keep them safe, or that they could be used to cause harm — or take harmful actions on their own. It also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash for the company's views on policy and regulation.

Amodei himself has issued some of the AI world's sharpest warnings about the possibility of AI spiraling out of control and causing harm, and urged AI companies to "pace the frontier," or to slow the development of their most capable models.

Anthropic has also clashed with the Pentagon this year over how the military can use its models. Amodei has drawn a line in the sand when it comes to using Anthropic's AI for autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans.

In response, the Pentagon blacklisted Anthropic and designated it a "supply chain risk" — a label previously reserved for entities affiliated with U.S. adversaries. Anthropic has sued the Pentagon in two federal district courts. Those legal battles remain ongoing.
Editor's note: This story was updated to add additional information from Anthropic's prospectus. Oct. 26, 2026

items.title: The Simpsons' brilliant parody of The Nightmare Before Christmas is proof that handmade creativity is on the rise
paragraphs: Over the last couple of years, I've worried that AI will take over animation, and that everything will end up looking slick and perfect… but really boring. This weekend, though, has eased my fears.

On Friday, Laika’s Wildwood, the studio’s sixth feature, opened in cinemas worldwide. I've already written about how its focus on stop-motion is what we all need in the AI era. So it's fantastic news that the movie seems to be doing well at the box office so far.

Shortly after that, we got The Simpsons’ Treehouse of Horror XXXVII opener: a stop-motion homage to The Nightmare Before Christmas. Bart is Jack Skellington, Marge is Sally, Homer is the two-faced Mayor, Santa’s Little Helper is Zero, and Ned Flanders is a bug-stuffed Oogie Boogie. Together, they belt out a parody version of This Is Halloween, replaced by the words "Simpsons Halloween".
The Simpsons | Nightmare Before Christmas Treehouse of Horror XXXVII by Stoopid Buddy Stoodios - YouTube

Since 1990, the Halloween specials have sat deliciously outside the show’s continuity. Characters die gruesome deaths, Springfield gets destroyed, but the following week everything's back to normal. In the new opener, Lisa (dressed as a witch) even spells it out in song: "Halloween episodes are not canon". And brilliantly, that freedom extends to the animation style itself.

Thematically, this sequence and Laika's Wildwood have almost nothing in common. But what matters is that both were made the slow, handmade way: with puppets, physical sets, and people moving them frame by frame. That's truly a lovely thing to see.

The Simpsons sequence came from Burbank’s Stoopid Buddy Stoodios, best known for Robot Chicken, which uses retro toys, action figures and dolls in stop-motion animation to deliver pop-culture parodies.

The studio could have used 3D printing. It chose not to. Co-founder John Harvatine IV told Animation World Network. “We kind of just did old school the whole way, from sculpting by hand." Similarly, sculptor Jim McKenzie told Entertainment Weekly: “I think in a time of AI, to be involved with something that’s truly handmade, it’s very special these days." Hear, hear.

It’s fitting that The Simpsons chose Nightmare as its Halloween tribute. When director Henry Selick’s chaotic classic arrived in 1993, it proved that a stop-motion feature could be a mainstream hit, and set him on the path to Coraline, the film that launched Laika.
The Simpsons - Nightmare Before Christmas - At Stoopid Buddy Stoodios - Behind The Scenes - YouTube

Back then, stop-motion was seen as very old hat, a thing of the past. Three decades later, it feels like a refreshing antidote to AI and overly slick CG, and this Simpsons opener plays right into that idea.
These gruesome puppet caricatures might only be on screen for half a minute, but they’re part of a much bigger fightback for handmade animation and creativity in general. Two enthusiastic thumbs up.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: To buy or to rent? – level 1
paragraphs: Twin sisters Morgan and Lisa move into the same kind of house. Morgan buys her home. Lisa rents hers.

Morgan must pay a lot of money in the beginning. She repairs the house when things break. After 30 years, Morgan pays off her home loan, and her house becomes worth a lot of money. She buys the house for 400,000 dollars. After 30 years, she can sell it for 1.3 million. Lisa pays rent every month. She does not pay for repairs. She saves money. She has a retirement account. After 30 years, she pays 900,000 dollars for rent. But she has 500,000 in her retirement account.
In the end, Morgan makes more money by buying. But Lisa is free to move. She can spend on hobbies, not a house.

Difficult words: twin sister (a girl who is born at the same time to the same mother as another child), rent (the money which you pay when you live in someone’s house or flat), retirement account (an account where you save money for the time after finishing work).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman
paragraphs: Prosecutors in Japan have filed formal charges against a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media.

Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcaster NHK reported.

Ballard had initially been arrested in Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges.

NHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings.
Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station, Japanese media reported.

While being questioned by police, Ballard denied having a hand in Yagi’s killing, saying, “I don’t know anything about it,” NHK reported. But during subsequent questioning Ballard was alleged to have “made statements that partially hinted at his involvement”, the broadcaster reported.
A statement reported by NHK and reported to Yagi’s family on Sunday expressed a hope that Ballard “will confront what he has done and make amends commensurate with what he has done”.
“She lost her life at the young age of 39,” the statement from Yagi’s family added. “She … wanted to live much, much longer.”

Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban for US military members stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based.
Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies.
A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman.
US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61.
The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972.
There were 80 such arrests in 2024, constituting a 20-year high.

After Ballard’s arrest, Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, said: “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.”

items.title: Sunlight at night: US startup’s demonstration of lighting Earth from space draws criticism
paragraphs: Locals in a rural area of California were recently startled to see dazzlingly bright light shining down from nearby mountains at night, illuminating a swathe of the desert below.
Unbeknown to them, the strange nocturnal illumination was the latest step in a company’s plan to erect thousands of giant mirrors in space to reflect sunlight on to the Earth during night-time.

The night-time light demonstration, near the town of Lone Pine in the Sierra Nevada region, was conducted by a US startup called Reflect Orbital, which has an almost sci-fi aim to launch 50,000 satellites into space in the next decade to illuminate parts of the world at night.

In July, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved Reflect Orbital’s proposal to launch an initial demonstration satellite next year, which will orbit the Earth and, via a 59ft-diameter mirror, reflect sunlight in 3-mile-wide beams in strengths from moonlight up to the brightness of the sun at noon.

The demonstration in California, undertaken earlier this month, showcased what this would look like on the ground, to the bewilderment of locals, one of whom called the lights “blinding”. Large mobile lights were erected near Mount Whitney, with Reflect Orbital comparing the radiance to that of a full moon.

This provided, the company said, a realistic simulation of one of the benefits of this technology: to help search-and-rescue teams and other emergency responders at night. Other planned uses include bathing crops in sunlight, replacing broken streetlights and even providing solar power for military operations, all summoned by the tap of a button on an app.

“Search-and-rescue teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who would use our technology,” said a spokesperson for Reflect Orbital, which partnered with a local search-and-rescue team for the demonstration.
“We’ll keep working closely with local communities and authorities wherever we operate, and are excited to show how this technology can help save lives.”

A coalition of environmentalists and astronomers are far less excited about Reflect Orbital’s ambitions, however. These groups have criticized the company and the FCC for threatening a harmful change to the separation of night and day that will affect everything from people’s sleep to wildlife and the ability to see the stars from Earth.

“This is an idiotic project,” said Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney with Earthjustice, an environmental group. “There are a huge number of unresolved questions and significant potential impacts. Literally all of life on Earth evolved based on the rhythm of day and night and there is a ton of data showing that messing with this is not a good idea.”

“There needs to be some sort of discussion and analysis before we grant these people the right to fundamentally alter the night sky,” he added. “The proposal for 50,000 of these satellite mirrors is crazy and would really end the night sky as we know it.”

In August, four groups represented by Earthjustice asked the FCC to reconsider its approval, citing concerns that opening up the skies to mirrored satellites, which would ascend to about 400 miles (645km) above the Earth’s surface before reflecting light back, would cause a litany of problems.
Animals such as birds, insects and mammals rely on the reliable change between day and night to feed, shelter and mate, with any change to this being potentially disastrous for some species.

Astronomers, meanwhile, have complained that this night-time glare would worsen existing light pollution and spur an overall rush to add more satellites to orbit – Elon Musk’s SpaceX plans to place 1 million celestial datacenters around Earth – that will obscure the stars and cause more space debris that could descend as pollution back to our world.

There are also concerns that the scrambling of night and day will harm people’s health by disrupting their circadian rhythms as they sleep. Looking directly at the unusual glaring sunlight at night would also, much like doing so during a solar eclipse, harm people’s eyes.

Reflect Orbital has said its technology will actually aid the environment by boosting the energy output of solar panels when sunlight is pointed at them during night-time, thereby reducing reliance on fossil fuels.

But some climate scientists have warned against meddling with the amount of sun’s energy reaching Earth. Proposals for solar geoengineering, in which particles are sprayed into the atmosphere to deflect sunlight away from Earth instead of toward it, have also prompted fierce opposition.

“Global warming is happening because the Earth has a radiative imbalance due to the massive amounts of greenhouse gases we’ve dumped into the atmosphere,” said David Ho, a climate scientist at the University of Hawaii.

“Some people are promoting the already unhinged idea of installing space mirrors facing away from the Earth to reflect the sun’s energy in order to decrease global warming. Imagine wanting to turn those mirrors around so that the Earth gets hotter.”

Reflect Orbital said it has had “substantive discussions” with scientists and astronomers on the use of its technology so that areas such as astronomical sites, national parks and other wildlife-rich areas are avoided.

“We welcome oversight and want to play a role in shaping it,” a spokesperson said. “We believe it is our responsibility to work alongside governments, scientists and regulators rather than ahead of them.”

items.title: Don’t judge me if I 3D print my own Wicker husband
paragraphs: After watching the bonkers trailer for the raunchy fantasy romance Wicker, I found myself getting slightly jealous – I wish I had my own Wicker husband. Well, thanks to good ol' 3D printers, my prayers have been answered.

As part of Regal Movies' new popcorn bucket promo, you can now 3D-print your own Wicker husband (well, at least a part of him). Is it a bit cheeky getting moviegoers to print their own popcorn buckets? Yes. Is it a bit stingy that the deal only got you a small popcorn? Absolutely. Do I still want a 3D-printed version of Alexander Skarsgård's rippling Wicker bod? Definitely.
Print Your Own Wicker Husband - Regal Prop Shop - YouTube

Straight from Regal's Prop Shop, the 3D-printed Wicker popcorn bucket was created using 3D scans of Skarsgård's costume (note the design is just the torso, so get your mind out of the gutter). Those brave enough to bring their freshly printed Wicker husband to the movie theatre received a free small popcorn for their efforts.

Unsurprisingly, the design is wonderfully detailed and, popcorn novelty aside, a playful prop for fans. The print files are entirely free, so your Wicker man is well within reach, provided you have your own setup (or a kind, unquestioning friend who will print it for you).
For more creative inspiration, check out these 3D printing essentials or take a look at our guide to the fastest way to get comfortable with 3D software

items.title: This might be why Apple iPhone Duo screens are cracking in exactly the same place
paragraphs: Apple's folding iPhone has, by all accounts, got off to a cracking start. Pre-orders quickly sold out, with delivery dates now extending well into 2027. It seems that after a string of somewhat disappointing launches such as the iPhone Air and Vision Pro, Apple has a bonafide hit on its hands. But as always happens in the first few days of a brand new product launch, a few snags are coming into focus.

One of the more curious issues facing some iPhone Duo units is the screen cracking in one very specific location. This involves a thin crack down the centre hinge, and a line of stuck bright white pixels across the right side of the display. The result has aready led to some amusing wallpaper designs making light of the issue.

But why are multiple Duo models breaking in the same way? Well, now that teardowns of the device have begun, we might have an answer. iFixit has revealed an area of concentrated components around the hinge, with a different shape to the rest of the hinge, which could be causing excess stress on the screen.

"To see where the stresses build up from folding, we built a 3D hinge model from teardown footage, patents, and CT scans, then compared it with the reported damage locations," reports iFixit. "The breaks cluster near the transition from the gap for the crossing flex cable to the central hinge support. The damage we’re seeing in photos isn’t right where the display cable passes through the hinge, but slightly lower, at a point where several edges meet and change how the thin display is supported as it bends... The screen’s curved fold comes down onto it, creating a small stress hotspot near the reported break location."

Looks like @iFixit has identified the part of the hinge on the iPhone Duo that may be causing the screen cracking and breaking issues. clip: iFixit (@ifixit) https://t.co/DfvPo5U3z5 https://t.co/MBMvatAnXjOctober 26, 2026

While it's too early to tell the scale of the problem, it seems at least a few units from this early batch of iPhone Duos might feature a subtle design flaw. Right now, early adopters are likely stress testing the product more than the average user, and the fault could be limited to a handful of units, leading to an outsized impression of the issue. If anything, it shows just how much more intricate the design of these foldable needs to be – and that not even Apple is necessarily immune to the difficulties of creating a durable device that can happily fold in half.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: Stone-covered roof provides "absolute camouflage" for Gamaya Farms eco-resort in India
paragraphs: Architecture studio Biome Environmental Solutions has used a hill-like roof covered in local stone and walls of compressed earth bricks to conceal this eco-resort within its site in India.
Named Gamaya Farms, the resort is located in the town of Vikarabad, near Hyderabad and has a total built area of 854 square metres.
It comprises a series of individual guesthouses and farm plots organised around a shared amenities block at its centre.

Biome Environmental Solutions designed each building to offer a different spatial experience of the surrounding landscape, from the hill-like vaulted roof of the central pavilion to a mixture of elevated and subterranean guesthouses.
“Gamaya Farms redefines architectural iconism not through bold geometry, but through absolute camouflage and tectonic erasure,” director Anurag Tamhankar told Dezeen.
“Rather than treating the program as a monolithic footprint, the master plan deconstructs the traditional resort layout into distinct, site-specific architectural typologies,” he added.

“Taking cues from the surrounding hills and forest to create an intervention that transitions out of the ground, the design disperses the program across decentralised pockets of the land, offering distinct sensory experiences.”

The curved, single-storey pavilion at the centre of Gamaya Farms contains the main entrance and reception at its western end. This leads into a large multi-purpose hall and dining room, as well as utility areas and bathrooms.

Large, circular windows set in exposed earth-block walls fill these spaces with light, and are shaded by the vaulted form of the pavilion’s hill-like roof, which extends to shelter a paved terrace to the north.
Punctured by rows of large, arched openings, this roof was constructed using shotcrete, or sprayed concrete, applied over chicken and weld mesh and topped with a layer of unworked local rubble.
In front of the central pavilion, four guesthouses are partially sunken into a slope, with narrow, dark entrance stairs opening out into bedrooms with large, north-facing windows.
Further toward the wooded edges of the site are two Forest Pavilions – cylindrical structures that are perched atop concrete stilts and accessed via spiral staircases in yellow-painted steel.
The lower levels of these guesthouses contain bathrooms lined in smooth, curved plaster, while above, their circular bedrooms are wrapped by glazing and a balcony with yellow-painted railings.
“The subterranean cottages, sunk into the ground, preserve the expansive view from the pavilion, while getting their own private views,” Tamhankar eplained.
“The isolated forest cottages are tucked into the woodland perimeter, with a 360-degree view of the forest canopy,” he added.

Another resort in India recently featured on Dezeen is The Earthen Retreat by AKSH Architects, which comprises a cluster of small abandoned buildings coated in mud and lime plaster, and Serenity by Ma+rs, which is distinguished by its thatched roofs.

items.title: Stunning photos capture October's Hunter's Moon around the world
paragraphs: A good view for the passengers of this plane flying over San Francisco Bay in California, US
The October full Moon lit up skies around the world this weekend.
Full Moons throughout the year have traditionally been given names that reflect what is going on in nature.
This particular full moon is known by several names, including the Hunter's Moon, a name rooted in historical traditions in the Northern Hemisphere.
The Hunter's Moon is known to sit in the sky for a particularly long time - similar to the preceding Harvest Moon - giving hunters extra light in the skies.
The Hunter's Moon over Stoney Middleton in Derbyshire, UK
An autumn glow as the Hunter's Moon rises behind the skyline of midtown Manhattan in New York City, US

The Moon can take on an orange or reddish hue when it is low in the sky due to the scattering of short wavelength blue light as it passes through a large depth of the atmosphere, as shown here as it rises behind the Basilica of the Madonna dei Martiri in Molfetta, Italy
A view of the moon from Kimmeridge in Dorset, UK
The full moon glowing a beautiful burnt orange over the Galata Tower in Istanbul, Turkey
A clear view of the Moon in Felixstowe, Suffolk
Moonrise in Baghdad's Firdous Square, Iraq
The Hunter's Moon setting in San Francisco, California, US
