items.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
paragraphs: The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.
“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”
Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.
“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”

Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.
The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.

The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.

Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.

“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.
Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.
“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.

When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.

Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”

US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”
Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.

Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”
Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.
“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.

US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.
Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.

Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.

His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.
Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.
The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.

Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.
“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.

Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.

Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.
Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.
Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”

Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.
“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”
Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.

Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.
Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.
Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.
David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”
The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”
Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.

Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.
Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.
Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”
In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.

Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.
El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.

Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.
Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.
For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.
“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.

Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

items.title: Storm Boelo leaves 90,000 without power as Met Office issues new wind warning
paragraphs: A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.
The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said around 90,000 properties are still without power as of Monday.
Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s in north London and a 60-year-old in Dumfries and Galloway.
The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for strong winds from 18:00 on Monday to 03:00 on Tuesday across the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland and eastern parts of Northern Ireland.
Another yellow warning kicks in from 03:00 across northern parts of Scotland.
Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen which brought similar levels of disruption.

Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England.

"Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," Slade told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.

On Sunday, a man in his 20s was pronounced dead in north London after the car he was driving was hit by a falling tree. It came hours after a 60-year-old man died in Dumfries and Galloway, in western Scotland.
Disruption to travel continued on Monday, and some schools in Scotland have been shut either due to lack of power, heating, water or damage.

Another weather warning has been issued by the Met Office for later this week. The yellow warning of wind, external, covers much of Scotland, as well as parts of northern England and Northern Ireland from 03:00 to 23:59 on Tuesday.
In Scotland, Network Rail said the Crianlarich to Oban and Inverness to Wick and Thurso lines remained closed, but work to restore them was ongoing.
ScotRail said the "vast majority" of its services were running as normal.

West coast ferry operator CalMac said some of its services could be cancelled at short notice, while passengers on NorthLink Ferries are advised that there is the "possibility of disruption" to services until Thursday.
Monday morning will bring rain to many parts of south-west England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
This will move quickly north-eastwards reaching central, eastern and northern England, as well as most of Scotland, by around lunchtime.

Winds will also strengthen throughout Monday, and it will turn even windier overnight as the area of low pressure passes close to Northern Ireland and north-west Scotland with gusts peaking on Tuesday.
While showers are forecast for Wednesday, conditions are expected to calm down midweek and most places will be dry by the end of the day.
Additional reporting by Ben Rich, lead weather presenter.

items.title: Stefano Boeri Architetti to transform industrial site into residential neighbourhood in Tbilisi
paragraphs: Italian studio Stefano Boeri Architetti has revealed plans to overhaul a former factory on an industrial site in Tbilisi, Georgia, and add a series of colourful housing blocks alongside it.
The studio recently won the competition to design the Loco Park masterplan, which will add housing, green spaces and community spaces to the Georgian capital.

Aiming to celebrate the site’s industrial heritage, Stefano Boeri Architetti will renovate an existing Soviet-era locomotive factory, rebuilding some of its former architectural features with a contemporary spin.

“The new Loco Park neighbourhood will combine the memory of the large Soviet-era locomotive factory with a vision of a contemporary, vibrant space that is green and open to everyone,” said Stefano Boeri Architetti founder Stefano Boeri.
“The buildings of Loco Park will be islands in an urban archipelago, distinct yet connected by a network of tree-lined pedestrian public spaces for the whole city to enjoy.”
A series of new buildings will be built on the site, providing a mix of homes and community spaces dispersed in an open green space populated with sports facilities, parks and boulevards.
Apartments will occupy the upper levels of the buildings, while shops, cafes and workshops will be located on the ground floors.
Landscaping will connect with the surrounding city, providing public space for the wider community in Tbilisi.

Renders of the Loco Park masterplan show a colourful series of block buildings of different rectangular forms, which Stefano Boeri Architetti said are designed to have their “own identity while remaining integrated into the context”.

Stefano Boeri Architetti carried out colour mapping research in Tbilisi to identify colours commonly found in the city’s architecture, which influenced the brick finishes chosen to clad the buildings, including blue-grey, terracotta, green, taupe and white.

“We set out to capture Loco Park’s identity through a simple, balanced and contemporary design, inspired by Tbilisi’s extraordinarily rich colour palette, local materials and traces of the area’s industrial history,” said Stefano Boeri Architetti partner Pietro Chiodi.
“Colour and brick thus give each building its own identity while bringing them together into a coherent whole.”
The buildings will also be distinguished by varying roofline silhouettes, including vaulted, sawtooth and pitched roofs, designed to recall the shapes of traditional industrial buildings.
Terraced roofs will be topped with planting and, elsewhere in the development, greenhouses and communal spaces will be created as spaces for residents to socialise.

Other projects recently unveiled by Stefano Boeri Architetti include plans to transform a historic transportation depot in Rome into a greenery-covered public space, and designs for a monastery in Milan with a sail-like roof.
The images are by Stefano Boeri Architetti.

items.title: Sudan paramilitary drone strikes cause mass power cuts in eastern states
paragraphs: Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.

The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity.
All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has been at war with the RSF, its former ally, since April 2023.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people who are already facing the world’s largest hunger crisis.
Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao, in Gedaref, said the power had been out there since early morning.

“My son is diabetic, his insulin has to be stored in the fridge,” he said over the phone, adding that he feared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoiled. “We have no idea when the power will come back,” he said.
Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams.
Sudan’s war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.
In the first three weeks of October, drone strikes killed more than 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally.
Africa’s third largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people.
The majority of Sudan’s hospitals have been forced to close, at least 8 million children are out of school and swathes of the country cannot access basic services.

Abdelhafez Daafallah, a 54-year-old farmer, said by phone from Al-Junaid town in Al-Jazira: “The electricity had just started to improve three months ago, the power station the militia had destroyed was just repaired and we had hope our irrigation pumps would finally start running again.
“We hoped we would be able to finally get back to farming, but now the station has been hit,” he said, frustrated after nearly four years unable to work his land.
Farmers in Al-Jazira have struggled to rehabilitate and replant their land since the army recaptured the state from the RSF last year.

To the east, in Gedaref, Ibrahim Mohammed, 37, a grocer, said he was “already facing power cuts for hours before the strike”. “Now I have chicken in the fridge, we either lose our entire stock, or will be forced to sell it off at any price, which is still a loss,” he said.
Sudan is also grappling with unprecedented inflation and its currency has lost more than 25% of its value in recent weeks.

items.title: ‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adults
paragraphs: Chinese young adults looking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having pets or children have found an answer: raising bricks.

Bricks may not be as cuddly as cats or as life-affirming as human offspring, but they also cost next to nothing. “No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick,” wrote one brick parent on social media.

Raising “brick babies” is easier than house plants, involving spraying them with water a few times a day and waiting for moss spores already present in the atmosphere to attach themselves and grow. One Chinese media article praised the bricks as being “practically immortal”: “If you forget to water them, the moss goes dormant. If you remember to water them again, the greenery returns.”
A hashtag related to the trend has attracted more than 5m views on Weibo, a Chinese social media platform.

Chinese commentators have linked the trend to young people looking for low-effort routes to finding meaning in life. One brick parent told Chinese media that the hobby created “a sense of accomplishment no less than completing a long-term project”.

One user on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like platform, also known as Rednote, posted a picture of their rusty-coloured brick baby, saying “no output required, no KPIs to hit, no need to beg it to bloom [and] no comparing its growth with others”.
Another user wrote: “My friends asked if I’d lost my mind. I said no, I’m just starting to raise a brick.”

“A brick gives me a sense of certainty that feels way more grounded than a lot of relationships. Psychologists call this ‘zero-energy emotional companionship.’ It fulfils your need for company without demanding any obligation to give love in return.”

Chinese young people are increasingly shunning the traditional expectations of society such as having children and grinding out long hours in strenuous jobs, assuming they can find one in the first place. Nearly one in five 16- 24-year-olds, excluding students, are unemployed, according to official statistics. Some estimates put the employment rate much higher.

China’s birthrate is in stubborn decline and fell to a record low last year. Faced with a sluggish job market after years of studying in an intensely competitive educational environment, many young people are choosing to drop out of the rat race, and opting instead for “lying flat” – pursuing a low effort, low stress lifestyle, well-suited to raising bricks.
The trend of raising bricks has become so popular that Chinese media has started to warn about the health risks.

Cultivating moss could lead to the spread of mould, with some “brick parents” reportedly complaining of suffering from itchy eyes and a runny nose. Xuedong Li, a retired moss professor from Beijing’s Capital Normal University, urged brick parents to raise their mossy babies in an enclosed environment. “It is best to wear disposable gloves and a mask during handling to reduce spore inhalation and skin contact,” Li told Chinese media.

items.title: What do we still need to know about the Tyne nurdle spill?
paragraphs: The pellets have washed up on several North East beaches
On 19 July about 18 tonnes of plastic nurdles, consisting of about one billion tiny balls, spilled into the River Tyne after a crash between ships at the Port of Tyne.
It is believed to be the worst recorded incident of its type in Europe.
In the months since, teams of volunteers have joined in efforts to collect the microplastics that continue to wash up on north-east England's coast.
But several questions remain. So what do we know about the spill right now - and what are we still waiting to find out?
A wind turbine installation vessel called the Wind Orca collided with a container ship berthed at the Port of Tyne.
A gantry crane on the quayside collapsed and ended up lying across the ship.

Two containers on the BG Orange were full of nurdles. These are pre-production plastic pellets, about the size of a lentil, which are used as the raw material to manufacture nearly all everyday plastic goods.
About 18 tonnes of these pellets spilled into the water because of the crash.
Northumbria Police said it was investigating the collision and so far, no-one has been arrested. The Marine Accident Investigation Branch is also investigating.

The Port of Tyne previously said it, along with others, had asked the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) to consider enforcing safer transportation methods for nurdles, something environmental groups have long called for.
By the end of September about 28% of the nurdles had been recovered, according to scientists.

But the Port of Tyne, the Environment Agency and the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority (MSA) said the numbers of nurdles washing up ashore had already "reduced significantly" by then and numbers were continuing to fall.

They said they believed the full recovery of the 18 tonnes was not achievable. When asked what percentage recovery rate would be considered a success, the bodies said they would measure success via various metrics including shoreline surveys.
The pellets from the spill have been found along the English coast from Northumberland to North Yorkshire.
On Friday the Danish Environment Protection Agency confirmed pellets found on the country's western coast had also likely originated from the Tyne spill.
Dr Matthew Perks at Newcastle University and his colleagues are monitoring the movement of the nurdles and examining how the pellets may deteriorate in water.
The team's modelling so far suggests about one in eight of the billion nurdles remain in the Tyne estuary and high river flows could flush these microplastics downstream in the autumn.
Perks said this was a crucial opportunity to collect the pellets.
The Danish Environment Protection Agency said the pellets along the Wadden Sea coast looked similar to those from the Tyne spill
Nevertheless he said it was unclear how far some of the nurdles could really travel.
"As time goes by, it becomes more difficult to pinpoint the areas where these nurdles are likely to be," he said.
It is also unclear when the nurdles will start breaking down into nanoplastics. "That will change the way they behave," he said.
Professor Bhavani Narayanaswamy at the Scottish Association for Marine Science said it could be months or years before we understood the full impact of the spill.
She said the nurdles could affect wildlife in various ways, including getting stuck in animal digestive tracts and adsorbing chemicals which then may be toxic to wildlife when ingested.
Prof Narayanaswamy said there was little research on the long-term impact of plastic pollution on animals compared with its immediate effects.
Dan Turner, who coordinates the North East England Beached Bird Survey, said the group had collected several dead birds along the coast which they would be testing for nurdles next month.
"It is quite possible that the seabirds have mistaken the plastic for fish eggs," he previously told the BBC.
Birds have been seen appearing to eat nurdles on a beach in Tynemouth
Recovery is largely being paid for by insurers representing BG Orange, which was carrying the pellets, as well as local councils and the Port of Tyne.
Thousands of volunteers have also been involved in the clean-up.
The Port of Tyne and the local authorities involved have been told to record their costs so they can seek compensation from the insurers of those ultimately found responsible.

The multi-agency group, consisting of the North East MSA, Port of Tyne and the EA, said the nurdle recovery programme was continuing but it had increasingly moved away from "large-scale clean-up activity" towards "targeted recovery and monitoring".
Environmental charity Fidra said it was unclear how long the clean-up would need to continue, considering the fact that nurdles could stay in water for years.
It said a long-term plan was required to tackle the pollution and the plans should be "adequately resourced" with responsibility clearly defined.
Volunteer Lou Shackleton said there was still a core group of individuals who gave up their spare time to monitor and recover nurdles on local beach.
She said the group needed all the help they could get.
"If you're happy to wrap up against the rain and the wind... come and join us," she said.

items.title: Apple Music unveils logo that was physically "made by sound"
paragraphs: Technology brand Apple has revealed the first rebrand for its Apple Music service, which was made in collaboration with musician Fred Again by passing sound waves through a pool of oil.

Created as part of the service’s first rebrand since Apple Music launched in 2015, the logo has a wave-like aesthetic that was created through a physical process at a time when digital design and artificial intelligence are at the forefront of creative processes.
According to Apple, the core concept was to give Apple Music a distinctive sound and create a logo that was “made by sound”.
“For the rebrand of Apple Music, we wanted sound to create the visuals,” said Apple. “How do we take this idea of music and distill it into something visually beautiful?”
The creation process was revealed in a video released by Apple, which showed an application icon-shaped piece of plastic placed in a shallow pool of mineral oil.

Musical frequencies, created by Fred Again in collaboration with NEST Acoustics, were translated into physical vibrations using a transducer. These vibrations moved the oil to produce the wave-like effect on the logo.

“Essentially, the idea was to create the perfect sound wave,” said Apple. “We take a frequency and we play it through a rig. This rig then moves a large amount of liquid at the frequency of the notes.”
“We partnered with one of the world’s best music artists to create the notes for the final mnemonic,” it continued. “And then we used that sound to create the visuals.”

Along with the wave-like overlay, the typology of the Apple Music logo has been amended to align with wider Apple visual identities. Sat alongside the apple icon, the M in music has been made lowercase.
The typology was changed to a custom version of Apple’s SF Pro typeface in an entirely lowercase, bold letterform.
Apple unveiled the new logo last week along with an additional musical note icon.

The Apple Music identity was teased earlier in the month, when the company unveiled its Apple Music Hall venue in Battersea, London. The logo is placed on the wall within the venue, which has an industrial aesthetic to match the renovated power station it sits within.

items.title: Discover the process and Photoshop brushes behind this fantasy book cover
paragraphs: The client commissioned me to design an original book cover for a new fantasy novel, A Bleeding of Heavens, whose central protagonist is a powerful dragon. They hoped the overall atmosphere would echo the iconic scene of Daenerys travelling with her fleet across the ocean at sunset in Game of Thrones.

Once I got the design requirements, I started planning the overall layout right away. I depicted the main dragon in a vivid dynamic stance, dashing forward from a distance in the frame, straight towards audiences with its mouth wide open in a fierce roar.

Floating clouds and sailing fleets spread across the sea in the lower part of the picture. The huge dragon and the tiny distant ships form a sharp contrast, building remarkable spatial depth. The whole scene is set against a glowing backlit sunset sky, and striking light rays enrich the visual layers.

For the back cover, I drew the other two dragons from the novel locked in an intense battle. I arranged the three dragons with clear visual hierarchy, and concentrated the finest details on the main dragon’s head on the front cover to highlight the core character.
If you want to follow a similar process, you'll need digital art software, and you might want one of the best drawing tablets to work on.

I quickly sketched out the overall composition and mood. Using simple photobashing, I overlaid some scene photos on the bottom layer, then blended elements into the scene with broad textured brushstrokes. For the dragon, I referred to 3D models posed in Blender.

After the client approved the sketch, I moved on to lighting rendering. Following backlighting rules, I focused on reflections across the sea, rim-lit clouds and subsurface scattering on the dragon’s wings. Once roughly 60–70% complete, I sent the draft for detail checks.

The client quickly approved most elements and requested that the lower fleet should be depicted in battle to match the chaotic tone of Jasmine Young’s fantasy novel (the fifth in the Dragon Breaker series). I revised accordingly and refined the artwork to final completion.

I use cloud brushes to quickly block out shapes. I intentionally vary the size of near and distant clouds to create depth. Additionally, it’s important to differentiate warm and cool tones between sunlit areas and shadowed back sides of the clouds. As you can see in the illustration, I tint the rear sides of the clouds with cool blue hues.
Given the top-down perspective requiring abundant details, I added figures on ships and multicoloured foliage atop island hills to amplify the sense of scale.
The vivid red on the dragon’s wings and bright pink within clouds stem from subsurface light reflection, enhancing the overall luminous effect.
My tip for detailing: paint sea foam only on lit water and leave shadowed areas under ships sparse. This draws eyes to highlights, saves work and boosts visual impact.
For the ships, I arranged multiple vessel orientations with 3D models in Blender to create a chaotic layout and avoid tedious perspective issues.
Here’s my tip for cloud painting: keep shadows unified and focus on lit areas to build volume, while keeping the scene’s perspective in mind.

items.title: Storm Boelo clears but more wind and rain bears down on UK
paragraphs: After a weekend of heavy downpours and severe gales, Storm Boelo is moving away from the UK and the weather has turned calmer.
However, this may not last long as another deep area of low pressure is already approaching from the Atlantic.
As this moves to the north-west of the country during Monday and Tuesday it will bring another dose of rain and gales.
A Met Office yellow wind warning has issued for much of Scotland, as well as parts of northern England and Northern Ireland, on Tuesday.
However, this latest weather system is unlikely to be as widely disruptive as Storm Boelo - or Storm Austen which came before it - and has not, so far, been named.
The next name on the list for the 2026/2027 season is Chloe.
Monday morning will bring rain to many parts of south-west England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
This will move quickly north-eastwards reaching central, eastern and northern England, as well as most of Scotland, by around lunchtime.
It will also be rather misty and murky over some coasts and hills.
As the rain clears, slightly drier conditions will spread across the UK from the south-west.
While many areas will remain cloudy a few bright or sunny spells are possible, especially in Wales and south-west England.
Southerly winds will bring warmer air than of late, especially in the south where temperatures may peak at 18 or 19C.
The wettest weather will affect Scotland by Monday afternoon
After a breezy start to Monday, winds will strengthen once again during the day, with widespread gusts of 30-40mph and 50mph gusts likely in many coastal areas.
It will turn even windier overnight as the area of low pressure passes close to Northern Ireland and north-west Scotland with gusts peaking on Tuesday.
A Met Office yellow warning covers almost the entirety of Scotland - apart from Shetland - extending into the north coast of Northern Ireland and the far north of Northern England.
The yellow Met Office warning is valid from 03:00 until 23:59 GMT on Tuesday
Widespread gusts of 50-60mph are expected, with the possibility of speeds exceeding 70mph around some exposed coasts.
The Met Office warning suggests that there is a low risk of significant impacts, with the chance of travel disruption, power cuts, damage to buildings and some flying debris.
While this weather system is not expected to be as severe as Storm Boelo, its impacts could be magnified coming so soon after the previous storm.
High pressure will build close to the UK from midweek onwards meaning the weather should gradually calm down.
Showers will continue on Wednesday but most places are expected to be dry by the end of the day.
Under light winds on Thursday morning, mist and fog could cause some travel disruption across some parts of the country. This should largely clear to leave a dry day with sunny spells.

A weather front could bring rain back into western parts on Friday but high pressure is then expected to rebuild with most computer weather models suggesting a drier and calmer spell is likely to develop over the weekend and into next week.
You can always check your local forecast and the weather warnings for where you are on the BBC Weather website and app

items.title: UK poised to miss reduced aid spending target of 0.3% of national income
paragraphs: The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.
Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.
The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.

However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates.
Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”.

Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts to Africa that are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said.

The CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) budget.
The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target.
The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence.
Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget.
She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set.
“Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut.
“The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.”
Charities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries.

The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s government hit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.
The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m.

The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiative Gavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support.

The Conservative party and Reform UK have pledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank.

An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.
“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”

items.title: Think Architecture's fragmented House on a Slope overlooks Lake Zurich
paragraphs: A cluster of interconnected volumes in dark limestone and cedar gradually descend down a narrow and steeply sloping site overlooking Lake Zurich at House on a Slope by Swiss studio Think Architecture.
Designed to sit harmoniously within the surrounding terrain, the 1,000-square-metre private home is split into two distinct blocks connected by a “subterranean art corridor”.
“The brief was to bring a very large programme into a narrow, steeply sloping site with as much sensitivity as possible,” Think Architecture creative director Marco Zbinden told Dezeen.

“We were interested in the quiet rhythm of the neighbouring houses, their individual scale, and the way they sit within the landscape. Breaking the residence into smaller volumes allowed us to respond to that context without losing the generosity of the interior,” he continued.
“From the outside, the house feels less like a single monumental object and more like a group of familiar structures that have always belonged to the hillside.”
Intended to emulate the surrounding landscape, the lakeside home was divided into two blocks, a “family house above, and a more grounded, protective house for children and guests below”.

“They are intimately connected through a corridor – filled with art – and the central garden level, which becomes the social heart of the home,” said Zbinden. “There, the architecture opens up, materials continue from outside to inside, and the different parts of the family’s life naturally meet.”

The larger, upper block, which is entered at street level, contains all the main living spaces including the kitchen, living room and dining room. These spaces are arrange over the first and lower floors, with large cedar-clad-timber windows giving views down the hillside. Several bedrooms are located on the top floor.

The lower level of the home opens up to a garden and large pool with a planted roof terrace sitting on the roof of the lower block. Clad in dark-limestone, this lower block is more enclosed with additional bedrooms for the family.
Carefully positioned openings within both structures allowed for the planting of native trees, ensuring a seamless transition into the mature foliage of the hillside.
Think Architecture designed the upper interior spaces to be open and airy, while the spaces in the lower block were more enclosed and calm.
“The interiors were conceived as a direct continuation of the architecture, extending its material language into the most private and lived-in spaces,” said Zbinden.
“We worked with a limited palette of bog oak, cedar, oak, Belgian bluestone, terrazzo, and patinated brass. Materials that are tactile, honest, and become more beautiful as they age,” he continued.
“The aim was to create spaces that felt warm and enveloping rather than decorated: quiet rooms shaped by light, texture, and proportion, where one can truly slow down and feel at home.”

House with a Slope is the most recent addition to a number of homes overlooking Lake Zurich completed by Think Architecture in recent months, including a minimal hilltop home and a home next to a vineyard.

items.title: Roca releases innovative all-in-one Avant toilet
paragraphs: Spanish bathroom brand Roca has rethought conventional toilet design with Avant, integrating the cistern within the toilet itself.
For the Avant toilet, Roca designed the cistern to sit within the bowl, removing the external cistern on its floor-standing model and the concealed cistern and flush plate on its wall-hung version.
Avant’s cistern uses flushing technology based on the Venturi effect. Here, fluid pressure drops when liquid is funnelled from a larger pipe section to a smaller one.

This creates a powerful suction in the tank, which is needed for the flush. As the components are concealed within the wall, this gives Avant a more minimalist appearance but also offers benefits in space, aesthetics, installation and maintenance.
The integrated aesthetic also makes bathrooms more adaptable and practical for different design needs and interiors.

“The removal of an external cistern or the flush plate further enhances the overall aesthetic of the bathroom, and its neutral, minimalist design blends seamlessly into any bathroom style, adding a touch of modernity,” said Roca.

Another innovative element is that the Avant is also powered without electricity, but if water pressure or flow is insufficient in a building, the Avant-E model is best suited – an electric version suitable for a wider range of plumbing systems.

The Avant also features dual-flush options, side-mounted flush buttons, a soft-close seat and cover and Roca Rimless Vortex. According to Roca, it meets the highest hygiene standards and operates with splash-free, low-consumption flushing, reducing water consumption.
The toilet is also covered in Supraglaze, a custom finish that mitigates the build-up of dirt, germs and residue, making cleaning simple and further increasing hygiene.
The result is an efficient, minimalist toilet ideal for compact spaces, easy to install and maintain.
“Avant not only brings a modern aesthetic to the bathroom, but it also reduces flush noise, providing a quieter, more comfortable experience than conventional toilets,” said Roca.
Founded in Spain in 1917, Roca now operates in 170 countries, with a special focus on sustainability and craftsmanship.
The company produces high-end, design-forward bathroom appliances, including everything from toilets to sinks, hardware and faucets.

It recently released modular bathroom furniture that can be adjusted to fit different scales and colourful taps in collaboration with designer Inma Bermúdez, in bright green, blue and yellow finishes.
To learn more about the Avant toilet, visit Roca’s website.

items.title: Sharon Osbourne: 'I visit Ozzy's grave every day'
paragraphs: Sharon Osbourne spoke to BBC News as the family prepares to release a film about Ozzy's final concert with Black Sabbath
It's been 15 months since Ozzy Osbourne died, at the age of 76, at his home in Buckinghamshire.
Although he had suffered from health problems for years, including Parkinson's disease and a fractured vertebra, his death was a shock.
Less than three weeks beforehand, he had been on stage in Birmingham, playing a triumphant farewell concert.
"He was just so, so happy," recalls his wife Sharon.
"He was online, going through the reviews and saying, 'There's something terribly wrong', and I'm like, 'Why?'
"He goes, 'I didn't get slagged by anybody. Why are people being nice to me?'

On the morning he died, Ozzy had woken up early and gone downstairs for his usual morning workout. Shortly afterwards, he had a heart attack. An air ambulance was called and paramedics tried to save him. But it was too late.
"We'd spoken in the night. Ozzy had woken in the night and he asked me to kiss him twice, and I did.
"And then he said, 'Hold me, hold me tight,' and I did.
"And then the next thing I know, it's early in the morning, and someone comes rushing into the room saying, 'Come down now'.
Sharon and Ozzy Osbourne, pictured in 2017 after renewing their wedding vows
"You've lost the love of your life, so you don't just wake up and go, 'I'm fine now. I'm cured'.
"You never get over it. But you learn to live with it, and that's what I'm trying to do. So you either sit in a room and don't come out, or you accept it, befriend it, and that's it."

The affection among Ozzy's fans was apparent before the singer's funeral. Thousands of people lined the streets of Birmingham, laying floral tributes and singing Black Sabbath songs as Ozzy's body was transported through his home city in a hearse topped by a purple floral tribute in the shape of a cross.
Sharon says he would have been mystified by the outpouring of love.
"He'd have been like, 'What's the matter with you guys? Go home!'" she says.
But for the family, the public response was a huge source of comfort.

Daughter Kelly said last year: "I never could have imagined it to be as helpful as it has been to know that we're not alone in our grief and our sadness, and that the rest of the world loved him as much as we did."
Sharon says the fans' cards and messages were all collected, sorted and photographed; while the flowers were composted for the family garden, where Ozzy is buried.
"There was no way I could put Ozzy in a public graveyard," she says.

"I've seen what happens to other people in the public eye. There's no peace because people want to come and they want to pay their respects. That's an ongoing thing, and I wanted Ozzy to rest and just be."
"Of course, every day. I can see him from my window."
She still talks to him regularly, she says. Asked what she discusses, she puts a finger to her lips and gives a gentle "shh".
Ozzy's family - including children Jack and Kelly - stopped to read the tributes during his funeral procession last July
Ozzy and Sharon's relationship spanned more than 50 years.

They met in 1970 and married in 1982. Their time together could be turbulent - he was arrested for attempting to murder her in 1989 (she dropped the charges), and they split briefly in 2016 amid rumours of infidelity - but the couple maintained that they were soulmates.
"It was an unusual relationship because we had such highs and such terrible lows," she admits. But at the end of his life, "he knew" how much he was loved.

You can see proof of that love - from his family, his fans and his bandmates – in a new documentary about his final gig at Birmingham's Villa Park last year, when he reunited with heavy rock legends Black Sabbath.
Titled Back To The Beginning, it features more than 25 of the songs played at that star-studded concert, including Ozzy's solo set and Sabbath's entire performance.
In backstage footage, fellow A-list performers discuss the star's influence in awestruck tones.
"If there was no Sabbath, there's no Metallica," says the band's frontman James Hetfield. "It's as simple as that."
Yungblud, whose version of Changes was one of the concert's emotional high points, talks about how, as a kid who didn't fit in, Ozzy changed his life.
"The fact he was celebrated for his madness and his individuality gave me hope."
Watch: Black Sabbath blast out Iron Man at final gig
Sharon says the concert was Ozzy's final wish: the one thing that would make him happy after years of deteriorating health.
Six months before the show, Ozzy fell and fractured his vertebrae. In recovery, he caught pneumonia three times. After surgery on his back, he caught sepsis and nearly died.
Two weeks before the show, doctors urged him to call it off.
"They came to see us at the house and they said, 'You can't do this. We're advising you not to do this. Your heart's too weak'," Sharon recalls.

But the singer was determined to see it through. In the film, it's hard to believe he's so ill. Although he performs seated on a throne, his eyes are full of life and his voice is powerful. As he looks out at the crowd, he seems elated.
Backstage, Sharon admits, "the whole family was terrified". But something changed when Ozzy entered the stadium.
"He was sat in his dressing room, watching everybody on a screen performing, and he was like, 'I just can't believe they're all here'.

"It's amazing what support and love and determination can do for you, because [before the show] he was somebody that couldn't breathe. He had a lung condition. He had a heart condition. He had terrible, terrible agony from his spine. He had blood clots and he had Parkinson's.
"Some days just to even talk was an effort, let alone sing. And I don't know how he did it, but he did it.
"And you saw it in his eyes, in his face. It just made him feel like he was alive again."
Ozzy is survived by Sharon, their three children (left-right: Kelly, Aimee and Jack) and three children from his previous marriage
The effect was so galvanising that, when he came off stage, Ozzy declared he wanted to go on tour.
"He was raring to go," Sharon laughs. "He was like, 'I can do this, and the fans don't mind if I'm sat down'."
It's an incredible and rare thing, I suggest, to be able to grant your partner their last wish.
Ozzy may have suffered immense pain in his final years, but he was able to say goodbye in style.
"To quote one of his songs, he was flying high again," Sharon says.
"He was just floating for those last 17 days. It was great. It was joyous."

items.title: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders
paragraphs: When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level.

As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials kick off an important meeting this week, discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions.

The “fifth plenum” began on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption.

As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.

Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.
He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty.

Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.

Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s.
“Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said.

The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy.

The meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.

Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”.

In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said.
The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.

In January, Zhang Youxia, China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC)
A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline.
Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.

Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.

Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.

items.title: Phantom Blade Zero review: dark wuxia martial arts masters with an apprentice's execution
paragraphs: Phantom Blade Zero has a lot going for it to distinguish itself from other AAA Souls-inspired games emerging from China in recent years, thanks to its painstaking martial-arts mocap combat and unique kung-fu-punk vision, but several frustrating design choices keep it from being a work of a grand master.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Phantom Blade Zero wants you to feel like a kung fu master from the opening moments, and you should, since you play as Soul, an elite assassin for the Order. Even after a fateful duel leaves him with 66 days to live, there’s no cheap Metroid-style reset, and his martial arts prowess keeps growing.

Whether taking on another fearsome warrior one-on-one or a group of enemies, there’s a fluid confidence to his moveset that captures the spirit of the classic martial arts films that have inspired studio S-Game's ambitious debut, itself based on the indie RPG Rainblood: Town of Death that director Soulframe Liang made more than 15 years ago.

While China’s first AAA hits like Black Myth: Wukong and Wuchang: Fallen Feathers have leveraged both Unreal Engine 5 and the overwhelming influence of Soulslikes, S-Game tries to carve out its own identity, which it has coined as ‘kungfupunk’. Aesthetically, that means a curious blend of traditional Chinese culture with the modern: steel-factory architecture clashing with bamboo forests and temples from a more classic wuxia setting, and music where elegant pipa strings give way to electric-guitar rock riffs. More literally, it’s about how Sha-Chi, the energy that powers your kung fu (in-game, it’s basically your stamina gauge used for heavy combos and guarding attacks), also powers other technologies.

But it's definitely the kung fu that's centre-stage here, with all of the fighting styles and movements in-game captured by real martial artists, notably with the involvement of Hong Kong martial arts legend Donnie Yen (he also plays a character, albeit one you don't strictly encounter on the main story path, while spending most of it behind a mask) and his stunt team.

Even though your combos are essentially just spamming light or heavy attacks, your fighting style changes depending on the weapon you use, such as the one-handed Jagged Steel, which inflicts bleed damage, or the weighty two-handed Scarlet Wraithblade, which leaves energy-draining red spider lilies on the ground. The action can often feel too fast for its own good, so you're usually focused on your flurry of attacks before waiting to react to an enemy's blue or red attacks to parry or dodge, but hitting the prompt to unleash a finishing move is pretty satisfying.

Since most bosses drop new weapons, there's a thrill in getting a new toy to play with, and the game has more than 50 to find and master. It can feel a little overwhelming, and some may feel more gimmicky than useful, like a sword that gives you unpredictable drunken-martial-arts movements, so I naturally stuck to a few favourites, especially since I needed to prioritise upgrading them with my limited resources.

Nonetheless, there's an incentive to master more than one weapon, as switching automatically gives you a full Sha-Chi gauge. I often used up a gauge with one weapon, then quickly swapped to another to keep my offensive momentum going (a cooldown period does prevent you from just exploiting this).

Special weapons called Phantom Edges have limited uses but, used at the right time, can turn the tide in encounters, like a large axe that smashes through enemy shields or a chain sickle that tears through multiple surrounding enemies. Some even serve Metroidvania-style exploration, letting you access areas you couldn't reach before.

But despite some interesting designs, it's hard not to see these as glorified keycards, with most leading to little more than a small room and a chest for your trouble. Even though the chain doubles as a grappling hook, it's a bit disappointing once you realise that, like other traversal options such as running up cliffs or wall-running, it's limited to a button prompt at prescribed points in the environment.

This is one of the frustrating aspects of Phantom Blade Zero's rich, dense Wulin, even as it takes you from the bottom of a valley to mountain peaks, plus a massive lake you can explore by boat. It may all look pleasing to the eye, but it suffers from environments where you regularly bump up against invisible barriers as you try to parse the artistically rendered map (albeit elegantly emulating a Chinese ink wash painting that fills up the more checkpoints you come across).

This is especially annoying when a quest marker is supposedly close by, but you still have to wander aimlessly until you spot an interaction prompt, or discover there's actually a long-winded detour you're supposed to take instead. Doors that require specific keys are one thing, but I catch myself sighing when I approach a ledge you would expect to mantle in a similar game, only for Soul's kung fu skills to be arbitrarily eluded.

Another question you might have about Phantom Blade Zero is whether it's a Soulslike. In many ways, it isn't. For instance, its checkpoints don't revive defeated enemies when you rest at them, and you also don't lose any resources permanently if you don't recover them. It nonetheless has some similarities, such as some labyrinthine level design where you'll encounter your share of doors inconveniently locked from your side, but it almost seems to turn into a Soulslike in challenge the moment you encounter bosses with hard-hitting attacks and where you have very limited heals (which you won't even be able to upgrade meaningfully until the game's midpoint).

On the one hand, some difficulty spikes are mitigated by bosses with a second phase, which also have a checkpoint so you're not forced to go through the first phase with fewer resources, and there are also difficulty options. The accessories you find and equip can also make a difference, especially ones that widen the parry and dodge windows, but my major gripe remains how spongy these boss fights feel, even for those that come back with a second phase.

This isn't unique to Phantom Blade Zero (see also Control Resonant, until Remedy patched it at launch), but it makes you question the point of staggering your opponent when, in this state, all your heaviest attacks still only chip away at their health. In many fights, it also makes your aggressive momentum push the enemy back until you inevitably get stuck on geometry. When it hits the camera, some cool-looking finishing moves get framed awkwardly, with parts of the environment obscuring the shot.

Even though I was testing on PS5 Pro, I still ran into some pretty glaring technical issues during my playthrough, mostly in the latter half of the game, which I think came down to optimisation and bugs, since they persisted even after I turned off ray tracing and set the graphics to Performance mode. Sometimes the audio got knocked way out of balance between the voice acting and music, and in a couple of cases the big puddles I came across didn't show reflections so much as they looked more like a big mirror or a hole in the ground.

Most egregious, however, were framerate drops during combat that devolved into a slideshow, spoiling several major boss fights. I should be relieved they didn't kill me, since most of these happened when I was already locked into my (likely very VFX-laden) attack animations against a staggered opponent.

That may make it seem like I have a lot to be down about Phantom Blade Zero, but there is still plenty to admire, including cultural and artistic flourishes I can't share in this review. The Wulin's centrepiece, Pangzhen, is the kind of labyrinthine town that deserves to be talked about in the same breath as Bloodborne's Yharnam, so rich and dense with secrets and lore, and home to some of the game's best bosses, while there's clearly been a lot of thought that has gone into the intriguing characters and deep questlines that offer meaningful rewards, including having an impact on the ending you'll get. It's just a shame that the version I got to play still needed a bit more time in the oven.

A final note: S-Game released a patch that supposedly resolves most of the above issues, but it came after I finished my playthrough, so I didn't have a chance to go through it again to make sure every issue I encountered was fixed.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

items.title: Data centre debate heats up ahead of US midterms - here's what you need to know
paragraphs: ByDaniel Thomas and the Visual Journalism Team
Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.
These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.
They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.
But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.
In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.
It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows.
Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing.
There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map, external, a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites.
That's up sharply from 2021, when there were around 8,000, external operational sites.
As the chart below shows, data centres are most densely clustered in the US which has 4,767 sites. It is followed by Europe, where the UK and Germany lead.

Data centres have typically been located near to cities where it's easier to access high voltage power lines or water resources for cooling. But as they get bigger, more are being built in rural areas.
Data centres vary wildly in size, ranging from ones that fit inside a garden shed to others covering vast expanses of land.

The world's largest operational data centre is widely reported to be one run by China Telecom in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, covering an area of approximately one million square metres (10.7 million sq ft). That is equivalent to about 140 Fifa football pitches.
However, much larger sites are under construction as the graphic below shows.
All these sites are being built exclusively to provide the immense computing power needed to run AI services.
For instance, Colossus 2, which is part of the wider Colossus campus, will house hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips made by tech giant Nvidia.

It will also be used to train xAI's chatbot Grok. Elon Musk's company will use 41 methane gas turbines to help power the site, which activists say could "significantly increase" local air pollution, external. Local regulators say the turbines will meet air quality standards.

The pressure data centres put on local resources has sparked increasing concern. These facilities can use significant amounts of water to cool their systems, which could lead to water shortages, some experts say.
Data centres worldwide are also thought to consume more electricity than the whole of France, as the chart below shows.
This growing hunger for power is driving up carbon emissions, analysis shows, while putting pressure on local grids, which some fear could push up energy prices.
With others worried about the noise data centres make and the space they take up, a public backlash is gathering steam.
Some 16 US states have proposed laws to ban or temporarily block new facilities, and it could be a key issue in November's midterm elections.
Outside the US, opposition to data centres has emerged in countries like Mexico, France, Indonesia and the UK.
But supporters say data centres are critical to national security, and the development of AI.
They also say they are good for the economy, external, attracting investment, generating tax revenue and creating jobs in areas like construction.
A recent report by the Brookings Center, external suggests data centres do create local jobs, although fewer than industry advocates claim.
The type of data centre matters too. So-called hyperscale facilities - massive sites owned and run by tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft - have a bigger positive effect on jobs, it found.
But "colocation" facilities, which lease space to remote tenants without a local presence, brought fewer benefits.
As the debate over their merits intensifies, the data centre rollout continues.
This year, the tech industry is expected to spend a combined $765bn, external ($544bn) on AI infrastructure in 2026, with this topping $1tn next year.
But as concerns about the environmental impact grow, the tech industry is exploring alternatives.
One idea is to put data centres in space, external or on the Moon, where they could harness abundant solar energy.
Others predict that more AI processing could eventually be carried out by the hardware already inside our computers and smartphones, reducing the need for vast data centres altogether.
Additional reporting and design by Erwan Rivault, Matt Faraci and Dominic Bailey.

items.title: Man killed by falling tree as Storm Boelo brings more severe weather to UK
paragraphs: A 60-year-old man has died after being hit by a falling tree in southern Scotland as Storm Boelo continues to bring severe weather to the UK.
Police Scotland said the man was pronounced dead at the scene following the incident near Castle Douglas in Dumfries and Galloway at about 10:30 on Sunday.

The harsh weather battering the UK has left more than 47,000 customers in Scotland without power, Scottish and Southern Electricity Networks said on Sunday, while 2,610 properties have faced outages in Cumbria in England.
Those still without electricity have faced delays as the dangerous conditions were "limiting network engineers' opportunities to safely start the work", the ENA added.
Wind gusts peaked on Sunday morning at 85mph in Machrihanish, in Argyll and Bute, and 84mph in both Stornoway in the Outer Hebrides, and Capel Curig in north Wales.
An amber wind warning issued by the Met Office will remain in place until 21:00 on Sunday across Scotland and parts of northern England.

A yellow warning that also covers other areas of the north of England, including Liverpool, Manchester, Leeds, Sheffield and Newcastle-upon-Tyne, as well as parts of the East and West Midlands and North Wales, is in place until 21:00 on Sunday.
The Met Office has urged people to "stay indoors as much as possible", adding: "If you do go out, try not to walk, or shelter, close to buildings and trees."
The strongest gusts have continued to spread eastwards across the UK on Sunday.
Four flood warnings have been issued for parts of England and Wales on Sunday, while there are 17 flood warnings in place in Scotland.
High rainfall totals have been recorded in the Scottish Highlands, peaking in Cluanie Inn which received 130mm.
Scottish government ministers and officials gathered on Sunday afternoon to discuss the impact of Storm Boelo.
In a statement, the Scottish government said while conditions may ease later on Sunday, there is potential for adverse weather to return in the coming days.
Police in Scotland have warned against unnecessary road journeys and ferry services have been cancelled.
Some flights to and from Belfast, Glasgow, Aberdeen and Dublin airports have been cancelled and train services across the UK have faced disruption.

Jason Kelly, the Met Office's chief forecaster, said: "People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies. Secure loose items outside, plan ahead if you are travelling and keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings for your area."
Events across the country planned for the weekend have been cancelled due to the weather.
In Merseyside, a River of Light event was called off for the second day in a row, and Knowsley Safari Park has announced that it was closed on Sunday due to "high winds".
Several markets across the North West have also been cancelled due to the weather, including Quayside Makers Market in Salford and Macclesfield Treacle Market in Cheshire.
In the East Midlands, Worksop Half Marathon was called off, and closures were announced at Wollaton Hall and Deer Park, Robin Hood's Wheelgate Park and Twinlakes Theme Park.

items.title: These beautiful buds bring expertly tuned audiophile sound to wireless inner-ear headphones
paragraphs: With the many wireless earbuds we've tested over the years, we've found that manufacturers tend to prioritise noise-cancelling algorithms over high quality, neutral audio fidelity. The Status Audio Pro X broke that mold and did so very well, and now they've taken things further.

While the standard Pro X use Status Audio's default signature tuning alongside an open EQ that lets you customise your own sound profiles via the app, the new GoldenSound Edition featues a locked, specialised sound profile from renowned audio engineer Cameron "GoldenSound" Oatley.
There are plenty of great over-ear wireless headphones, but for inner-ear earphones, the Status Pro really stand out right now.

At the heart of the Status Audio Pro X is a triple-driver configuration, combining a 12mm dynamic driver for deep sub-bass with dual Knowles-balanced armatures for highs and mids. The standard signature profile delivers impressive instrument separation and a weighty sub bass partnered with splashes of high end, but with a rich midrange presence for an engaging V-shape sound signature.

The GoldenSound Edition feature an additional locked profile developed using the specialised Brüel & Kjær 5128 head and torso simulator. This targets a natural, balanced timbre, smoother treble and improved mid-range cohesion for a more acoustic-friendly and realistic presentation. You to switch back to the standard Pro X tuning using the app.

They also have a sharp aesthetic with a matte black and matte gold finish on the earbuds, with a matte black charging case and a matte gold lid stamped with both the Status Audio and GoldenSound logos.
