items.title: US adds wrongful detention warning to China travel advisory
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

The U.S. State Department has added a wrongful detention warning to its travel advisory for mainland China, cautioning that Americans face a serious risk of being detained without a fair legal process.
The advisory, updated October 19, keeps China at Level 2 — “Exercise Increased Caution” but adds a “D” risk indicator for wrongful detention.
The advisory warns that Chinese authorities may enforce local laws arbitrarily and impose exit bans without a fair and transparent legal process.
In an emailed statement to VOA, the State Department said it had determined that “Americans are at serious risk of wrongful detention in China.”

“The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans,” a State Department spokesperson told VOA, adding that the administration was committed to securing the release of Americans wrongfully detained overseas.

The department identifies several groups that may face heightened risks, including Americans of Chinese descent, people involved in business disputes, and those with current or past ties to U.S. law enforcement, the military, intelligence agencies or the federal government.
The House Select Committee on China called the new “D” indicator “a serious warning to all Americans” in a social media post Tuesday.
The State Department has formally designated two U.S. citizens detained in China as wrongfully detained: Chinese American seismologist Chen Youlin and Myanmar-born American scholar Min Zin.
Chen had worked with Chinese researchers on a U.S. government-funded public research project examining seismic signals from underground nuclear tests in North Korea.

Chinese authorities arrested Chen on November 5, 2024, as he prepared to return to the United States after visiting family in China. On May 1, 2025, China accused him of espionage. The State Department designated his case as wrongful detention in March 2026.

Min Zin, who studies Myanmar politics and China-Myanmar relations, was detained by Chinese authorities after traveling to China’s southern Yunnan province for a conference in June this year. Beijing accused him of suspected espionage that endangered China's national security. The State Department designated his case as wrongful detention on August 20.
The designations make securing the release of both men a U.S. government priority.
President Donald Trump said he raised the cases of detained Americans and Chinese political prisoners with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their White House meeting at the end of September.
The State Department also confirmed to VOA that Washington had directly raised Chen's and Min Zin's cases with Beijing.
Chen's wife, Rong Yufang, welcomed the updated travel advisory in a written statement sent to VOA through Global Reach, a nonprofit organization working to secure her husband's release.

“I am grateful to Secretary Rubio for taking this action,” she said. “He has tried for months to quietly resolve my husband’s wrongful detention in China, and President Trump has even asked President Xi twice about Youlin.”

Aung Maw Zin, Min Zin’s brother, told VOA on Wednesday that “we are glad to see this small but important step that could help ensure that no other American family has to endure the nightmare our family has been living through since June.”

The United States previously placed China at Level 3, with a “D” indicator for wrongful detention. The advisory was downgraded to Level 2 and the indicator removed on November 27, 2024, after three Americans detained in China for years were released in a prisoner exchange between Washington and Beijing.
Upcoming summits could bring renewed pressure
Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer at Global Reach, told VOA that the espionage allegations against Chen were fabricated.
Lebson said Trump could press for a resolution when he meets Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen and the G20 meeting at Mar-a-Lago over the next two months.
“President Xi can expect President Trump to continue raising the need to resolve this case while the State Department increases the costs associated with holding two U.S. citizens,” Lebson said.

Beijing has rejected allegations of wrongful detention, maintaining that its judicial authorities handle cases in accordance with the law.The Chinese Embassy in Washington has yet not responded to VOA's request for comment.

items.title: US says wartime command transfer to South Korea remains conditions based
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

The United States has reiterated that wartime operational control, or OPCON, of allied forces on the Korean Peninsula will transition to South Korea only after mutually agreed conditions are met, despite renewed calls from Seoul to accelerate the process.

“The transition of wartime operational control (OPCON) remains a conditions-based process mutually agreed upon by the United States and the Republic of Korea,” a U.S. Department of Defense official told VOA on Monday, speaking on background.

“Both nations remain committed to ensuring that the necessary conditions are met before any transition occurs,” the official said. “We will not prejudge decisions or outcomes of this bilateral process.”
Wartime OPCON refers to the authority to direct military operations during a conflict.

Under the current U.S.-South Korea combined defense structure, a U.S. general serves as commander of the Combined Forces Command, which would oversee allied military operations in wartime. CFC was established in 1978 with a goal to "deter, or defeat if necessary, outside aggression against" South Korea. It unified U.S. and South Korean forces under a single war-fighting command.

Although South Korea regained peacetime OPCON in 1994, plans to transfer wartime OPCON were repeatedly postponed before the allies adopted a conditions-based approach in 2014, leaving the timing of the transition undecided.
The comments come as South Korean President Lee Jae Myung pushes for a faster transition of wartime command authority.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Lee said South Korea should “swiftly” regain wartime OPCON, arguing that the country possesses sufficient military capabilities to assume greater responsibility for its own defense. According to South Korean media reports, Lee suggested that “regaining” or “restoring” wartime OPCON would be more appropriate terms than “transferring” it.

The issue gained renewed attention last week after Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of U.S. Forces Korea, said the conditions surrounding the transition had evolved since the allies established their original framework.

“Because the conditions have changed, because we’ve changed our plan, we have new standards which we have to uphold,” Brunson said at a policy forum in Washington, citing an evolving security environment that includes North Korea’s continued weapons development and recent missile activities.
The Pentagon did not say whether the formal criteria for the transition had been revised.

The two allies have agreed to a conditions-based process that includes assessments of South Korea’s military capabilities and its ability to lead combined operations. While the Lee administration has expressed interest in completing the transition before the end of its term in 2030, Washington and Seoul have not publicly announced a target date.
Patrick Cronin, chair for Asia-Pacific security at the Hudson Institute, told VOA earlier this year that the OPCON transition carries both political and military significance.

Politically, the transition symbolizes “regaining full sovereignty” for many South Koreans, Cronin said. Militarily, however, he argued that the focus should remain on how the change would affect deterrence and the alliance’s ability to respond effectively to regional threats.
Sungwon Baik from VOA's Korean service contributed to this report.

items.title: Former Afghan soldiers fear deportation from Iran
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.
“We are in a very difficult situation in Iran,” said a former Afghan soldier, adding that “there is always the fear of being deported to Afghanistan.”
The 37-year-old former soldier, who requested not to be named for security reasons, told VOA that he fled Afghanistan soon after the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
Remembering his forced deportation and brief detention by the Taliban, he fears being deported again as Iran continues the forcible expulsion of Afghans.
The United Nations said on Oct. 12 that Iran deported nearly half a million Afghan nationals back to Afghanistan in 2026.

In 2025, about 1.9 million Afghans returned from Iran, including 1.26 million who were deported. Iran hosts the largest Afghan refugee community in the world. According to the U.N., there are 4.4 million Afghan nationals living in Iran. This includes 1.4 million undocumented Afghans.

“I live in hiding, with no documents. I go to work in the morning and come straight back home. I don’t go out at all anywhere,” the former soldier said, adding that he fears being arrested and deported.
He added that he would rather endure the difficult situation living in Iran than be forced to return to Afghanistan, where his life would be in danger.
His story is just one of the many involving former Afghan security personnel who live in fear of being deported to Afghanistan and arrested by the Taliban.

In its latest report released last week, the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan said that it documented at least four killings and 14 arbitrary arrests and detentions of former Afghan security personnel between July 1 and Sep. 30, 2026.
The report said that despite the Taliban’s announcement of a general amnesty, former Afghan officials who return to the country remain at risk.
Under Taliban rule, harassment, detention and killings are not limited to former security personnel, as activists are also at risk.
Khalid Qaderi, an Afghan writer and journalist, was arrested in 2022 and accused “of spreading anti-regime propaganda and committing espionage for foreign media outlets.”

Qaderi, who was in the Taliban’s prison for 10 months, told VOA that after he was transferred to the Taliban’s Intelligence prison, he got to know that his Facebook posts and private conversations were used as evidence against him.

“There I realized that all my Facebook posts that I had written against the Taliban, and a collection of my voice messages in which I spoke against the Taliban in very private settings, were used against me, calling it propaganda against the regime," said Qaderi.
He added that the Taliban’s officials in the detention center in the western city of Herat tortured him.
After his release, Qaderi left Afghanistan.
“We either had to be quiet, or we had to leave the country, and I obviously chose to leave the country, at least not to be silenced,” he said.
In its quarterly report, UNAMA documented at least 443 arbitrary arrests and detentions and 97 incidents of ill-treatment of Afghan women and men.

items.title: Iran steps up pressure on Kurdish opposition in Iraq
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdi article.
With a lull in the U.S. Iran conflict and the September completion of the withdrawal of American forces from Iraq, Iran appears to be increasing pressure on Iranian Kurdish opposition groups.

The actions against Kurdish groups based in Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan Region are a test of Baghdad's independence and analysts are warning Tehran retains considerable influence over Iraqi political decisions.

Iranian news agencies reported that Iraqi and Iranian officials agreed during talks on Monday to relocate members of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups from the Kurdistan Region. Iranian Ambassador to Iraq Mohammad Kazem al-Sadegh said Tuesday that both countries had agreed to expel groups Tehran describes as separatist terrorists or hand their members over to Iran.
Iraqi officials confirmed the meeting, attended by representatives of the Kurdistan Regional Government, but made no mention of an agreement to expel or extradite opposition members.
Iraq's National Security Advisory Agency said the discussions, chaired by National Security Advisor Qassim Aboudi, focused on resolving outstanding issues under a bilateral security agreement.
The conflicting accounts highlight the political sensitivities surrounding Iranian Kurdish groups, which have maintained bases in northern Iraq for decades.
Hazhar Barnji, U.S. representative of the Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran (KDPI), told VOA that the party had received no official notification of any relocation decision.
"To date, we have not received such official communication or indication from either the Iraqi federal government or the Kurdistan Regional Government," Barnji said.
He said the party respected Iraqi sovereignty and international law, while its principal political activities remained focused on Iranian Kurdistan.

Washington-based Iraqi political figure Entifadh Qanbar said Iran's influence over armed factions continued to constrain Baghdad's decision-making despite American efforts to weaken Tehran's regional reach.
"In reality, Iraq is currently governed by armed groups and the will of those forces," Qanbar told VOA, arguing that Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had little ability to restrain them.
"Iraq will not emerge from Tehran's control unless a fundamental political change takes place," he said.

Political analyst Isam Fayli told VOA that Tehran's concerns extended beyond border security to fears that Kurdish opposition movements could gain broader support inside Iran and emerge as a more significant political challenge.

Fayli warned that Iraq handing opposition members to Iran could raise serious legal and humanitarian concerns. He suggested international assistance in finding safe resettlement arrangements, citing the relocation of members of the exiled Iranian opposition group Mujahedin-e Khalq.
Sheikh Ghaith al-Tamimi, head of the Iraqi Citizenship Project, said Iraq's own history demonstrated the limitations of military approaches to Kurdish political demands.

He said Baghdad's security cooperation with neighboring countries must respect constitutional and international obligations rather than become an instrument for settling another government's political disputes.

The changing U.S. military presence, Tamimi argued, presents a crucial test of whether Iraqi institutions can make independent security decisions or remain vulnerable to foreign influence and powerful armed factions.

For Iranian Kurdish opposition groups, the immediate question is whether Tehran's reported agreement with Baghdad will translate into concrete action, given that previous agreements between the two governments have failed to result in the expulsion of these groups from Iraqi Kurdistan.

items.title: Pupils who designed a badge sent to space meet NASA astronaut
paragraphs: Pupils at the school in Cemaes got the chance to ask question to a NASA astronaut
Pupils at a school on Anglesey were "very excited" when they met virtually with a NASA astronaut.
Students at Ysgol Cemaes were able to put their questions to Frank Rubio on Wednesday, who is set to be part of the crew for the Artemis III mission.
Rubio also spent more than a year aboard the International Space Station (ISS) after a fault with the spacecraft that was due to bring him and his fellow astronauts back to Earth.
During the virtual session, pupils asked him about his experiences of living and working in space, as well as the challenges and excitement of space travel.
Astronaut Frank Rubio was stranded on the ISS for 371 days
This is not the first time pupils at the primary school have had the chance to speak with astronauts.
Earlier this year, they took part in a project to design a badge that was sent into space, later seeing it float in zero gravity aboard the ISS.
The opportunity was made possible by former pupil Dr Melanie Coathup, a scientist who works closely with astronauts and has helped inspire the school's growing links with the space industry.
Guto Rhys, acting headteacher, said the students were "extremely excited" ahead of the meeting, and had "been looking at videos of life on the ISS and life in space".
The school's headteacher says the pupils were very excited to talk to an astronaut
The pupils had prepared many questions to ask Rubio.
Harry, 9 and his friend Sofia, 8, were among those listening to the astronaut talk about his experiences.
Harry said: "The most interesting thing I've done today is learning about NASA and Frank Rubio."
The pupils had been busy preparing in the classroom ahead of the meeting, according to Sofia.
She said: "In the school today, we've been learning about Frank Rubio. We learned that if you're sick in space, there are medical kits to help.
"We've been watching some videos about how to brush your teeth and sleep in space."
Harry and Sofia were both delighted to meet Frank Rubio
Lola, 9, was also in the hall for the talk on Wednesday. She was delighted to see Rubio holding a badge that one of the pupils at the school had designed.
"We've been learning about Frank Rubio and that he was supposed to stay in space for six months, but he ended up staying there for a year," she said.
"We got to design a badge to go up to space and it was my cousin who won and her badge got to go up to space."
Lola and Ruby say they're lucky to be able to have such a close connection with NASA as a school
Speaking to a real astronaut was "very cool" according to Ruby, 10, "because no other schools in Wales will get that experience".
"The most interesting thing that I learned today was that there is a space station up in space," she said.
The school plans to design a new badge very soon, with the plan to send another one up to space next year.

items.title: Olivier Mourgue obituary
paragraphs: Olivier Mourgue always wanted to design the future. Growing up in Paris in the 1950s, he took against the ornate antique furniture of his parents’ apartment, the formality of a dining room with a table surrounded by elaborately uncomfortable chairs and a living room dominated by a sofa used only on special occasions. “Furniture like that has nothing to do with life,” he would suggest later. “One is never at ease in such rooms.”

Mourgue, who has died aged 87, set out to design furniture that belonged to the modern world, and blurred the boundaries between furniture and architecture. In his view, that meant that it should be flexible, informal, affordable and as close to the floor as possible. He succeeded in a way that he could not have expected.

The film director Stanley Kubrick made Mourgue’s designs an essential part of popular culture’s expectations of how the future would look, even though Mourgue’s work was produced by the thousand rather than in millions. Kubrick used a cluster of Mourgue’s Djinn armchairs to equip the lobby of the Hilton hotel orbiting the moon on Space Station V for one of the key scenes of 2001: A Space Odyssey. The Djinn seemed to float almost weightless, like a colourful bubble of air. There were no conventional arms or legs to be seen. Instead there was a lightweight steel structure and some sturdy rubber webbing to support the foam upholstery, all hidden inside a seamless surface.

Kubrick had a preternatural gift for finding what might be called “real” objects, such as Djinn, from his own time, that seemed to belong to the future. He used them to give a sense of authenticity to his sets. Kubrick filmed A Space Odyssey in 1968, when Djinn looked entirely at home in a plausible version of 2001 that did not yet exist. Almost 60 years later, Djinn still looks like a version of the future, fluid and colourful, covered with a specially made stretch fabric that was available in 15 different bright colours and light enough to carry under your arm.

Mourgue wanted to do more than change the way that things looked. He believed in designing furniture that reflected the way that people want to live. He created a low-cost range of mass-produced designs for the department store chain Prisunic, in the days when it was a French version of Ikea, selling through its catalogue as well as its network of stores. The 1969 Prisunic edition launched a collection that Mourgue described as “bringing beauty at the price of the ugly”. It included bookcases, beds, tables, and seating made from lightweight chipboard that could be easily dismantled if required. One piece was a floor-cushion seat with raised edges that formed a place to sit.

Mourgue was born in Paris, to Denise (nee Lesieur), a physiotherapist, and Jean, who owned an art supply store. His uncle, Pierre Mourgue, was a successful illustrator, working for Vogue and Harper’s Bazaar in the US. Olivier’s younger brother, Pascal, also became a successful furniture designer.

Mourgue was influenced by the radical spirit of 1968, and impatient with tradition. But he was also the product of one France’s historic institutions. At the age of 14 he went to the École Boulle, a school named after Louis XIV’s cabinet maker, André-Charles Boulle, and set up to train apprentices in the art of marquetry.

After graduating, he studied at the École Nationale Superieure des Art Decoratifs. He also went to lectures at the Conservatoire National des Arts et Metiers by the architect and designer Jean Prouvé, whose ideas about prefabrication would have a lasting impact on Mourgue. He spent six months interning as a furniture designer for the Stockholm department store Nordiska Komaniet. His travels in Sweden and Finland, in those days Europe’s leading centres for innovative design, gave him an important new perspective.

Mourgue was still a student in 1959 when he designed Joker, his first chair to go into production. One of his teachers at the Boulle school introduced him to the Bernard family, founders of the Airborne furniture company. He caused something of a stir at Airborne’s factory in Montreuil, on the outskirts of Paris, when he arrived on his Solex moped carrying a full-scale prototype. It was the beginning of a long collaboration. Airborne launched Joker in 1964 and made the Djinn range, which included a two-seater sofa and a chaise longue. The company also manufactured a version of Montreal, the lounge chair that Mourgue designed for the French national pavilion of the 1967 Expo.

In 1966 Mourgue had set up his own studio in Paris. His projects included a consultancy for the motor manufacturer Renault for a low-cost version of the Renault 4 and lighting for the French company Disderot.

Despite Mourgue’s radical approach, he was part of the teams that designed the French national pavilions for both the Montreal Expo in 1967, and the one in Osaka in 1970. He designed the Bouloum chaise longue for Osaka and gave it a playfully anthropomorphic human form. But then the French state has always been determined to present itself as modern and forward looking. It was the Mobilier National, the state-run foundation originally set up in 1663 as the Royal Furniture Depository, that made the Montreal chair from fibreglass.

The Mobilier National was also responsible for Mourgue’s most radical project, an experimental scheme to equip 500 flats in the prefabricated Grand’Mare social housing development in Rouen with a furniture system. The architect was Marcel Lods, one of Prouvé’s collaborators. Mourgue used factory-made steel and glass components for the project; Lods designed the 80m² floor-plan. Mourgue came up with a series of prefabricated units that could in theory be used to take the place of internal walls to equip it. There was a sleeping pod on wheels, a kitchen that could be shifted as required and an integrated bathroom unit that could be plumbed in where needed.

Mourgue had a personal fondness for mobility. In the 1970s he built himself a series of travelling studios, one based on a Land Rover, another on a VW van. By now married with children, he took his family on an extended tour of central Europe on a specially adapted Saviem truck made by Renault for military use. In the 1970s he began to teach, first in Paris at the École Nationale Supérieure des Art Décoratifs, then, after moving to Brittany, at the École des Beaux Arts in Brest, where he was a charismatic and inspiring presence for 30 years, retiring in 2004.

Alongside his design work, Mourgue pursued painting and sculpture. He created a series of what he called “Imaginary Gardens and Little Theatres”, exhibited in 1992 at the Sainsbury Centre at the University of East Anglia, among other places. They can be seen as a more personal exploration of possible futures.
Mourgue is survived by his wife, Anne Turlan, a kindergarden teacher, and their five children, Thomas, Mikael, Armel, Gaetan and Maria.

items.title: Sir Donald Insall obituary
paragraphs: Donald Insall, doyen of conservation architects, who has died aged 100, was very clear about the distinction between preserving buildings and conserving them. “Preservation,” he pronounced, “is what you do for marmalade.” Though Insall could see the value of preservation, he was an adroit conservationist rather than a stodgy marmalade maker, always seeing how historic buildings could be revived and put to new uses.

Marshalling teams of architects, craftsmen and builders, he brought Windsor Castle back from the brink following the devastating “annus horribilis” fire of 1992. The exacting rescue scheme encompassed a range of strategies, from complete restoration to renewal in spirit. “As well as keeping things as they were, or putting them back as one thinks they were – which is chancy and not the main aim – we had to find new solutions to parts that had been irreparably destroyed,” Insall told Country Life in 2018.

Other high-profile projects included the renovation of Kelmscott Manor, the Oxfordshire country home of the writer, designer and socialist William Morris, following its acquisition by the Society of Antiquaries in 1961, and the restoration of Kedleston Hall in Derbyshire, Robert Adam’s Palladian masterpiece, now in the care of the National Trust. “Kedleston was our first big job,” Insall recalled. “I used to take a scooter on the train, hop off at Derby and go to the hall, where I was met by the butler and the dogs. Once or twice, Lord Scarsdale, the owner, came on the back of the scooter for a ride around the estate.”

Insall was also involved in the lengthy rebuilding of Wotton House in Buckinghamshire, which had previously been remodelled by John Soane following a fire in 1820. Derelict and teetering on the brink of destruction, it was bought in 1957 by the enterprising Elaine Brunner, daughter of King George V’s valet, who had first arrived there, chauffeured by an antique dealer friend, to scavenge columns to adorn her swimming pool and then embarked on a decades-long programme of restoration.

Commissioned by custodians of the country’s most significant historic buildings, from town halls to royal palaces, Insall changed the scope and ambition of conservation practice, shaping pioneering approaches to heritage management at a time when historic buildings were widely seen as impediments to progress rather than assets to be cherished. In deftly addressing issues of heritage, sustainability and contemporary use, his approach has a renewed resonance and relevance. When Insall once worked for the College of Arms, he was granted a personal coat of arms. Aptly, he chose the motto “Bring Forth the Best”.

The son of Phyllis (nee Hill) and William Insall, he was born in Bristol into a family of long established manufacturers of traditional luggage, such as trunks, cricket bags and portmanteaux. He attended Bristol grammar school, and his interest in architecture was piqued when his father commissioned and built a new family home at Henleaze, in the north of the city. During the blitz, Insall witnessed the wartime destruction of Bristol’s ancient churches and historic buildings, and in 1942 started architectural studies at the Royal West of England Academy School of Architecture. He saw wartime service from 1944 in the Coldstream Guards, completing his education after being demobbed in 1948.

Insall studied civic design in London at the Royal Academy Schools and later at the RA’s School of Planning. In 1951 he was a Lethaby scholar with the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, the organisation founded by William Morris in 1877 in response to the activities of Victorian architects, whose misconceived enthusiasm for restoration often caused calamitous damage. As a Lethaby scholar, Insall worked with and learned from an array of traditional craftsmen, including thatchers and lime plasterers, going on to spend 18 months measuring and surveying Winchester college for the medieval historian John Harvey.

It proved a formative education in which he got to know and understand historic buildings from different periods. He claimed to have no favourites. “I love them all,” he said, relishing how social change was reflected in architecture. “It’s all part of a lively continuity.” What also mattered to him was not just the quality of individual buildings, but their wider contextual relationships with streets, towns and cities. The role of conservation architects was, Insall believed, to help make “every place to be truly more itself”.

Insall initially joined Phillimore and Jenkins, a London-based practice specialising in the restoration of country houses in the greatly altered postwar milieu. In 1958, together with a fellow Lethaby scholar, Peter Locke, he founded Donald Insall Associates, working from the kitchen table in his flat in Belgravia. His father and then his wife, Libby (nee Moss), a lawyer, whom he married in 1964, did the accounts. From these tentative beginnings, the practice is now over 100 strong, operating out of eight offices across England and Wales.

With modernism then in the ascendancy, it was a bleak time for historic buildings. Country houses that did not find a saviour were all too often demolished, as were urban swathes of Victorian and Georgian terraces. While conservation fired Insall’s imagination, taking an interest in old houses was regarded as perplexingly antiquarian, as he recounted to Country Life. “Nice to meet you, but when will your father be coming?” asked the builder on one early job.

Insall’s 1968 study of Chester was a landmark for urban conservation and town planning. Undertaken as a part of a government pilot project surveying four historic towns (the others were Bath, Chichester and York), it recognised for the first time the importance of groups of structures with historic or architectural value. Insall and his team “crawled in overalls” over some 400 buildings, evaluating their merits and advocating that the best ones should be retained.

This led to his appointment as conservation consultant for Chester, and, ultimately, to the establishment of municipal conservation officers in local councils across the country. It also helped formulate many of the principles that underpin today’s conservation management plans and historic building appraisals.

Over time, Insall became a driving force in the workings of the Ancient Monuments Board and the Historic Buildings Council for England. There he befriended the architectural historian John Summerson, and the historians and conservation activists Nikolaus Pevsner and John Betjeman. These liaisons seeded the formation of English Heritage in 1984, of which Insall was a founding commissioner.

Conservation techniques are continually evolving and Insall kept abreast of developments. In the decade-long restoration of Westminster Hall completed in 2020, for instance, nanolime (nano-sized particles of calcium hydroxide dissolved in alcohol) was used to consolidate weathered limestone, and latex poultices employed to remove staining. Insall was also a thoughtful writer, summarising his philosophy, principles and practice in Living Buildings (2008), reprinted a decade later with a foreword by the then Prince of Wales.

For the last three years, Insall projects have won the Europa Nostra award, Europe’s highest accolade for heritage conservation: for the restoration of Westminster Hall (2024), the saving from dereliction of the 18th-century Camellia House at Wentworth Woodhouse, in South Yorkshire (2025) and the revitalisation of Rochdale’s imposing neo-Gothic Town Hall (2026).

Whether resplendent in elegant tweed suits on Instagram, commuting to the office on a BMW 750 motorbike, or vertiginously face to face with Nelson at the top of his column, Insall cultivated a suavely swashbuckling persona, laced with charm and humour. Though he retired as practice chairman in 1998, he continued to work as a consultant until his death.

“Buildings are so very much like people,” he observed. “They all have their own characters, their own strengths and weaknesses, their own message, their own background in terms of the influences that have made them. People change throughout their lives – so does a building.”
Insall was knighted in 2010. He is survived by Libby and their three children, Robert, Christopher and Hilary.

items.title: Why has a crumbling bottle plant been rebuilt in Paris? The stunning show suggesting the future is Ghana-shaped
paragraphs: Ibrahim Mahama has dug through the ruins of post-colonial Ghana, sorted through the ashes of its ancient history, picked through the industrial detritus, the corporate waste, the piles of rubbish, and found something pretty unique: hope.

Sit on one of the Asante stools in his circular Parliament of Ghosts and you can almost feel a new future being worked out right in front of you. It’s the first installation in this huge exhibition at the Fondation Cartier in Paris, and it sums Mahama up pretty neatly. He’s looking at the collapse of the Ghanaian government in 1966, the way the hope of the post-colonial project was crushed in a military coup, and he’s looking at ancient Ghanaian history, at the empires that fell centuries ago and the way colonialism tore them to shreds. But he’s not lamenting any of them. He’s not mourning. Instead, he’s reclaiming them, asking how things can be rebuilt, how we can move forwards by learning from the past.

And he does it over and over. In 2024 he bought an old bottle factory – a symbol of industry and its collapse. He’s rebuilt it here, in the centre of Paris. Its steel roof beams, rusted and crumbling, reach up to the ceiling, its walls are lined with thousands of green bottles in Coca-Cola, Schweppes, Kool and Club Minerals crates. It’s a whole history of manufacturing, of commerce in West Africa post-independence. Not left to rot, but rebuilt and reconfigured into something new.
Nearby, he’s taken some of those bottles and piled them around a collection of local pottery. The industrial meets the artisanal, two lost arts creating a new one.

But this huge show isn’t really about Mahama, it’s about the people around him. Most of the work here is by nine other artists and collectives. Mahama runs three art centres near Tamale in Ghana, giving time, space and opportunities to local artists. Their work is given priority here, alongside art by his mentors and collaborators. He’s taken this massive exhibition opportunity and used it as a chance to celebrate his community. It’s almost as if he’s trying to make the rest of us feel bad.

Way up on the top floor, a long scroll of jute and bark by Dorothy Akpene Amenuke undulates across the floor. If it looks like Mahama’s work, it should: she was his art teacher back in 2013. Knowledge, and the past, gets reconfigured and reshaped once again.

Nearby, the wall of a farmhouse has been built by artist and architect Courage Dzidula Kpodo out of red earth clay, a material lost as modernism brought in concrete. Now, historic methods become a kind of resistance, a symbol of tradition’s ability to endure.

Those core ideas get repeated through pretty much every presentation here. Influential 97-year-old photographer James Barnor captures the communities around Mahama in large format, grainy Polaroids. Gideon Appah’s hazy, dream-like paintings imagine fictional Ghanaian youths staring out to sea, congregating on beaches in utopian, idealised visions of the country’s past. Some of the works are absolutely stunning, like Peter Doig and Noah Davis transported to Accra.

The best work, appropriately enough, isn’t by one artist but a collective. On the top floor, a bunch of lumpy, surreal sculptures of birds, bodies and men wrestling bulls is by the Congolese Plantation Workers Art League (CATPC). Each one is made of chocolate, sculpted in the DRC but poured into moulds in Amsterdam. Everything they make from selling the art goes towards buying back land confiscated in the early 20th century by the Lever Brothers, who we now know as Unilever. The work is a whole conversation about global trade taking place in sculptural form, an act of resistance and reclamation through chocolate.

This exhibition is essentially an ambitious, ultra-idealistic group show of West African art. It is art exhibition as political utopianism. Which is great, even if not everything in it is good. And the real draw is Mahama, with his archival approach to monumental installation art, and it’s a shame to not get a load more of it.

Mahama has sacrificed himself for the greater good, basically. But this collaborative approach is the point: he’s saying collective action, community, togetherness, that’s how we’ll build a future. It might sound a bit cloying and earnest, but then you see the results, you see the art and the ideas, you see the community and the hope and the idealism and you eventually say: “Get me a one-way ticket to Accra. I’m in.”

items.title: Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?
paragraphs: Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.
Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."

The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5tn (£1.1tn) and SpaceX at $2tn (£1.5tn), a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.
Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.
"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, the Chief Technology Advisor at The Futurum Group, a market research company.

The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.
Musk, the CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.
Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.
The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.
Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year.
Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?

But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as CEO of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions.
Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors.
He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said.
But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added.
"There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said.
SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 1.5%.
Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine.
In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said.
Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models.
Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus.
Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the Cybertruck and Model 3
Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said.
"The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added.
The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights.
The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January.
The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year.
The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider.
A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said.
"The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said.
However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.
The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month.
Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Musk valued around $1tn.
"I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said.
The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.

items.title: US relations with Central Asia a priority, says Secretary Rubio
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says U.S. relations with Central Asian nations is a priority.

He made the statement after a meeting Monday with his counterparts from Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan at the C5+1 Forum in the historic Silk Road city of Samarkand in Uzbekistan.

“Let there be no doubt that the United States wants to be a partner of this region and wants to be a partner of this country. We already are, and we intend to build that and grow it,” said Rubio at the U.S.-Uzbekistan Business and Investment Council.
During the meeting with the Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, Rubio pledged government and private sector cooperation, with the announcement of 54 agreements and proposed projects.
"There were agreements achieved worth $12 billion, and for us, it’s a great achievement," President Mirziyoyev said Monday.
The C5+1 diplomatic forum aims to bring together the five Central Asian countries and the United States to discuss security, trade and other concerns.

Washington has given special attention to trying to secure greater access to Central Asia’s rare earth minerals, a priority underscored by Rubio’s visit to Samarkand with a delegation of more than 200 U.S. business leaders, the State Department said.

items.title: Ukraine showcases its defense tech at the AUSA Expo 2026
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.

For the first time ever, the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington hosted the Ukrainian Defense Tech Pavilion. Organized by Fenicks Group, the pavilion brought together 17 Ukrainian companies to showcase their aerial and ground drones, and their communications systems.

Following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine rapidly expanded its drone production and made technical innovations to adapt its Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) to the demands of modern warfare.

The president of North Carolina-based Fenicks Group, Enrique Herrera, said, “The Ukrainian technologies that the United States is really looking for, that we're trying to bring from Ukraine to the United States, is the counter-UAS systems, the unmanned ground systems ... the one-way attack systems.”

One of the pavilion participants, Tencore, a Ukrainian producer of ground drones, known for their evacuation missions at the frontline in Ukraine, signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Canadian defense firm Dominion Dynamics during the AUSA conference.

The partnership is part of a larger defense cooperation deal that will include the manufacture of thousands of battle-tested drones and uncrewed systems in the next two years, with one-third earmarked for Ukraine's defense, according to a statement from the two companies.
In his remarks at the AUSA, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth acknowledged that the U.S. has learned a lot from Ukraine, though he noted that Ukraine’s vulnerability is its reliance on Chinese parts.

"We've learned a lot from Ukraine, but you can't use everything that's in Ukraine because of all the Chinese components involved in it," Hegseth said. "So, you've got to be able to ensure that we take the best of that and the lessons learned."

The United States, Ukraine and the EU, are among the countries limiting reliance on Chinese components in defense production. President Donald Trump signed an order in July making it harder to for U.S. weapons producers to purchase supplies from China.

Michael C. Horowitz, senior fellow for technology and innovation program at the Council on Foreign Relations, told VOA that Ukraine still must rely on Chinese components to defend itself. “Very often what is available and cheap are the Chinese components. He remarked that ensuring independence from China is “absolutely existential from the point of view of cybersecurity.”

The Pentagon has noted Ukraine’s progress in limiting purchases of components from China. “Most of the drone companies that you would go to see in Ukraine have brought their supply chains onshore,” said Travis Metz, recently promoted to acting director of the Defense Innovation Unit, told the podcast School of War in September.

Several Ukrainian companies have participated in the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance competition, which is aimed at purchasing small lethal drones and creating a U.S. industrial capability to produce such drones at scale. A Ukrainian company was selected to build a facility in Ohio.

Still, Derek Berlin of the New York-based Palisade Bergschrund company says cooperation could be moving faster, but says “Ukraine is fighting an active conflict, and it's very hard to focus on international markets when you're fighting for your survival. Ukraine would be much better able to share its technologies internationally if we were able to bring peace about in a lasting way for Ukraine,” he told the VOA at the AUSA conference.

Berlin says other factors impeding Ukraine’s access to U.S. markets include Ukraine’s complex export system, especially for intellectual property, and a complicated U.S. procurement program. “The companies that have been working in this market for 50, 100 years — even for some of the defense companies — still need to hire teams of people to figure out how to productively do procurement in the United States.”
